explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport caused by ATP7B mutations, in which copper accumulates in the liver and then spills into other tissues, notably the basal ganglia and cornea. It should be considered in anyone under 40 with unexplained liver disease, particularly when neurological or psychiatric features accompany it, because the neurological form is frequently misattributed to a primary psychiatric disorder for years. No single test is diagnostic: caeruloplasmin is low in most but not all patients and is an acute phase reactant that can be falsely normal, urinary copper is raised, and Kayser-Fleischer rings are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement but in only about half of those presenting with liver disease alone. Two supporting clues are Coombs negative haemolytic anaemia from copper release and a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase. Treatment with chelation using penicillamine or trientine, or with zinc to block absorption, is lifelong and highly effective if started before irreversible damage, and first-degree relatives require screening.
key_points: Consider Wilson disease in anyone under 40 with unexplained liver disease, especially with neurological or psychiatric features
Diagnosis combines low caeruloplasmin, raised 24 hour urinary copper and slit lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings
Total serum copper is unhelpful alone because it tracks caeruloplasmin
Coombs negative haemolysis and a low alkaline phosphatase are supportive clues
Treatment is lifelong chelation or zinc, and first-degree relatives must be screened
explanation.pearls: A ratio of alkaline phosphatase to total bilirubin below 4 in acute liver failure is highly suggestive of Wilson disease and should prompt immediate transplant unit referral, since fulminant Wilsonian failure is almost always fatal without transplantation.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.rationale: Biopsy with quantitative metal measurement can be informative but is invasive and would be arranged only after non-invasive testing is equivocal; iron studies are already normal, so measuring tissue iron answers the wrong question. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.rationale: Brain imaging can show basal ganglia changes and supports the diagnosis, but it is not the confirmatory test and is arranged alongside or after the biochemical assessment rather than in place of it. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.rationale: Repeating a negative autoimmune panel is unlikely to change the answer and does not explain the neurological signs, the anaemia with a negative direct antiglobulin test, or the low alkaline phosphatase. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Total serum copper largely reflects the copper bound to caeruloplasmin, so it falls as caeruloplasmin falls and can appear normal despite a high free copper fraction; it is not a useful standalone test. Caeruloplasmin and urinary copper are the tests to rely on instead. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.rationale: Hepatitis with a movement disorder and a psychiatric or academic decline in a young adult, alongside Coombs negative anaemia and a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase, is the combination that points to Wilson disease, and the diagnosis is built from a low caeruloplasmin, raised 24 hour urinary copper and Kayser-Fleischer rings. No single one of these is sufficient alone, which is why they are requested together. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

explanation.summary: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a disorder of the presynaptic neuromuscular junction caused by antibodies against voltage gated calcium channels, which reduce the quantal release of acetylcholine. The clinical signature is the mirror image of myasthenia gravis: proximal lower limb weakness dominates, ocular and bulbar involvement is mild or absent, autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation and erectile dysfunction are common, and both power and reflexes improve transiently after sustained contraction as calcium accumulates in the nerve terminal. Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, overwhelmingly associated with small cell lung cancer, and the neurological syndrome commonly precedes the radiological detection of the tumour by months, so surveillance imaging is repeated if the initial scan is clear. Treatment of the tumour often improves the neurological syndrome, and symptomatic treatment uses amifampridine to prolong nerve terminal depolarisation, with immunosuppression or immunoglobulin for more severe disease. Recognising the syndrome matters practically because these patients are exquisitely sensitive to neuromuscular blocking agents during anaesthesia.
key_points: Proximal weakness, autonomic features and areflexia that reverses after contraction distinguish it from myasthenia gravis
Antibodies to voltage gated calcium channels confirm the diagnosis
About half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always small cell lung cancer, so chest imaging is mandatory
Electrophysiology shows an increment after high frequency stimulation or brief maximal contraction, not a decrement
Patients are highly sensitive to neuromuscular blocking agents, which matters before any anaesthetic
explanation.pearls: If the initial chest computed tomography is clear in a smoker with confirmed Lambert-Eaton syndrome, repeat imaging every 3 to 6 months for at least 2 years, since the neurological syndrome commonly precedes detectable small cell lung cancer.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

options.rationale: This is the workup for myasthenia gravis, which characteristically involves ocular and bulbar muscles, worsens with sustained effort rather than improving, and preserves reflexes; the thymus rather than the lung is the associated structure. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

options.rationale: Proximal weakness that improves with sustained effort, reflexes that return after contraction, and autonomic features such as dry mouth and erectile dysfunction describe Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, confirmed by antibodies to the presynaptic voltage gated calcium channel. About half of cases are paraneoplastic and almost always from small cell lung cancer, so chest imaging is part of the same request in a heavy smoker. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

options.rationale: Low frequency repetitive stimulation at 2 to 3 Hz demonstrates the decrement of myasthenia gravis; the presynaptic disorder here requires high frequency stimulation or brief maximal voluntary contraction to show the characteristic post-exercise increment. The distinguishing feature is decrement versus increment. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

options.rationale: Muscle biopsy investigates an inflammatory or metabolic myopathy, which a normal creatine kinase and the post-exercise facilitation of both power and reflexes make improbable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Empirical immunosuppression before a diagnosis risks masking or delaying identification of an underlying malignancy, which is the priority in a 62-year-old smoker with this syndrome. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

explanation.summary: Pulmonary arterial hypertension complicating connective tissue disease, particularly systemic sclerosis, carries a worse prognosis than the idiopathic form, and an isolated reduction in diffusing capacity with normal lung volumes and no parenchymal disease is the classic early signal. The diagnostic pathway is deliberately sequential because the treatment is expensive, the drugs are hazardous in the wrong group, and the differential spans five distinct haemodynamic groups. Echocardiography is the screening test but systematically over and under-estimates pressures and cannot distinguish pre-capillary from post-capillary disease, which requires a measured pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. Before catheterisation, lung disease must be excluded by imaging and function testing and chronic thromboembolic disease by ventilation perfusion scanning, which is the test of choice because computed tomography angiography misses chronic organised thrombus. Screening annually with echocardiography and diffusing capacity in systemic sclerosis is recommended precisely because earlier treatment improves outcomes.
key_points: An isolated fall in diffusing capacity with normal volumes suggests pulmonary vascular disease
Echocardiography screens but cannot separate pre-capillary from post-capillary hypertension
Right heart catheterisation with wedge pressure measurement is required before targeted therapy
Ventilation perfusion scanning excludes chronic thromboembolic disease more reliably than computed tomography angiography
Systemic sclerosis warrants annual screening because early treatment improves outcomes
explanation.pearls: Giving a pulmonary vasodilator to a patient whose hypertension is post-capillary can precipitate acute pulmonary oedema, which is why a measured wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg is required before targeted therapy begins.

options.rationale: Echocardiography estimates pulmonary pressures indirectly and cannot measure pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, which is what separates pre-capillary pulmonary arterial hypertension from post-capillary disease due to left heart pathology. Targeted vasodilator therapy is harmful in post-capillary disease and is only subsidised and justified once catheterisation has confirmed the haemodynamic diagnosis. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

Starting targeted therapy on echocardiographic estimates alone risks treating post-capillary hypertension, in which pulmonary vasodilation increases transpulmonary flow into a congested left atrium and precipitates pulmonary oedema. It becomes appropriate once catheterisation confirms pre-capillary haemodynamics. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

High dose calcium channel blockade benefits only the small minority who demonstrate acute vasoreactivity at catheterisation, and vasoreactive responders are very rare in connective tissue disease associated disease. Empirical use in non-responders causes systemic hypotension and right ventricular decompensation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

Anticoagulation is directed at chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, which the ventilation perfusion scan has effectively excluded by showing no mismatched segmental defects. It would be indicated if that scan had shown mismatched defects warranting pulmonary angiography. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

Long term oxygen is prescribed for sustained resting hypoxaemia with an arterial oxygen tension at or below 55 mmHg, and her saturation is 94 per cent on room air. Oxygen would become appropriate if she developed resting hypoxaemia meeting those criteria. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

explanation.summary: Congenital long QT syndrome is regularly misdiagnosed as epilepsy, because the cerebral hypoperfusion of a self-terminating polymorphic ventricular tachycardia produces brief limb jerking that observers describe as a fit. The distinguishing features are the abruptness of onset without aura, the speed of full recovery without postictal confusion, and above all the trigger. Trigger patterns map onto genotype with unusual fidelity: exertion and particularly swimming point to the potassium channel subtype, sudden auditory startle to the sodium-potassium subtype, and events during sleep or rest to the sodium channel subtype. A family history of drowning in a competent swimmer, of sudden infant death, or of unexplained single-vehicle accidents is highly relevant and should be sought explicitly. Beta blockade is the foundation of treatment, with non-selective agents outperforming selective ones, while an implantable defibrillator is reserved for aborted cardiac arrest or recurrent syncope despite adequate beta blockade, and avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs is a lifelong requirement.
key_points: Convulsive syncope with rapid full recovery and no postictal confusion suggests arrhythmia rather than epilepsy
Swimming and sudden auditory startle are characteristic triggers in specific genotypes
Family history of drowning, sudden infant death or unexplained accidents is highly relevant
Non-selective beta blockers are preferred over selective agents such as metoprolol
Cascade screening of first-degree relatives is required because inheritance is autosomal dominant
explanation.pearls: A competent swimmer who drowns in calm water should raise suspicion of the potassium channel subtype of long QT syndrome in the family, since swimming is its signature trigger and the diagnosis is frequently made only after a relative presents.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Long QT syndrome

options.rationale: The brief jerking described occurred after the patient was already on the ground and is typical of convulsive syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion rather than of a primary seizure. Rapid recovery without postictal confusion and a normal electroencephalogram argue against epilepsy, which is a common misdiagnosis in this condition. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

Syncope triggered by swimming and by sudden auditory startle with a prolonged corrected QT interval and a family history of unexplained drowning indicates congenital long QT syndrome, in which beta blockade substantially reduces cardiac events. Non-selective agents such as nadolol and propranolol are preferred over selective agents, and cascade screening of first-degree relatives is essential because inheritance is autosomal dominant. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

Pacing does not prevent the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that causes syncope in this condition and does not address the repolarisation abnormality. Pacing has a limited role in pause-dependent arrhythmia or in symptomatic bradycardia resulting from beta blockade. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

Ablation targets a discrete arrhythmic focus or circuit, and this is a diffuse genetic disorder of ion channel repolarisation with no such target. Ablation would be appropriate for an accessory pathway or a focal ventricular tachycardia in a structurally normal heart. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

Intravenous magnesium terminates established torsades de pointes but oral supplementation does not prevent events in congenital long QT syndrome, and her magnesium is already normal. Magnesium would be given acutely for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in progress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Brugada syndrome is an inherited sodium channelopathy in which reduced inward sodium current creates a transmural voltage gradient in the right ventricular outflow tract, producing the coved ST elevation of the type 1 pattern and a substrate for phase 2 reentry and ventricular fibrillation. Its defining clinical feature is that the electrocardiogram is dynamic: the pattern waxes and wanes, and fever is the most important and most treatable unmasking factor because elevated temperature further impairs sodium channel kinetics. This makes a febrile illness a genuine emergency in an affected patient rather than an incidental finding, and antipyresis is therapeutic rather than merely symptomatic. Events characteristically occur at rest or during sleep and in males of South East Asian background at disproportionate rates, which is the opposite pattern to the exertional syncope of long QT syndrome or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Sodium channel blocking drugs, cocaine and excess alcohol all accentuate the phenotype and must be avoided lifelong, while an implantable defibrillator remains the only proven treatment for those with aborted arrest or arrhythmic syncope.
key_points: Fever unmasks the type 1 coved pattern and markedly increases arrhythmic risk
Aggressive antipyresis is an antiarrhythmic intervention, not merely symptomatic care
Events occur at rest or during sleep rather than with exertion
Sodium channel blockers, cocaine and excess alcohol accentuate the phenotype and are avoided
An implantable defibrillator is the only proven therapy after arrhythmic syncope or aborted arrest
explanation.pearls: Give paracetamol early and at full dose for any febrile illness in a patient with a Brugada pattern, and record a repeat electrocardiogram once afebrile, because the type 1 morphology may disappear entirely and the diagnosis be wrongly discarded.

options.rationale: The ST elevation is confined to the right precordial leads with a coved morphology and inverted T waves, the troponin is not elevated and there is no chest pain, so this is not an occlusive infarction. Reperfusion would be correct for regional ST elevation with reciprocal change and a compatible ischaemic history. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

Amiodarone does not prevent arrhythmia in this condition and sodium channel blocking antiarrhythmics accentuate the electrocardiographic pattern and the arrhythmic risk. Isoprenaline is the agent used for recurrent ventricular fibrillation in this setting, by increasing calcium current and heart rate. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

Fever unmasks the type 1 coved pattern of Brugada syndrome by accentuating sodium channel dysfunction, and the arrhythmic risk is at its highest while the temperature is elevated, so aggressive antipyresis is itself an antiarrhythmic intervention. Continuous monitoring is required because ventricular fibrillation can occur without warning, and the syncope with a family history of nocturnal sudden death marks him as high risk. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

Provocation testing is used to unmask the pattern when the baseline tracing is non-diagnostic, and the diagnostic type 1 pattern is already present, so the challenge would add arrhythmic risk without diagnostic gain. It would be appropriate in an afebrile patient with only a saddleback pattern and a suggestive history. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

Imaging is used to exclude structural mimics such as arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy but does not change the immediate priority of controlling the fever that is driving current risk. It would be a reasonable part of the subsequent workup once he is stable and afebrile. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

explanation.summary: Rheumatic mitral stenosis remains an important cause of maternal morbidity in Australia, disproportionately affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and people who grew up in the Pacific and South East Asia, and pregnancy is frequently the event that unmasks it. The physiology explains why: cardiac output rises by up to half by the early third trimester and tachycardia shortens diastole, and since the stenotic valve fills only during diastole, both changes raise left atrial pressure steeply. New atrial fibrillation compounds this by removing atrial systole and shortening filling time further, which is often the final trigger for pulmonary oedema. Medical management with rate control, cautious diuresis and anticoagulation is first-line, but failure of medical therapy in severe stenosis before term requires mechanical relief because the haemodynamic burden will only increase. Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty is strongly preferred over surgery, with abdominal shielding and minimised screening time, and valve morphology determines suitability, while anticoagulation matters because left atrial stasis with atrial fibrillation carries a high thromboembolic risk in an already prothrombotic pregnancy.
key_points: Cardiac output rises through pregnancy and tachycardia shortens diastolic filling, worsening the gradient
New atrial fibrillation removes atrial systole and often precipitates decompensation
Balloon valvuloplasty suits pliable non-calcified valves without regurgitation or left atrial thrombus
Cardiopulmonary bypass carries fetal mortality of roughly 20 to 30 per cent and is a second choice
Anticoagulate for atrial fibrillation with mitral stenosis regardless of any risk score
explanation.pearls: Atrial fibrillation with rheumatic mitral stenosis is an absolute indication for warfarin rather than a direct oral anticoagulant, since the direct agents have not been shown safe in this valve lesion and are specifically excluded from that indication.

options.rationale: Cardiopulmonary bypass in pregnancy carries fetal mortality of roughly 20 to 30 per cent through non-pulsatile placental perfusion, so it is reserved for valves unsuitable for percutaneous treatment. Replacement would be appropriate for a heavily calcified valve, significant mitral regurgitation or left atrial thrombus. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

Medical therapy is the correct first step but she has already failed it while cardiac output demands continue to rise until around 32 weeks, so deferring intervention allows further deterioration. Ongoing medical management alone would be reasonable for moderate stenosis with symptoms controlled on rate control and diuretics. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

Delivery at 26 weeks commits the infant to extreme prematurity and the immediate haemodynamic stress of birth and autotransfusion is poorly tolerated in severe mitral stenosis. Delivery would be the priority if the fetus were near term or if maternal collapse were imminent and irreversible. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

Severe mitral stenosis with pulmonary oedema refractory to medical therapy in pregnancy warrants mechanical relief of the obstruction, and pliable non-calcified leaflets with commissural fusion, no regurgitation and no left atrial thrombus make this valve ideally suited to balloon valvuloplasty. The percutaneous route avoids cardiopulmonary bypass, which carries substantial fetal loss rates, and rate control plus anticoagulation are established first because the new atrial fibrillation is driving the decompensation. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

Restoring sinus rhythm improves diastolic filling time and is a valuable adjunct, but it leaves a valve area of 0.9 cm2 obstructing flow and recurrence of atrial fibrillation is likely while the left atrium remains pressurised. Cardioversion alone would suffice if the underlying valve lesion were mild. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

explanation.summary: Immune-related colitis is among the most common serious toxicities of checkpoint inhibition and is substantially more frequent and more severe with combination cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 and programmed death 1 blockade than with either agent alone. Onset is typically weeks to months after starting treatment and can occur after the drug has been stopped, since the immune activation outlasts drug exposure, so the diagnosis must be considered in any patient who has ever received these agents. Grading drives management: mild disease is managed symptomatically while continuing treatment, moderate disease prompts withholding the drug and starting corticosteroid, and severe disease requires admission, high dose corticosteroid and early escalation. Infection must be excluded because the treatment is immunosuppression, but exclusion should not delay therapy when the clinical picture is convincing, and cytomegalovirus reactivation should be reconsidered in anyone who fails to respond. Corticosteroid non-response by around day 3 is the trigger for infliximab or vedolizumab, and untreated or slowly treated colitis progresses to perforation, which carries high mortality in this population.
key_points: Combination checkpoint blockade causes more frequent and more severe colitis than single agent therapy
Onset is typically weeks to months after initiation and can follow drug cessation
Blood in stool, nocturnal symptoms and more than six extra stools daily indicate severe disease
Exclude infection but do not delay corticosteroid when the clinical picture is convincing
Escalate to infliximab or vedolizumab if there is no response after about 3 days of corticosteroid
explanation.pearls: Reconsider cytomegalovirus colitis by requesting tissue polymerase chain reaction on colonic biopsies in any patient whose immune colitis fails to respond to corticosteroid, because serology showing past exposure does not distinguish latent infection from active reactivation unmasked by immunosuppression.

options.rationale: Antimotility agents are appropriate for mild grade 1 diarrhoea but risk masking progression and precipitating toxic dilatation in established immune colitis. Loperamide would be reasonable for fewer than four extra stools daily with no blood, no nocturnal symptoms and normal inflammatory markers. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

Clostridioides difficile is an important differential in this population but the toxin assay is negative and there has been no antibiotic exposure or healthcare contact to support it. Vancomycin would be indicated if toxin or nucleic acid testing were positive alongside compatible symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Infliximab is the standard second-line agent for immune colitis but is reserved for patients who fail to improve after roughly 3 days of adequate corticosteroid. Starting it first exposes the patient to infection risk before establishing whether steroid alone will control the colitis. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

Endoscopy usefully assesses severity and excludes cytomegalovirus colitis, but deferring treatment until it can be arranged risks progression in a patient with an established clinical and radiological diagnosis. Colonoscopy should proceed alongside, not before, corticosteroid therapy in grade 3 disease. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

Nine stools daily with blood, nocturnal symptoms and radiological colitis after infection has been excluded is grade 3 immune-related colitis, which requires immunotherapy to be withheld and high dose corticosteroid started promptly. Delay is the principal driver of perforation and death in this complication, so treatment begins on clinical and radiological grounds rather than awaiting endoscopy. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

explanation.summary: The single most useful discriminator in dysphagia is whether solids alone or solids and liquids are affected, because mechanical obstruction narrows a lumen progressively and therefore troubles solids first, while a motility disorder disrupts coordinated transit and affects both from the outset. Nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food, weight loss and a complete lack of response to acid suppression all reinforce that picture here. Endoscopy remains the necessary first investigation in any adult with dysphagia because malignancy must be excluded and eosinophilic oesophagitis is now a common finding requiring biopsies even when the mucosa looks normal. A normal endoscopy in this setting is an informative result rather than a dead end, and high resolution manometry then classifies the disorder and, in achalasia, identifies the subtype that predicts response to pneumatic dilatation and to myotomy. Pseudoachalasia from a tumour infiltrating the gastro-oesophageal junction remains an important mimic, particularly with short symptom duration and rapid weight loss in an older patient.
key_points: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset indicates a motility disorder
Solid food dysphagia progressing to liquids suggests mechanical narrowing
Endoscopy is the necessary first test to exclude malignancy and eosinophilic oesophagitis
Take oesophageal biopsies even when the mucosa appears normal
High resolution manometry is the definitive test and subtypes achalasia to guide treatment
explanation.pearls: Failure to respond to a full dose proton pump inhibitor trial in a patient with regurgitation should prompt manometry rather than dose escalation, because achalasia is regularly mislabelled as refractory reflux for years before the correct test is ordered.

options.rationale: Empirical dilatation treats a presumed structural narrowing, and the endoscopy specifically found no stricture, so this intervenes before the mechanism is known. Dilatation would be appropriate for a confirmed peptic or fibrotic stricture causing solid food dysphagia. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

Reflux monitoring quantifies acid exposure in suspected gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and her symptoms did not respond to full dose acid suppression and are not reflux-typical. It would be indicated for refractory heartburn or regurgitation where reflux remains the leading hypothesis. (Source: GESA: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease)

Staging imaging follows a tissue diagnosis of malignancy, and endoscopy with biopsy has already excluded a mucosal lesion in the segment being imaged. It would be the next step if endoscopy had shown an infiltrating mass or ulcerated lesion. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset points to a motility disorder rather than a mechanical obstruction, which typically begins with solids alone and progresses. With endoscopy having excluded mucosal and structural disease, manometry is the definitive test and is required to make the diagnosis and to subtype it. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

Videofluoroscopy assesses oropharyngeal swallowing, which produces coughing, choking and nasal regurgitation at the moment of swallowing rather than food lodging retrosternally. It would be the right test for a patient with a neurological cause of transfer dysphagia. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is now the commonest cause of food impaction in young adults and is strongly associated with the atopic diathesis of asthma, rhinitis and eczema. The history of long-standing adaptive eating behaviour, such as chewing excessively, cutting food finely and drinking with every mouthful, is characteristic and frequently goes unreported unless asked about directly, because patients regard it as normal. Diagnosis requires at least 15 eosinophils per high power field on oesophageal biopsy with symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction, and biopsies must be taken from both proximal and distal oesophagus since the disease is patchy. Proton pump inhibitors are now understood as a treatment rather than a diagnostic filter, resolving inflammation in a meaningful proportion of patients, and non-response simply moves therapy along. The three established options are topical corticosteroids, dietary elimination and, in refractory disease, biologic therapy, with dilatation reserved for fixed strictures, and the treatment goal is histological remission because ongoing inflammation drives the fibrosis that ultimately causes strictures.
key_points: Suspect the diagnosis in any young adult with food impaction, especially with an atopic history
Diagnosis requires 15 or more eosinophils per high power field with oesophageal symptoms
Take biopsies from both proximal and distal oesophagus because involvement is patchy
Proton pump inhibitors are a treatment, not a diagnostic filter; non-response moves therapy on
Corticosteroid must be swallowed, not inhaled, and histological remission is the treatment target
explanation.pearls: Rinse the mouth and avoid eating or drinking for 30 minutes after a swallowed corticosteroid dose, because oesophageal candidiasis is the main adverse effect and adherence to that instruction largely prevents it.

options.rationale: The corticosteroid must be swallowed rather than inhaled so that it coats the oesophageal mucosa, and inhaled delivery sends the drug to the lungs where it does nothing for this condition. Inhaled delivery is correct for his asthma, which is a separate indication. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Systemic corticosteroid is effective but exposes a young man to cumulative toxicity for a chronic relapsing condition that topical therapy controls. Oral steroid is reserved for severe disease with malnutrition or stricturing requiring rapid control. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Allergy testing predicts food triggers poorly in this condition, so elimination diets are structured empirically, most commonly by removing the six or the two most common trigger food groups. Dietary therapy is a legitimate alternative to topical steroid but should not be directed by skin prick results. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Dilatation relieves fibrostenotic narrowing mechanically but does nothing for the underlying eosinophilic inflammation, which will continue to remodel the oesophagus. It is appropriate for a persistent stricture causing symptoms despite adequate anti-inflammatory therapy. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Persisting symptoms with more than 15 eosinophils per high power field after an adequate proton pump inhibitor trial confirms eosinophilic oesophagitis not responsive to acid suppression, and swallowed topical corticosteroid is the standard next-line therapy. Histological reassessment is required because symptoms correlate poorly with inflammation and untreated inflammation drives progressive fibrostenotic remodelling. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is substantially underdiagnosed, with typical delays of many years between first symptoms and recognition, largely because emphysema is assumed to require smoking. The protein is a protease inhibitor produced in the liver that protects alveolar tissue from neutrophil elastase, so deficiency allows unopposed proteolysis in the lower zones where perfusion and neutrophil traffic are greatest, producing the characteristic basal panlobular pattern that contrasts with the upper zone centrilobular emphysema of smoking. The same mutation causes liver disease through accumulation of misfolded protein in hepatocytes, which is why unexplained cirrhosis in a relative is such a useful clue. Testing is recommended for all patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and particularly those presenting young, never-smokers, those with a basal predominant distribution and those with a suggestive family history. Diagnosis changes management: smoking avoidance becomes critical, family members warrant testing and counselling, and augmentation therapy may be considered in selected patients.
key_points: Suspect deficiency in emphysema that is early onset, in a never-smoker, or basal predominant
Panlobular lower zone emphysema contrasts with upper zone centrilobular disease from smoking
Unexplained liver disease in the patient or family is an important associated clue
Serum concentration is the screening test, followed by phenotyping or genotyping
Diagnosis has implications for family screening and counselling as well as for the patient
explanation.pearls: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is an acute phase reactant, so a level measured during an infection or exacerbation can be falsely normal in a deficient patient; recheck when the C-reactive protein has settled.

options.rationale: Emphysema in a lifelong non-smoker under 45 with lower zone panlobular distribution and a family history of both early emphysema and unexplained cirrhosis is the classic presentation of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Serum concentration is the appropriate screening test and phenotyping or genotyping follows a low result to characterise the variant. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X Plan)

Allergic assessment supports an asthma diagnosis, and the fixed obstruction with only 4 per cent bronchodilator reversibility and emphysema on imaging argues against that. Testing would be appropriate for variable airflow obstruction with significant bronchodilator response and a compatible history. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X Plan)

Cystic fibrosis produces bronchiectasis with upper lobe predominance, purulent sputum and pancreatic and gastrointestinal features rather than isolated lower zone panlobular emphysema. It would be worth testing for bronchiectasis with recurrent infections and malabsorption. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X Plan)

Sarcoidosis causes upper zone predominant interstitial change with hilar lymphadenopathy and a restrictive or mixed pattern, not obstructive physiology with panlobular emphysema. It would be considered for bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with reticulonodular infiltrates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Vasculitis affecting the lung presents with nodules, cavities, haemorrhage or infiltrates alongside renal or upper airway involvement, none of which is present. Testing would be appropriate for haemoptysis with pulmonary infiltrates and an active urinary sediment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Occupational asthma accounts for a meaningful share of adult onset asthma and is important because it is potentially curable if exposure ceases early, while continued exposure leads to fixed airflow obstruction. Isocyanates in two-pack spray paints are among the commonest Australian causes, alongside flour, wood dusts, latex and laboratory animal proteins. The history of symptoms improving away from work and on holidays is suggestive but not sufficient, since recall is unreliable and the consequences of a diagnosis are severe for the worker. Serial peak flow monitoring, ideally four or more readings daily across at least 2 weeks working and 2 weeks away, is the accessible objective test, with specific inhalation challenge available only in specialised centres, and timing of assessment matters because spirometry performed after a break from exposure is frequently normal, as happened here. Prognosis depends heavily on the interval between symptom onset and removal from exposure, so investigation should be prompt rather than leisurely.
key_points: Adult onset asthma with symptoms improving away from work should prompt an occupational assessment
Isocyanates in two-pack spray paints are a common Australian sensitiser
Normal spirometry after time away from exposure does not exclude the diagnosis
Serial peak flow diaries across periods at and away from work provide objective confirmation
Prognosis depends on how early exposure ceases, so avoid delay in investigating
explanation.pearls: Ask what day of the week the patient is being assessed: a Monday morning clinic after a weekend away from exposure is the least likely time to capture the airflow obstruction that confirms occupational asthma.

sources.label: Safe Work Australia: Occupational respiratory disease

options.rationale: Removing a worker from their trade has major financial and legal consequences and should follow objective confirmation rather than history alone, which is unreliable in isolation. Immediate removal would be justified once the diagnosis is objectively established, since continued exposure worsens long-term outcome. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

A single normal spirometry taken after a weekend away from exposure cannot exclude occupational asthma, because airflow obstruction recovers between exposures early in the disease. Serial peak flow diaries across at least 2 weeks at work and 2 weeks away demonstrate the work-related pattern objectively, which is required before advising a change that will end his livelihood. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

Treating the inflammation while exposure continues allows progressive airway remodelling and permanent impairment, which is what distinguishes this from ordinary asthma management. Controller therapy is appropriate but only alongside exposure control, not as a substitute for it. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

Cross-sectional imaging investigates hypersensitivity pneumonitis or interstitial disease, which cause breathlessness with crackles and restrictive physiology rather than episodic wheeze with normal spirometry. It would be indicated if there were crackles, hypoxaemia or a restrictive pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Common aeroallergen testing does not address workplace sensitisers such as isocyanates, and a negative result would not exclude occupational asthma. Specific immunological testing to the workplace agent, where available, is the relevant investigation rather than a standard environmental panel. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

explanation.summary: Exertional syncope in a young person with a family history of sudden death is a presentation that demands explanation rather than reassurance, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cardiac cause of sudden death in young athletes. The physical signs follow directly from the physiology: a hypertrophied septum narrows the outflow tract during systole, and anything that reduces ventricular cavity size increases the obstruction. Standing from squatting drops preload and makes the murmur louder, while squatting and sustained handgrip increase preload and afterload respectively and make it quieter, which is the exact reverse of a fixed valvular lesion. The electrocardiogram is abnormal in the great majority of patients and deep narrow Q waves reflect septal hypertrophy rather than infarction. Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and quantifies the gradient, after which risk stratification determines whether an implantable defibrillator is indicated, and first-degree relatives require screening because inheritance is autosomal dominant.
key_points: Exertional syncope with a family history of sudden death requires cardiac investigation, not reassurance
Reduced preload increases dynamic obstruction, so standing from squatting makes the murmur louder
Handgrip increases afterload and softens a dynamic murmur while intensifying a regurgitant one
A sharp rapid upstroke pulse without carotid radiation contrasts with the slow rising pulse of valvular stenosis
Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so first-degree relatives require screening
explanation.pearls: Deep narrow Q waves in the inferolateral leads of a young patient represent septal hypertrophy rather than prior infarction, and their presence alongside left ventricular hypertrophy should prompt echocardiography before any exercise clearance is given.

options.rationale: A fixed valvular lesion produces a murmur that softens rather than intensifies on standing, because reduced stroke volume decreases flow across the fixed orifice, and it characteristically radiates to the carotids with a slow rising pulse. Both give a harsh mid-systolic murmur with exertional syncope, but the pulse character and response to manoeuvres are opposite. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

A septal defect produces a pansystolic rather than mid-systolic murmur and would not generate exertional syncope with a double apical impulse and inferolateral Q waves. It would be the diagnosis for a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a thrill and a normal pulse character. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

A murmur that intensifies with standing from squatting and softens with handgrip indicates dynamic obstruction, because reduced preload and afterload bring the hypertrophied septum and mitral apparatus closer together. The sharp rapid upstroke pulse, double apical impulse, absence of carotid radiation and inferolateral Q waves complete the picture. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

Prolapse produces a mid-systolic click with a late systolic murmur at the apex, and although the click moves earlier on standing there is no click described here. It would be the diagnosis with an audible click and an apical late systolic murmur. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

Pulmonary stenosis produces an upper left sternal edge murmur with an ejection click and right ventricular hypertrophy on the electrocardiogram, not left ventricular hypertrophy with inferolateral Q waves. It would be suggested by right axis deviation and a click varying with respiration. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

explanation.summary: Australia experienced a marked resurgence of silicosis driven by the engineered stone benchtop industry, where the material contains a far higher crystalline silica content than natural stone and dry cutting generates extremely high respirable dust concentrations. The disease has been seen in young workers after unusually short latency, in contrast to the decades-long course of classical silicosis from mining. Diagnosis rests on occupational history with characteristic imaging showing upper zone predominant small nodules, and calcified hilar nodes are a supportive feature. There is no disease-modifying drug therapy, which makes exposure control and early detection the entire strategy, and notification is both a legal duty and the mechanism by which other exposed workers are identified. Associated risks require active surveillance, since tuberculosis, autoimmune connective tissue disease, chronic kidney disease and lung cancer all occur at increased rates and progression continues for years after exposure ceases.
key_points: Engineered stone has very high crystalline silica content and dry cutting produces extreme dust exposure
Silicosis is notifiable in Australian jurisdictions and notification triggers co-worker screening
No pharmacological therapy alters the disease, so exposure cessation is the primary intervention
Upper zone predominant nodules with calcified hilar nodes are characteristic on imaging
Screen for tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, renal impairment and lung cancer on an ongoing basis
explanation.pearls: Tuberculosis risk is increased several-fold in silicosis and remains elevated for life, so annual screening continues even after the worker has left the industry and regardless of how well the lung disease appears to be behaving.

sources.label: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust

options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not alter the natural history of silicosis and the fibrosis progresses even after exposure ends, so immunosuppression adds risk without benefit. Steroid therapy would be appropriate for sarcoidosis, which can produce a similar nodular pattern but lacks the exposure history. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Antifibrotics are established in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive fibrosing phenotypes, not as primary therapy for silicosis, and continuing exposure would undermine any benefit. Nintedanib would be considered for a progressive fibrosing course after specialist assessment, alongside exposure cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Silicosis substantially increases tuberculosis risk and screening is mandatory, but the interferon gamma release assay is negative and there are no clinical features of active disease. Treatment would be indicated for a positive screen with active disease, or preventive therapy for latent infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Silicosis is a notifiable occupational disease in Australian jurisdictions and there is no treatment that reverses established fibrosis, so exposure cessation is the only intervention that alters disease trajectory. Notification triggers workplace inspection and screening of co-workers, who share the same exposure and are frequently affected without symptoms. (Source: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust

options.rationale: The occupational history with a characteristic upper zone nodular pattern and calcified hilar nodes makes this a clinical and radiological diagnosis not requiring tissue. Biopsy would be considered only where imaging is atypical and an alternative diagnosis would change management. (Source: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust

explanation.summary: Constrictive pericarditis is one of the most frequently missed causes of right heart failure, and patients commonly accumulate years of gastroenterological investigation for ascites before the venous pressure is examined properly. The physiology is distinctive: a thickened non-compliant pericardium prevents transmission of intrathoracic pressure changes to the cardiac chambers, so inspiration no longer augments right-sided filling and the jugular venous pressure paradoxically rises, and the two ventricles become interdependent within a fixed total volume so that inspiratory right ventricular filling displaces the septum leftward. Distinguishing it from restrictive cardiomyopathy matters enormously because constriction is surgically curable by pericardiectomy while myocardial restriction is not. Helpful discriminators include normal wall thickness, a natriuretic peptide that is normal or only slightly elevated, and respiratory variation in inflow velocities. Prior cardiac surgery, mediastinal radiotherapy and tuberculosis are the leading causes, and radiation-induced constriction may appear decades after treatment.
key_points: A jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration is highly suggestive of constriction
Respirophasic septal shift and exaggerated mitral inflow variation reflect ventricular interdependence
Normal wall thickness with a normal or minimally raised natriuretic peptide favours constriction over restriction
Mediastinal radiotherapy, prior cardiac surgery and tuberculosis are the main causes
Constriction is surgically curable by pericardiectomy, unlike restrictive cardiomyopathy
explanation.pearls: A brain natriuretic peptide that is normal or only marginally elevated in a patient with florid right heart failure argues strongly for constriction, because the normal myocardium is not stretched, whereas infiltrative restriction drives the peptide substantially higher.

options.rationale: Infiltrative myocardial disease typically thickens the ventricular walls and produces a markedly elevated natriuretic peptide, whereas the walls are normal here and the peptide is only marginally raised. Both cause right-sided failure with preserved ejection fraction, but respiratory interdependence with septal shift is a pericardial phenomenon absent in myocardial restriction. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

Hepatic ascites is not accompanied by an elevated jugular venous pressure, and the liver biopsy was normal, so the liver is congested rather than diseased. Cirrhosis would be the diagnosis with a normal venous pressure, stigmata of chronic liver disease and confirmatory histology. (Source: GESA: Ascites)

Significant tricuspid regurgitation produces a pansystolic murmur, large venous v waves and a pulsatile liver, and the echocardiogram reported normal valves. It would be the diagnosis with those examination findings and regurgitation demonstrated on colour Doppler. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

Pulmonary hypertension causes right ventricular dilatation and hypertrophy with a raised estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure, none of which is described on the echocardiogram. It would also be expected to cause exertional syncope and a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

A rigid pericardium isolates the heart from intrathoracic pressure changes, producing the respirophasic septal shift and exaggerated mitral inflow variation seen here as the ventricles compete for a fixed total volume. A jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration and prior mediastinal radiotherapy, a well recognised cause with a latency of decades, complete the picture. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

explanation.summary: Respiratory failure is the usual cause of death in motor neuron disease and arises from progressive weakness of the diaphragm and accessory muscles rather than from lung pathology. Because the diaphragm is loaded most when supine, the earliest measurable abnormality is a fall in vital capacity on lying flat and the earliest symptoms are orthopnoea, fragmented sleep, morning headache and daytime sleepiness, all of which precede any daytime rise in carbon dioxide. Monitoring therefore uses seated and supine forced vital capacity, sniff nasal inspiratory pressure and overnight oximetry at each clinic visit, because a single seated measurement will miss the transition. Non-invasive ventilation started at the point of nocturnal hypoventilation prolongs survival and improves quality of life and cognition, with the benefit greatest in patients without severe bulbar involvement. Discussions about ventilation, gastrostomy and advance care planning are held early while communication is intact, and are revisited as the disease progresses.
key_points: Supine vital capacity falls before seated vital capacity because the diaphragm is loaded lying flat
Morning headache, orthopnoea and daytime somnolence indicate nocturnal hypoventilation
A normal daytime carbon dioxide does not exclude nocturnal hypoventilation
Non-invasive ventilation improves both survival and quality of life when started at this stage
Oxygen without ventilatory support can worsen carbon dioxide retention
explanation.pearls: Place a gastrostomy while forced vital capacity is still above 50 per cent predicted; beyond that point the procedure carries a markedly higher risk of respiratory complications and radiologically inserted gastrostomy under non-invasive ventilation becomes the safer route.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

options.rationale: He has taken riluzole since diagnosis, and in any case it extends survival by a few months without altering diaphragmatic weakness or nocturnal hypoventilation. Deferring for three months allows a further substantial fall in vital capacity. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

Gastrostomy is indicated for dysphagia with weight loss or unsafe swallowing, and his swallow is normal with a stable weight. Placing a tube once vital capacity has fallen below 50 per cent predicted also becomes substantially more hazardous, which is an argument for doing it earlier when it is genuinely needed, not for doing it now. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

Oxygen alone treats the saturation without supporting ventilation and can worsen carbon dioxide retention by reducing hypoxic respiratory drive in a patient whose problem is pump failure. Supplemental oxygen is used only alongside ventilatory support or in the palliative phase. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

Orthopnoea, disturbed sleep, morning headache and daytime somnolence with a supine fall in vital capacity to 52 per cent predicted and significant nocturnal desaturation indicate diaphragmatic weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation, which is the trigger for non-invasive ventilation. Started at this point it improves survival by several months and improves quality of life more than any other intervention in this disease, and a normal daytime carbon dioxide does not exclude the diagnosis because hypoventilation appears first during sleep. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

Opioids and benzodiazepines are the mainstay of symptom control for dyspnoea in the terminal phase or when ventilation has been declined or withdrawn. Used now they would suppress an already failing respiratory drive in a man who is ambulant, eating normally and has months to years of useful function ahead. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

explanation.summary: Acromegaly is caused in almost all cases by a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma, and diagnosis is typically delayed by 7 to 10 years because the changes are insidious and the patient sees themselves daily. Comparison with old photographs is one of the most useful bedside manoeuvres available. Presenting complaints are often the complications rather than the appearance: carpal tunnel syndrome, obstructive sleep apnoea, hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes, arthropathy and cardiomyopathy. Insulin-like growth factor 1 is the screening test because it integrates pulsatile growth hormone secretion, and confirmation uses failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test, with imaging reserved for after biochemical proof. Transsphenoidal surgery is first-line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant, dopamine agonists and radiotherapy used for residual disease, and mortality, which is increased mainly through cardiovascular disease, returns towards normal once growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 are brought into the target range.
key_points: Insulin-like growth factor 1 is the screening test; random growth hormone is uninterpretable
Confirm with failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test
Image the pituitary only after biochemical confirmation
Compare with old photographs, since the changes are too gradual for the patient to notice
Screen for sleep apnoea, diabetes, hypertension, cardiomyopathy and colonic neoplasia
explanation.pearls: Colonoscopy is recommended at diagnosis in acromegaly and repeated according to findings and disease control, because growth hormone excess raises the risk of colonic adenomas and carcinoma independently of other factors.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Pituitary disorders

options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses with a short half-life, so a random level overlaps between health and disease and a normal value cannot exclude the diagnosis. Growth hormone is measured meaningfully only during a dynamic suppression test. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Imaging follows biochemical confirmation because incidental pituitary lesions are found in around 10 per cent of the population and an unconfirmed abnormality generates unnecessary surgery. Once excess secretion is proven, magnetic resonance imaging defines the adenoma and its relation to the optic chiasm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Insulin-like growth factor 1 is produced by the liver in response to integrated growth hormone exposure and has a long half-life, so a single age-matched measurement reflects average secretion over the preceding day and is the recommended screening test. A raised result is confirmed by failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 microgram/L during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, after which imaging is arranged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Cortisol screening addresses Cushing syndrome, which shares hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance with this presentation but produces central obesity, proximal myopathy, thin skin and striae rather than acral enlargement. Acral growth and coarsened features are not features of cortisol excess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

This is a confirmatory test for cortisol excess and is used after an abnormal first-line screen such as late night salivary cortisol or 24 hour urinary free cortisol. It examines an axis that is not implicated by the clinical findings here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin by oxidising its cobalt centre, which blocks methionine synthase and produces a functional deficiency regardless of dietary intake or absorption. The consequence is subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, giving the distinctive combination of sensory ataxia and absent ankle reflexes with extensor plantar responses, and a peripheral neuropathy often coexists. Serum cobalamin is frequently within the reference range because the assay measures total rather than active vitamin, so methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are the tests that establish functional deficiency. Haematological changes are commonly absent, and the neurological syndrome can occur with an entirely normal blood film, so a normal full blood count is no reassurance. Treatment is immediate parenteral hydroxocobalamin with cessation of exposure, and recovery is good when treatment starts within weeks but incomplete once the deficit has been established for months.
key_points: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin directly, so serum levels are often normal
Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine demonstrate functional deficiency when the level is normal
Neurological disease can occur without anaemia or macrocytosis
Sensory ataxia with absent ankle jerks and extensor plantars is the classic cord syndrome
Treat with parenteral hydroxocobalamin immediately; oral replacement is too slow
explanation.pearls: Never give folate before cobalamin when both may be deficient: correcting the megaloblastic anaemia removes the haematological signal while methylmalonic acid continues to accumulate, and the cord lesion progresses silently.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Vitamin B12 deficiency

options.rationale: Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt core of cobalamin, inactivating the vitamin while leaving the serum assay, which measures total cobalamin, within the reference range. Functional deficiency is demonstrated by the raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, which are the appropriate tests when the level is normal but the clinical picture is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

High dose oral replacement is effective for dietary and even for absorptive deficiency in the absence of neurological signs, and it acts too slowly for subacute combined degeneration where the window for recovery is measured in weeks. Parenteral loading is used whenever neurological involvement is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Imaging may show the characteristic inverted V signal change in the dorsal columns and is useful to document severity, but the biochemical and clinical picture is already diagnostic and treatment should not wait for a scan slot. Delay while imaging is arranged converts reversible deficit into permanent disability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Folate corrects the megaloblastic anaemia of cobalamin deficiency while allowing the neurological damage to progress unchecked, which is why folate is never given first when cobalamin deficiency is possible. His homocysteine is raised through the cobalamin dependent pathway, not from folate deficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Dorsal column loss with a positive Romberg sign, absent ankle reflexes and extensor plantar responses is subacute combined degeneration of the cord, and parenteral hydroxocobalamin is started immediately because recovery depends on how long the deficit has been present. Cessation of nitrous oxide is equally essential, since continued exposure will inactivate each replacement dose as it is given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism is several times more common in people with cancer than in the general population, and it is the second commonest cause of death in patients receiving chemotherapy. Risk is driven by tumour type, with pancreatic, gastric, brain, lung and haematological malignancies at the top, and by the presence of a central venous access device, recent surgery, immobility and certain chemotherapy and antiangiogenic agents. The treatment landscape shifted with trials showing direct oral anticoagulants are at least as effective as low molecular weight heparin, so they are now first choice for many patients, but the same trials identified a consistent excess of gastrointestinal and genitourinary bleeding in patients with unresected luminal tumours at those sites. Low molecular weight heparin therefore retains a clear place where mucosal bleeding risk is high, where absorption is unreliable from vomiting or gastrointestinal resection, and where drug interactions with anticancer therapy are a concern. Anticoagulation continues for a minimum of 6 months and indefinitely while the cancer remains active, with the platelet count guiding dose reduction rather than cessation.
key_points: Direct oral anticoagulants are first choice for many cancer associated thromboses
Avoid them with unresected luminal gastrointestinal or genitourinary tumours because of bleeding
Low molecular weight heparin is preferred when absorption or mucosal bleeding is a concern
Continue for at least 6 months and while the cancer remains active
Reduce the heparin dose rather than stopping it when the platelet count falls
explanation.pearls: Anticoagulate catheter associated upper limb thrombosis and keep the line in place if it is functioning and still needed; removal is required only for infection, malfunction or persistent symptoms despite anticoagulation.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Cancer associated thrombosis

options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are a reasonable choice for most cancer associated thrombosis and apixaban has the lowest bleeding signal of the class, but the trials consistently show excess major bleeding in patients with unresected luminal gastrointestinal tumours. An ulcerated antral lesion that is already bleeding is the specific situation in which the oral agents are avoided. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

Low molecular weight heparin remains the preferred agent for cancer associated thrombosis when there is an unresected luminal gastrointestinal tumour, active tumour bleeding, significant thrombocytopenia or concerns about oral absorption, all of which apply here. It is continued for at least 6 months and for as long as the cancer remains active or treatment continues, with the dose reduced rather than stopped if the platelet count falls further. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

Warfarin performs worse than low molecular weight heparin in cancer, with higher recurrence and bleeding rates, because chemotherapy, vomiting, altered nutrition and drug interactions make the international normalised ratio unstable. It is used when neither heparin nor an oral agent is feasible. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

A filter is reserved for patients in whom anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated, such as active uncontrolled haemorrhage or recent intracranial bleeding, and he has had no overt bleeding this admission. Filters prevent pulmonary embolism but increase recurrent deep vein thrombosis and do not treat the existing clot. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

Rivaroxaban carries the clearest excess of gastrointestinal bleeding of the oral agents in cancer trials, which is the wrong profile for an ulcerated gastric tumour. Three months is also too short, since anticoagulation continues while the malignancy is active. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

explanation.summary: Toxic alcohol poisoning is suspected whenever a high anion gap metabolic acidosis is accompanied by a raised osmolar gap, calculated as measured osmolality minus calculated osmolarity with a normal value below about 10. The gap is largest early, when the parent alcohol is still present, and falls as it is metabolised while the anion gap rises, so a normal osmolar gap late in the course does not exclude the diagnosis. Ethylene glycol and methanol are separated clinically by the target organ: ethylene glycol produces calcium oxalate crystalluria, hypocalcaemia and acute kidney injury, while methanol produces blurred vision, central scotomata and a hyperaemic optic disc from formic acid toxicity to the optic nerve. Treatment for both is blockade of alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole, or with an ethanol infusion where fomepizole is not immediately available, combined with bicarbonate and cofactor therapy, thiamine and pyridoxine for ethylene glycol and folinic acid for methanol. Haemodialysis is added for severe acidosis, end-organ injury or a high measured concentration, and it clears both the parent alcohol and its acid metabolites.
key_points: A high anion gap acidosis with an osmolar gap above 10 suggests toxic alcohol ingestion
The osmolar gap falls and the anion gap rises as the parent alcohol is metabolised
Oxalate crystalluria and renal injury indicate ethylene glycol; visual loss indicates methanol
Alcohol dehydrogenase blockade with fomepizole or ethanol stops metabolite production
Dialyse for severe acidosis, end-organ injury or a high measured concentration
explanation.pearls: Sodium fluorescein is added to many automotive coolants, which is why the urine can fluoresce under a Wood lamp in ethylene glycol ingestion; the finding supports the diagnosis when positive but is too unreliable to exclude it when negative.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Ethylene glycol poisoning

options.rationale: An anion gap of 32 with an osmolar gap of 38, an undetectable ethanol, calcium oxalate crystalluria and fluorescent urine identifies ethylene glycol rather than methanol, and preserved vision with normal fundi argues against the methanol optic neuropathy. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and stops further conversion to glycolic and oxalic acid, while haemodialysis is indicated here by a pH of 7.06 with acute kidney injury and removes both the parent alcohol and the accumulated metabolites. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Bicarbonate is a useful adjunct that reduces tissue distribution of the acid metabolites and is given alongside definitive therapy, but on its own it does nothing to stop ongoing metabolite production. Buffering a toxic alcohol poisoning while the parent compound continues to be converted is treating the number rather than the poisoning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Thiamine and glucose are given to every unwell person who drinks heavily and are entirely appropriate, but alcoholic ketoacidosis has been excluded by serum ketones of 0.2 mmol/L and cannot explain an osmolar gap of 38. Relying on this alone would allow renal failure and death from the acidosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Charcoal binds alcohols poorly, the ingestion is clearly hours old given the established metabolic acidosis and renal injury, and administering it to a confused vomiting patient risks aspiration. Decontamination has no role in toxic alcohol poisoning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Acetylcysteine treats paracetamol poisoning, which produces hepatic injury with transaminase rise rather than an early high anion gap acidosis with an osmolar gap. Massive paracetamol ingestion can cause a lactic acidosis, but the lactate here is 2.1 mmol/L. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program offers a free immunochemical faecal occult blood test every two years, with eligibility now extending from age 45 to 74 following the lowering of the starting age. The test detects human globin and so does not require dietary restriction, unlike the older guaiac based tests. Participation remains well below target and a substantial number of positive results are never followed up with colonoscopy, which is the single greatest weakness in the program and where general practice makes the most difference. Roughly 5 per cent of positive tests correspond to a cancer and a further third to an advanced adenoma, and the absence of symptoms carries no reassurance because the program exists precisely to find disease before symptoms appear. Colonoscopy is recommended within 30 days, with evidence of worsening stage at diagnosis and survival as the interval lengthens beyond about 120 days.
key_points: A positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test requires colonoscopy, not a repeat test
Target interval is within 30 days, with outcomes worsening beyond about 120 days
About 5 per cent of positive tests correspond to a cancer and a third to an advanced adenoma
Absence of symptoms and a normal haemoglobin do not reduce the need for colonoscopy
The program now covers ages 45 to 74 with two yearly testing
explanation.pearls: The immunochemical test detects human globin and is therefore specific to lower gastrointestinal bleeding, because globin from an upper gastrointestinal source is digested before reaching the colon; this is why it needs no dietary preparation and why a positive result should not be attributed to reflux or peptic ulcer disease.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.rationale: A positive screening test is not repeated to confirm it, because a repeat negative does not exclude the lesion that caused the original bleed and intermittent bleeding from a tumour is the rule rather than the exception. Repeat testing is for people whose kit was inadequate or spoiled. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.rationale: Computed tomography colonography is the alternative when colonoscopy is incomplete, refused or unsafe, and it cannot take biopsies or remove polyps, so any abnormality still requires colonoscopy afterwards. It is not the first choice in a fit 62-year-old. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.rationale: Around one in 20 people with a positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test has a colorectal cancer and about a third have an advanced adenoma, so colonoscopy is the required follow-up test regardless of whether symptoms are present. Australian guidance is that it should occur within 30 days of the positive result, and outcomes worsen measurably once the interval exceeds about 120 days. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.rationale: Anaemia is neither sensitive nor specific for colorectal neoplasia, and most screen-detected cancers are found in people with a normal haemoglobin, as his result illustrates. Using a normal blood count to withhold colonoscopy is a recognised route to delayed diagnosis. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.rationale: Sigmoidoscopy examines only to the splenic flexure and would miss the proximal lesions that account for a substantial minority of screen-detected cancers. The whole colon must be visualised after a positive faecal occult blood test. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

explanation.summary: Intravenous iron is indicated when oral iron is not tolerated or not absorbed, when losses exceed what oral replacement can match, or when repletion is needed quickly before surgery. Hypophosphataemia is an under-recognised complication that is specific to certain carbohydrate shells, occurring because they increase intact fibroblast growth factor 23, which causes renal phosphate wasting and suppresses calcitriol. It is far more frequent with ferric carboxymaltose than with ferric derisomaltose, iron sucrose or iron polymaltose, and although most cases are asymptomatic and transient, repeated infusions can produce persistent hypophosphataemia with proximal myopathy, bone pain and osteomalacic fractures. Phosphate is checked a fortnight after infusion in anyone receiving repeated doses, in malabsorption, malnutrition or vitamin D deficiency, and in those with existing bone disease. All modern preparations carry a low rate of hypersensitivity and the transient Fishbane reaction of flushing and back or chest tightness, which settles with stopping the infusion and does not by itself contraindicate re-exposure.
key_points: Hypophosphataemia after intravenous iron is mediated by fibroblast growth factor 23
The risk is substantially higher with ferric carboxymaltose than with other preparations
Repeated exposure can cause proximal myopathy, bone pain and osteomalacic fracture
Check phosphate about two weeks after infusion in those needing repeated doses
Switching preparation, rather than supplementing phosphate, is the way to prevent recurrence
explanation.pearls: The Fishbane reaction of facial flushing with chest or back tightness during an iron infusion is not anaphylaxis: there is no urticaria, wheeze or hypotension, and it settles within minutes of pausing the infusion, which can then be restarted at a slower rate.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines
BMJ Best Practice: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.rationale: Repeating the same preparation reproduces the mechanism that caused the problem, since ferric carboxymaltose raises intact fibroblast growth factor 23 and drives renal phosphate wasting, and recurrence rates on rechallenge are high. Monitoring the phosphate detects the complication rather than preventing it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Ferric carboxymaltose is the intravenous iron most strongly associated with fibroblast growth factor 23 mediated hypophosphataemia, and head to head trials show substantially lower rates with ferric derisomaltose, which delivers an equivalent single high dose. Switching preparation addresses the mechanism while still correcting the iron deficit in one visit, with a phosphate check to confirm the change has worked. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

She has already failed oral iron on intolerance grounds including a trial of alternate day dosing, which is the usual strategy for improving tolerance and absorption. Returning to it would leave her anaemic while ongoing menstrual losses continue. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Oral phosphate does not prevent the renal wasting driven by fibroblast growth factor 23 and can worsen it by further stimulating the hormone. Supplementation is used to treat symptomatic hypophosphataemia once it has occurred, not to enable a rechallenge. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or symptomatic anaemia that cannot wait for iron repletion, and a stable woman with a haemoglobin of 96 g/L does not meet that threshold. It also fails to replenish the iron stores that the marrow needs. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines
