explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis in people of northern European ancestry is overwhelmingly caused by homozygosity for the C282Y variant in HFE, which reduces hepcidin production and allows unregulated intestinal iron absorption. Penetrance is incomplete, so many homozygotes never develop clinical disease, and the decision to treat rests on the iron indices rather than on the genotype alone. Transferrin saturation rises first and is the more specific marker, while ferritin is an acute phase reactant that is also raised by alcohol, inflammation and metabolic dysfunction, which is why both are measured fasting and interpreted together with a C-reactive protein. Venesection is remarkably effective and, when started before cirrhosis develops, restores a normal life expectancy; established cirrhosis does not reverse and carries an ongoing hepatocellular carcinoma risk that requires six monthly surveillance. First-degree relatives are offered genetic and biochemical screening, since identifying them before organ damage occurs is the main benefit of making the diagnosis.
key_points: Transferrin saturation rises before ferritin and is the more specific marker of iron loading
Treat on the basis of the iron indices, not on the genotype alone, since penetrance is incomplete
Weekly venesection until ferritin reaches 50 to 100 microgram/L, then maintenance every 3 to 4 months
Life expectancy is normal if treatment starts before cirrhosis develops
Screen first-degree relatives genetically and biochemically
explanation.pearls: Arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints is the one manifestation that does not improve with venesection and can progress despite normal iron indices, so its presence should not be used to judge the adequacy of treatment.

options.rationale: Chelation is reserved for iron overload in people who cannot be venesected, principally those with transfusion dependent anaemias, and it carries renal, hepatic and gastrointestinal toxicity. Venesection is cheaper, faster and better tolerated in a man with normal haemoglobin. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

C282Y homozygosity with a fasting transferrin saturation above 45 per cent and a ferritin above the reference range, in the absence of inflammation or alcohol excess, establishes iron overload that warrants treatment. Weekly removal of 450 to 500 mL continues until the ferritin reaches 50 to 100 microgram/L, after which maintenance venesection every 3 to 4 months keeps it in that range. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

Dietary measures cannot remove the iron already deposited and have only a marginal effect on ongoing absorption, so they are an adjunct rather than a treatment. Avoiding iron and vitamin C supplements and uncooked shellfish is sensible advice alongside venesection. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

Biopsy is used to assess fibrosis when the ferritin exceeds 1000 microgram/L with raised transaminases and non-invasive assessment is equivocal, and here transient elastography at 4.8 kPa already indicates the absence of significant fibrosis. Venesection is started regardless of the fibrosis stage. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

Repeat fasting testing is the right step when a single raised ferritin could reflect inflammation, alcohol or metabolic syndrome, and that has already been done with concordant results and a normal C-reactive protein. Further delay allows continued deposition in liver, pancreas, heart and joints. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiectasis management rests on four pillars: airway clearance and exercise, treatment of exacerbations, long term suppression where exacerbations are frequent, and identification and treatment of the underlying cause. Pseudomonas aeruginosa occupies a special position because chronic infection with it marks a distinct trajectory, with more frequent exacerbations, greater sputum volume, accelerated decline in forced expiratory volume and increased mortality independent of other severity markers. For that reason a first isolation triggers an eradication attempt even in a clinically stable patient, borrowing the strategy established in cystic fibrosis, typically oral ciprofloxacin combined with an inhaled antipseudomonal agent. Once biofilm formation has occurred the organism is rarely cleared and management shifts to long term suppression with nebulised antibiotics. Investigation for a treatable underlying cause continues alongside, including immunoglobulins, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis serology, cystic fibrosis testing where appropriate, and consideration of primary ciliary dyskinesia.
key_points: Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection independently predicts decline and mortality
A first isolation warrants an eradication attempt even when the patient is stable
Typical regimen is oral ciprofloxacin plus a nebulised antipseudomonal agent with repeat cultures
Long term macrolides are for three or more exacerbations a year, after excluding mycobacteria
Inhaled corticosteroids are not routine in bronchiectasis without asthma or airflow obstruction
explanation.pearls: Exclude non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection with three sputum cultures before starting long term azithromycin in bronchiectasis: macrolide monotherapy against an unrecognised Mycobacterium avium complex infection induces resistance and removes the most effective drug from any future regimen.

options.rationale: A first isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in bronchiectasis is treated with an eradication attempt even when the patient is clinically stable, because chronic infection is independently associated with more exacerbations, faster lung function decline and higher mortality. The usual Australian regimen combines two weeks of oral ciprofloxacin with a course of nebulised tobramycin, with repeat cultures to confirm clearance. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

Long term macrolide therapy reduces exacerbation frequency in patients having three or more exacerbations a year, and she has had none for eight months. Starting a macrolide also requires excluding non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection first, or resistance may be induced. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

Waiting allows the organism to establish a biofilm, after which eradication becomes much less likely and treatment shifts to lifelong suppression. Observation is appropriate for organisms of low pathogenic significance in bronchiectasis, which Pseudomonas aeruginosa is not. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

Inhaled corticosteroids are not routinely indicated in bronchiectasis without coexisting asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and they increase the risk of respiratory infection including Pseudomonas colonisation. They do nothing to clear an established isolate. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

Resection is considered for localised disease causing recurrent severe exacerbations or massive haemoptysis that has failed medical management. Her disease is stable and this would not address an organism present throughout the airway. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

explanation.summary: Falls in older people are multifactorial, and a structured assessment covers gait and balance, vision, postural blood pressure, cognition, continence, footwear, home hazards and medications. Benzodiazepines, Z drugs, antipsychotics, anticholinergics, opioids and antidepressants are the principal culprit medicine classes, and benzodiazepines approximately double the risk of falls and hip fracture in this age group. Long term use is rarely justified for insomnia because tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops within weeks while the daytime psychomotor and cognitive impairment persists. Deprescribing succeeds far more often when the patient understands the rationale, when reduction is gradual rather than abrupt, and when non-pharmacological treatment for insomnia is offered in parallel. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia outperforms hypnotics for chronic insomnia at every age and its benefit persists after treatment ends.
key_points: Benzodiazepines roughly double the risk of falls and hip fracture in older people
Reduce by about 10 to 25 per cent every 2 to 4 weeks, slowing near the end of the taper
Never stop abruptly after long term use because of rebound, seizure and delirium risk
Z drugs carry the same risks and are not a safer substitute
Offer cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia alongside the taper
explanation.pearls: Switching to diazepam before tapering is genuinely useful for short half-life agents like alprazolam and oxazepam, where interdose withdrawal drives the difficulty, but it is counterproductive in frail older people because the active metabolite desmethyldiazepam has a half-life that can exceed 100 hours.

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after eleven years of continuous use risks rebound insomnia, anxiety, and in some cases seizures and delirium, and it almost always drives the patient to resume the drug. Melatonin is a reasonable adjunct during a taper but does not make abrupt withdrawal safe. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

Exercise based falls prevention reduces falls and should be arranged, but leaving the single most modifiable pharmacological risk factor in place treats around the problem. Benzodiazepine use roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture in older people. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

Benzodiazepine withdrawal in long term users is achieved by gradual dose reduction of roughly 10 to 25 per cent every 2 to 4 weeks, slowing further near the end where withdrawal symptoms are most pronounced. Pairing the taper with education and behavioural strategies for insomnia substantially increases the proportion who stop successfully. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

The so-called Z drugs carry the same falls, fracture and cognitive risks as benzodiazepines in older people and are not a safer substitute. Substitution also resets the dependence rather than reducing total sedative exposure. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

Conversion to a long-acting agent is a recognised technique that smooths withdrawal for short-acting drugs such as alprazolam, but temazepam has an intermediate half-life and tapers adequately in its own right. Diazepam accumulates markedly in older people with reduced renal and hepatic clearance, and the active metabolite prolongs the sedative and falls risk. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

explanation.summary: Prostate specific antigen testing is offered rather than recommended universally, because the mortality benefit is real but modest while overdiagnosis is substantial, and Australian guidance therefore builds the decision around an informed discussion. For men at average risk the recommendation is two yearly testing between 50 and 69 years for those who choose to be tested, with no testing where life expectancy is less than about 7 years. Family history modifies the starting age rather than the interval: a first-degree relative diagnosed under 60, or two or more affected relatives, moves the start to 45, and a very strong family history or a known BRCA2 mutation moves it to 40. A father diagnosed at 62 raises the relative risk modestly and does not by itself bring the start forward. Digital rectal examination is no longer recommended as an addition to antigen testing in asymptomatic men in general practice, and a raised result is now usually followed by multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging before any decision about biopsy.
key_points: Offer two yearly testing between 50 and 69 after discussing benefits and harms
A first-degree relative diagnosed under 60 brings the starting age forward to 45
A relative diagnosed after 60 raises risk modestly without changing the starting age
Digital rectal examination adds little in asymptomatic men and is no longer recommended
Do not test where life expectancy is less than about 7 years
explanation.pearls: A prostate specific antigen above the age specific 95th centile, which is 3.0 microgram/L for men in their fifties, prompts a repeat within 1 to 3 months before referral, because transient rises from ejaculation, cycling, prostatitis or instrumentation are common and a single raised value is not an indication for biopsy.

sources.label: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Prostate cancer screening

options.rationale: Digital rectal examination adds negligible diagnostic value to prostate specific antigen testing in asymptomatic men in primary care and is no longer recommended as part of screening. Ordering the antigen test without first discussing the benefits and harms also bypasses the consent process the guideline requires. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: Blanket advice against testing is not what Australian guidance recommends for a man aged 50 to 69 who asks about it, and deferring to 60 would forfeit a decade of the age band in which testing offers most benefit. Testing is not recommended in men whose life expectancy is under 7 years, which does not apply here. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: Multiparametric imaging is used after a raised prostate specific antigen to decide whether and where to biopsy, not as a first-line screening test in an asymptomatic man. Using it up front would generate incidental findings without an antigen result to interpret them against. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: Annual testing increases the detection of indolent disease and the associated overtreatment without a corresponding mortality benefit, which is why the recommended interval is every 2 years. The age band is also to 69 rather than to 70. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: Australian guidance is that men aged 50 to 69 who decide to be tested after being informed of the benefits and harms should be offered prostate specific antigen testing every 2 years, and a father diagnosed after 60 confers a modestly increased risk that does not change the starting age. The discussion covers the reduction in prostate cancer mortality set against overdiagnosis, biopsy complications, and the incontinence and erectile dysfunction that follow treatment of disease that would never have caused harm. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction distinguished from other drug eruptions by its long latency of 2 to 8 weeks, its systemic features and its tendency to persist and relapse after the drug is stopped. The characteristic combination is fever, an extensive morbilliform or oedematous eruption, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis, and involvement of at least one internal organ, most often the liver. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline account for the majority of cases. Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses occurs during the illness and contributes to the relapsing course and to the late complications, which include thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes appearing months afterwards. Mortality is around 5 to 10 per cent, mostly from fulminant hepatitis, and long term follow-up with thyroid and glucose monitoring is recommended.
key_points: Latency is 2 to 8 weeks, far longer than a simple morbilliform eruption
Look for fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and organ involvement
Allopurinol and the aromatic anticonvulsants are the commonest culprits
Withdraw the drug permanently and treat organ involvement with systemic corticosteroid
Wean corticosteroid over 8 to 12 weeks and monitor thyroid function for months afterwards
explanation.pearls: Test for HLA-B*58:01 before starting allopurinol in people of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean ancestry: carriage confers a markedly increased risk of severe cutaneous adverse reaction and the alternative urate lowering agent is febuxostat.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

options.rationale: Topical treatment and antihistamines are appropriate for a simple morbilliform drug eruption, which is confined to the skin without fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia or organ involvement. Restricting treatment to the skin here leaves a hepatitis and an acute kidney injury untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Immediate and permanent withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single most important intervention and determines outcome, so corticosteroid without withdrawal is inadequate. Allopurinol also has a long-acting metabolite, oxipurinol, so the reaction can continue to evolve for weeks after cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Burns unit transfer is the pathway for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which present with mucosal erosions, a positive Nikolsky sign and epidermal detachment. His mucosae are spared with no detachment, and the eosinophilia and hepatitis point to a different reaction pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Rash with fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia above 1.5 x10^9/L and hepatic and renal involvement 2 to 8 weeks after starting a drug is a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, and allopurinol is among the commonest causes. The drug is withdrawn permanently and systemic corticosteroid at 0.5 to 1 mg/kg is given for organ involvement, weaned slowly over 8 to 12 weeks because rapid reduction provokes relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Immunoglobulin is used in severe toxic epidermal necrolysis and in some refractory presentations, and it is not first-line treatment for this reaction pattern. Corticosteroid remains the mainstay where there is organ involvement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, which is shed in very high concentration in the birth products, urine and faeces of cattle, sheep and goats and is acquired by inhaling contaminated aerosols or dust, making abattoir workers, shearers, farmers and veterinarians the classical risk groups. Acute infection presents as an undifferentiated febrile illness with prominent headache, often retro-orbital, sweats and myalgia, frequently with a hepatitis and a normal or low white cell count with mild thrombocytopenia, and it may present as atypical pneumonia. The organism is intracellular and does not grow in routine blood culture, so serology using phase I and phase II antibodies is the diagnostic test, with a rising phase II titre indicating acute infection and a high phase I titre suggesting persistent focalised infection such as endocarditis. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for acute disease, and persistent infection requires prolonged doxycycline with hydroxychloroquine under specialist supervision. A vaccine is available in Australia and is recommended for at risk occupations, but it requires pre-vaccination skin testing and serology because vaccinating someone with prior exposure causes severe local reactions.
key_points: Livestock aerosol exposure in abattoir workers, shearers and farmers is the key history
Hepatitis with a normal white cell count and mild thrombocytopenia is typical
The organism is intracellular and does not grow in routine blood culture
Phase I and phase II serology separates acute from persistent focalised infection
Doxycycline is first line; beta-lactams are ineffective
explanation.pearls: Q fever vaccination in Australia requires pre-vaccination skin testing and serology, because giving the vaccine to someone with prior exposure produces severe local and systemic hypersensitivity reactions including sterile abscess formation.

options.rationale: Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular organism that will not grow in standard blood culture bottles, so repeat cultures will again be negative. Cephalosporins have no activity against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A prolonged febrile illness with hepatitis, thrombocytopenia and a normal white cell count in someone with intensive livestock exposure is Coxiella burnetii infection, which is not detected on routine blood culture and does not respond to beta-lactams. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice and serology distinguishes acute from persistent infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Brucellosis produces a very similar undulant febrile illness with hepatitis and is a reasonable differential, but it is exceptionally rare in Australia outside feral pig hunters and returned travellers. Its treatment is longer and combination based, so committing to it without supporting exposure is inappropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Viral hepatitis should be tested for, but the transaminase rise here is modest and accompanied by three weeks of high fever, sweats and weight loss, which acute viral hepatitis does not usually sustain. Supportive management alone leaves a treatable bacterial infection untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Imaging for occult malignancy is a reasonable step in a fever of unknown origin once infective causes with a clear exposure history have been excluded. Ordering it before testing the single most likely occupational diagnosis inverts the sequence. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Q fever)

explanation.summary: Calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis, historically called pseudogout, typically affects older adults and is frequently precipitated by intercurrent illness, surgery, trauma or metabolic disturbance, which is why it commonly appears several days into a hospital admission for something else. The knee and wrist are the joints most often involved, and chondrocalcinosis on plain radiography, seen as a thin line of calcification within fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, supports the diagnosis although it can be present without symptoms. Synovial fluid analysis is the definitive test, showing rhomboid or rod shaped crystals with weak positive birefringence, in contrast to the needle shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals of monosodium urate. The presence of crystals never excludes coexisting infection, so fluid must always be sent for Gram stain and culture and the two can occur together. Treatment of the acute attack is with intra-articular corticosteroid, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine or systemic corticosteroid, with the choice driven by renal function, age and comorbidity, and recurrent attacks should prompt screening for haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypophosphatasia and hypomagnesaemia.
key_points: Rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence distinguish this from monosodium urate
Chondrocalcinosis on radiography supports but does not confirm the diagnosis
Intercurrent illness or surgery is a classical trigger in hospital inpatients
Crystals do not exclude infection; always culture the fluid
Choose treatment by renal function and comorbidity rather than by default
explanation.pearls: Recurrent calcium pyrophosphate arthritis under the age of about 60 should prompt screening for haemochromatosis, primary hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia and hypophosphatasia, since these metabolic associations are treatable and are missed if the attack is simply managed symptomatically.

options.rationale: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are first line in younger patients with normal renal function but are contraindicated here, where they would worsen an already reduced glomerular filtration rate and add gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risk in a 78-year-old. Gastric protection does not address the renal hazard. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Allopurinol lowers urate and has no effect on calcium pyrophosphate crystals, and her urate is within the reference range so gout is not the diagnosis. Starting urate lowering therapy during an acute attack of any crystal arthritis can also prolong it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Septic arthritis must be considered and is the reason cultures were sent, but a negative Gram stain with identified crystals and a synovial white cell count of 22 000 per microlitre favours crystal disease, since septic counts are usually above 50 000 per microlitre. Committing to washout before culture results in a patient with an alternative explanation is disproportionate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals with cartilage calcification identify calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis, and intra-articular corticosteroid is the preferred treatment in an older patient with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL/min/1.73m2 because it avoids systemic drug exposure. Waiting for a negative culture is appropriate since injecting a septic joint would be harmful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Colchicine is effective in crystal arthritis but is renally cleared, and at this level of kidney function it accumulates and causes diarrhoea, myelosuppression and neuromyopathy. Dose reduction is required and even then it is a poorer choice than a local injection. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy is the commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and classically presents in young adults with visible haematuria occurring within one to two days of a mucosal infection, most often pharyngitis. This synpharyngitic timing is the key discriminator from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows a streptococcal infection after a latent period of one to three weeks and is accompanied by a low C3 and a raised antistreptolysin O titre. Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts confirm a glomerular source and make urological investigation unnecessary in a young patient. Prognosis is driven by the degree of proteinuria, the blood pressure and the glomerular filtration rate at presentation, and treatment begins with optimised supportive care including renin-angiotensin system blockade titrated to maximum tolerated dose, strict blood pressure targets, sodium restriction and cardiovascular risk management. Immunosuppression and newer targeted agents are reserved for those with persistent proteinuria above about 0.75 to 1 g per day despite several months of optimised supportive therapy, and renal biopsy is used to confirm the diagnosis and grade the histological risk.
key_points: Haematuria concurrent with the infection suggests immunoglobulin A nephropathy
A latent period of one to three weeks with low C3 suggests post-streptococcal disease instead
Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts localise bleeding to the glomerulus
Renin-angiotensin blockade with strict blood pressure control is the foundation of treatment
Proteinuria, blood pressure and filtration rate at presentation drive prognosis
explanation.pearls: Proteinuria above roughly 1 g per day sustained after several months of maximally tolerated renin-angiotensin blockade is the threshold at which additional immunosuppressive or targeted therapy is considered in immunoglobulin A nephropathy, so quantifying the protein excretion matters more than the visible haematuria that brought the patient in.

options.rationale: Visible haematuria occurring at the same time as a mucosal infection, with dysmorphic cells and red cell casts, normal complement and a negative autoimmune screen, is characteristic of immunoglobulin A nephropathy, and renin-angiotensin blockade with strict blood pressure control is the foundation of treatment. Nephrology referral establishes whether biopsy and additional therapy are needed given the proteinuria. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

Antibiotic treatment of the throat does not alter the renal process, and repeating urinalysis alone in a man with red cell casts and significant proteinuria under-investigates established glomerular disease. The haematuria will settle spontaneously and give false reassurance. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

Urological imaging and cystoscopy are the pathway for painless visible haematuria in an older patient or where the bleeding is non-glomerular. Dysmorphic red cells with casts and proteinuria localise the bleeding to the glomerulus and make a urological source very unlikely. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

Corticosteroids are considered only for patients who remain at high risk of progression despite maximal supportive therapy, and they carry substantial infective and metabolic toxicity. Starting them before optimised blood pressure and renin-angiotensin blockade reverses the accepted treatment order. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

Thin basement membrane nephropathy causes persistent microscopic haematuria without significant proteinuria and rarely produces visible haematuria linked to infection. A protein to creatinine ratio of 68 mg/mmol is well beyond what that diagnosis explains. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

explanation.summary: Paget disease of bone is a focal disorder of accelerated and disorganised bone remodelling that affects older adults and most commonly involves the pelvis, spine, femur, tibia and skull. Many cases are found incidentally through an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase, and the first step is to confirm that the enzyme is of bony rather than hepatic origin, which a normal gamma glutamyl transferase and normal transaminases achieve. The differential for a raised alkaline phosphatase with bone pain includes osteomalacia, which is distinguished by a low or low normal calcium, low phosphate, raised parathyroid hormone and low vitamin D, and metastatic bone disease, which produces destructive rather than expansile changes. Radiographic features of Paget disease include cortical thickening, coarse trabeculation, bone expansion and bowing, with a flame shaped or blade of grass lucent advancing front in long bones. Treatment with a potent bisphosphonate, usually a single zoledronic acid infusion, relieves bone pain and normalises turnover for years, and it is indicated for symptomatic disease or for asymptomatic disease at sites where complications such as deafness, nerve compression, fracture or joint destruction would be serious.
key_points: Confirm the bony origin of a raised alkaline phosphatase with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase
Normal calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D exclude osteomalacia
The flame shaped advancing lucent front is characteristic in long bones
Bone scan maps disease extent including clinically silent but risky sites
A single zoledronic acid infusion gives prolonged biochemical and symptomatic remission
explanation.pearls: New, severe or rapidly escalating pain in a previously stable pagetic bone, particularly with a soft tissue mass, should raise osteosarcoma, which complicates well under one per cent of cases but carries a very poor prognosis and requires urgent imaging and biopsy rather than escalation of bisphosphonate therapy.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Paget disease of bone

options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia, which raises alkaline phosphatase but produces a low or low normal calcium, a low phosphate and a raised parathyroid hormone. His vitamin D is adequate and his parathyroid hormone is normal, which excludes that mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Denosumab is given subcutaneously rather than orally and is not established therapy for this condition, where potent nitrogen containing bisphosphonates have the evidence base. It also carries a risk of rebound bone turnover when stopped. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A markedly raised alkaline phosphatase of bony origin with a normal liver panel, bone pain, bowing deformity and the characteristic radiographic advancing front establishes Paget disease of bone, and a bone scan maps the distribution including sites that are clinically silent but at risk. A single zoledronic acid infusion produces prolonged biochemical remission and relieves the pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Watchful waiting is reasonable for a mildly raised alkaline phosphatase of uncertain origin, but a level six times the upper limit with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase and characteristic radiology already establishes the diagnosis. Delay allows further deformity and hearing loss to accrue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Biopsy is indicated when a lytic lesion has features suspicious for sarcoma such as cortical destruction, a soft tissue mass or rapidly worsening pain, which are absent here. The radiographic appearance described is the typical advancing resorption front of the disease itself. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Paget disease of bone)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Paget disease of bone

explanation.summary: Syphilis has re-emerged in Australia with rising rates among men who have sex with men and a concerning increase in heterosexual and congenital infection, so any genital ulcer warrants testing regardless of the perceived risk profile. Primary syphilis presents as a chancre appearing about three weeks after exposure, classically single, painless, indurated with a clean base, and accompanied by firm non-tender regional lymphadenopathy, which distinguishes it from the painful vesicles and ulcers of herpes simplex and the painful ragged ulcer of chancroid. Diagnosis in Australian practice combines a treponemal screening immunoassay, a non-treponemal rapid plasma reagin titre for staging and monitoring, and direct detection from the lesion by polymerase chain reaction. Treatment of early syphilis, meaning primary, secondary or early latent infection of under two years duration, is a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin, while late latent disease or infection of unknown duration requires three weekly doses. Management is incomplete without contact tracing, testing for concurrent sexually transmissible infections including human immunodeficiency virus, and serological follow up demonstrating a fourfold fall in the rapid plasma reagin titre.
key_points: A painless indurated ulcer with non-tender nodes distinguishes chancre from herpes
Early syphilis under two years duration requires a single benzathine penicillin dose
Late latent or unknown duration infection requires three weekly doses
Azithromycin resistance is widespread and it should not be used
Follow up requires a fourfold fall in rapid plasma reagin titre and full contact tracing
explanation.pearls: Warn the patient about the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, a self-limiting fever, rigors and myalgia occurring within hours of the first penicillin dose from treponemal lysis, since it is commonly mistaken for penicillin allergy and leads to inappropriate avoidance of the best treatment.

options.rationale: Three weekly doses are the regimen for late latent syphilis, syphilis of unknown duration and tertiary disease, where slower treponemal replication requires prolonged treponemicidal levels. Applying it to early infection means two unnecessary injections. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Doxycycline for fourteen days is the recommended alternative for a patient with genuine penicillin hypersensitivity, and it requires good adherence and closer serological follow up. It is second line where penicillin can be given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This is empirical therapy for gonorrhoea and chlamydia, and azithromycin resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread in Australia so it should not be relied upon. Concurrent infections should be tested for and treated, but this regimen does not treat the confirmed diagnosis. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI management guidelines)

Antiviral therapy treats genital herpes, which characteristically produces painful grouped vesicles progressing to shallow tender ulcers with tender lymphadenopathy. The painless indurated ulcer with non-tender nodes and a positive treponemal polymerase chain reaction points elsewhere. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI management guidelines)

A painless indurated ulcer with confirmed Treponema pallidum and a reactive treponemal test is primary syphilis, which is treated with a single intramuscular dose of long-acting benzathine benzylpenicillin. Contact tracing covers partners from the three months preceding symptom onset, and serial rapid plasma reagin titres document the response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, an environmental saprophyte of soil and surface water across northern Australia and Southeast Asia, and cases cluster sharply in the wet season following heavy rainfall when the organism is brought to the surface and aerosolised. The dominant risk factors are diabetes, hazardous alcohol use, chronic kidney disease, chronic lung disease and immunosuppression, and the majority of cases occur in people with at least one. Pneumonia is the commonest presentation and may cavitate, and bacteraemic disease seeds abscesses in the spleen, liver, prostate, joints and occasionally the brain, so imaging to search for these collections is part of the standard workup. Treatment has two obligatory phases: an intensive intravenous phase of at least two weeks with meropenem or ceftazidime, extended considerably for deep seated disease, followed by an eradication phase of at least three months with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Omitting or shortening the eradication phase is the principal cause of relapse, and the organism is intrinsically resistant to penicillins, first and second generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides and macrolides.
key_points: Wet season soil and water exposure in northern Australia with diabetes is the classical setting
Cavitating pneumonia with splenic or hepatic abscesses is highly suggestive
The organism is intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides and to penicillin
Meropenem is preferred over ceftazidime in severe disease with shock
A three month oral eradication phase is mandatory to prevent relapse
explanation.pearls: Always image the prostate in men with melioidosis, since prostatic abscess is common, frequently asymptomatic, and is a recognised source of relapse when it is not drained alongside the antibiotic course.

options.rationale: Invasive fungal disease is a consideration in poorly controlled diabetes but typically involves the sinuses, orbit or brain in mucormycosis rather than producing this pattern. Gram negative bacilli in the blood cultures direct therapy away from antifungal cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Cavitating pneumonia with splenic abscesses and Gram negative bacteraemia in a diabetic man with soil and water exposure during the wet season in northern Australia is melioidosis until proven otherwise, and Burkholderia pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to many agents. Meropenem is preferred over ceftazidime in severe disease with septic shock, and the mandatory eradication phase prevents the relapse that follows inadequate treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This is the standard regimen for moderate community-acquired pneumonia and would be reasonable in a temperate setting without these risk features. Burkholderia pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to penicillin and the delay would be measured against a high mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Staphylococcus aureus is a genuine cause of cavitating pneumonia with distant abscesses and is the closest differential, but the blood cultures show Gram negative bacilli which excludes it. Burkholderia pseudomallei is also intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides, so this regimen would provide no effective cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This is a common empirical choice for Gram negative sepsis and has some activity against Burkholderia pseudomallei, but it is not the recommended agent and outcome data favour a carbapenem or ceftazidime. Adding gentamicin contributes nothing against this organism and risks further renal injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Ascites is the commonest decompensating event in cirrhosis and carries a poor prognosis, with roughly half of patients dying within two years of its onset, so its appearance should trigger consideration of liver transplantation assessment as well as symptom control. A serum ascites albumin gradient of 11 g/L or more confirms portal hypertension as the mechanism, and the initial treatment is sodium restriction with spironolactone and furosemide in a 100 to 40 mg ratio, titrated to a weight loss of about 0.5 kg daily in the absence of peripheral oedema. Diuretic resistant ascites is defined by a failure to respond despite maximal tolerated doses with genuine dietary adherence, and therapeutic large volume paracentesis is then the treatment of choice. Removing more than about 5 L without colloid replacement precipitates post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, a state of accentuated arterial vasodilatation with activation of the renin-angiotensin system that leads to renal impairment, hyponatraemia and shortened survival, and albumin at 6 to 8 g per litre removed prevents it. Coagulopathy as reflected in the international normalised ratio does not contraindicate paracentesis, and options beyond repeated drainage include transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt in selected patients and referral for transplantation.
key_points: A serum ascites albumin gradient of 11 g/L or more confirms portal hypertension
Diuretic resistance is defined by failure at maximal doses with genuine dietary adherence
Albumin 6 to 8 g per litre removed is required when more than about 5 L is drained
The prolonged international normalised ratio in cirrhosis does not predict bleeding at paracentesis
A neutrophil count of 250 per microlitre or more is required to diagnose peritoneal infection
explanation.pearls: Every new presentation of ascites, and every admission of a patient with known ascites, warrants a diagnostic tap with a neutrophil count, because spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is asymptomatic in a substantial minority and is missed entirely if the tap is only performed when the abdomen is tender.

sources.label: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis

options.rationale: She is already at the maximum recommended doses of both agents and is adherent to sodium restriction, which defines diuretic resistance rather than undertreatment. Pushing further risks hyponatraemia, acute kidney injury and encephalopathy without relieving the tense ascites. (Source: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis)
source_refs: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis

options.rationale: The prolonged international normalised ratio in cirrhosis reflects reduced synthesis of both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors and does not predict bleeding at paracentesis, which is very low risk. Plasma transfusion adds volume and transfusion risk without measurable benefit. (Source: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis)
source_refs: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis

options.rationale: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis requires an ascitic neutrophil count of 250 cells per microlitre or more, and hers is 90 with no fever or abdominal tenderness. Treating an uninfected fluid exposes her to unnecessary antibiotic pressure and does not relieve the distension. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Ascites that persists on maximal tolerated diuretics with dietary adherence is diuretic resistant, and therapeutic paracentesis relieves the symptoms faster and more safely than further diuretic escalation. Albumin replacement of roughly 6 to 8 g per litre removed prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction with its attendant renal failure and hyponatraemia whenever more than about 5 L is drained. (Source: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis)
source_refs: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis

options.rationale: Crystalloid does not maintain oncotic pressure and the sodium load promotes rapid reaccumulation of the ascites. Trials comparing colloid with saline after large volume drainage show higher rates of circulatory dysfunction and renal impairment with saline. (Source: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis)
source_refs: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis

explanation.summary: Strongyloides stercoralis is unique among human helminths in completing its entire life cycle within the host through autoinfection, so untreated infection persists for decades after a person leaves an endemic area, and in Australia it is endemic in parts of northern Australia as well as being common in migrants from Southeast Asia, the Pacific and sub-Saharan Africa. Chronic infection is usually asymptomatic or produces intermittent abdominal symptoms, an urticarial rash and a mild eosinophilia, which is frequently the only clue. Corticosteroids directly accelerate the autoinfective cycle through effects on the parasite itself, and hyperinfection syndrome produces massive larval migration with pneumonitis, ileus and Gram negative bacteraemia or meningitis from enteric organisms carried across the bowel wall, with a very high mortality. Serology is the screening test of choice since stool microscopy is insensitive, and treatment is ivermectin, usually as two doses two weeks apart with serological follow up to confirm cure. Screening before commencing corticosteroids or other immunosuppression in anyone with relevant residential or travel history is the standard of care, and when treatment cannot wait for the serology, presumptive ivermectin is given.
key_points: Autoinfection allows infection to persist for decades after leaving an endemic area
Eosinophilia may be the only sign of chronic infection and is suppressed by corticosteroids
Serology, not stool microscopy, is the screening test of choice
Corticosteroids directly precipitate hyperinfection with very high mortality
Ivermectin is the treatment; presumptive therapy is given when immunosuppression cannot wait
explanation.pearls: Recurrent Gram negative bacteraemia or Escherichia coli meningitis in an immunosuppressed patient from an endemic region should raise strongyloides hyperinfection, because migrating larvae carry enteric organisms across the bowel wall and the parasitic diagnosis is otherwise easily missed.

options.rationale: Strongyloides stercoralis persists for decades through autoinfection and corticosteroids specifically accelerate that cycle, precipitating hyperinfection and disseminated disease with a mortality that can exceed half of those affected. Eosinophilia with prolonged residence in an endemic area of northern Australia makes screening mandatory, and treatment should not wait when high dose corticosteroid is starting imminently. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Stool microscopy has poor sensitivity for Strongyloides because larval output is low and intermittent, and even serial specimens miss a substantial proportion of infections. Relying on negative stool microscopy provides false reassurance before immunosuppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Corticosteroids suppress the eosinophil count within hours, so repeating it after starting prednisolone destroys its diagnostic value. Delaying investigation also leaves the window in which hyperinfection develops unmonitored. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis is indicated against Pneumocystis jirovecii during prolonged high dose corticosteroid therapy and should be considered separately here. It does not treat Strongyloides, for which ivermectin is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Haematological investigation of eosinophilia is appropriate when the count is markedly raised without an identified cause, particularly above 1.5 x10^9/L with organ damage. A modest eosinophilia with a clear epidemiological exposure should first prompt parasitic screening. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Strongyloidiasis)

explanation.summary: Transfusion associated circulatory overload is among the most frequently reported causes of transfusion related morbidity and death, and is systematically underdiagnosed because it is mistaken for other acute reactions. It arises when the transfused volume exceeds what the circulation can accommodate, and the risk is concentrated in older patients, those with heart failure or renal impairment, small body size, and those receiving multiple units or concurrent intravenous fluids. The features that distinguish it are hypertension, a raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly and radiographic upper lobe venous diversion, alongside a rapid response to diuresis. Transfusion related acute lung injury is the principal differential and typically produces hypotension with fever, a normal jugular venous pressure and bilateral infiltrates without cardiomegaly, and it is managed with respiratory support rather than diuretics. Prevention in at risk patients includes transfusing one unit at a time with reassessment, using a slower infusion rate, and giving a diuretic between units where clinically appropriate.
key_points: Hypertension with a raised jugular venous pressure and oedema indicates circulatory overload
Transfusion related acute lung injury produces hypotension with a normal jugular venous pressure
Upper lobe venous diversion and cardiomegaly support the overload diagnosis
Rapid improvement with diuresis is both treatment and confirmation
Prevent by transfusing single units with reassessment in at risk patients
explanation.pearls: Prescribe one unit at a time with clinical reassessment before the next in any patient over 70 or with heart failure or renal impairment, since single unit transfusion policy is the most effective single measure for preventing transfusion associated circulatory overload.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions

options.rationale: Acute haemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility presents with fever, rigors, loin pain and dark urine, and this workup should be triggered by those features. Fluid loading a woman with pulmonary oedema on the basis of an unsupported suspicion would be harmful. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions

options.rationale: Premedication and a slower rate are the response to a mild febrile non-haemolytic or allergic reaction, and continuing the unit in established pulmonary oedema adds further volume. She has no fever and no allergic features. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions

options.rationale: Hypertension with a raised jugular venous pressure, new peripheral oedema and radiographic upper lobe venous diversion identify circulatory overload rather than an immune reaction, and diuresis with upright posture and oxygen reverses it. Stopping the transfusion halts further volume loading while the assessment continues. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions

options.rationale: This describes the management of transfusion related acute lung injury, which can resemble this presentation but characteristically produces hypotension, fever and a normal or low jugular venous pressure with no cardiomegaly. Withholding diuretics in genuine circulatory overload would prolong the hypoxaemia. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions

options.rationale: Anaphylaxis to a blood component causes urticaria, angio-oedema, wheeze and hypotension within minutes, and none of those features are present. Giving fluid to a patient in pulmonary oedema would worsen her condition considerably. (Source: ASCIA: Acute management of anaphylaxis)

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterised by a gait disorder, urinary urgency or incontinence and a subcortical cognitive impairment in the setting of communicating ventricular enlargement with a normal opening pressure, and its importance lies in being one of the few potentially reversible causes of dementia and gait failure in older adults. The gait is the earliest and most shunt responsive feature, described as magnetic or glue footed, with short wide based steps, reduced foot clearance, outward foot rotation and marked difficulty turning, while arm swing is typically preserved. Imaging findings that support the diagnosis beyond simple ventriculomegaly include an Evans index above 0.3, a callosal angle below about 90 degrees, and disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus with tight high convexity sulci alongside widened sylvian fissures. Because ventriculomegaly from atrophy is common and shunting carries meaningful surgical risk, prediction of response matters, and a high volume lumbar puncture removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid with objective timed gait measurement before and after, or extended external lumbar drainage in equivocal cases, is used to select surgical candidates. A positive test predicts benefit well, whereas a negative test does not entirely exclude response and may warrant extended drainage.
key_points: Gait is the earliest feature and the one most likely to respond to shunting
The cognitive profile is subcortical with preserved recall, unlike Alzheimer disease
A narrow callosal angle and tight high convexity sulci support the diagnosis
Ventriculomegaly alone predicts shunt response poorly and often reflects atrophy
High volume lumbar puncture with objective gait timing is the selection test
explanation.pearls: Measure the gait objectively with a timed up and go or a ten metre walk immediately before and two to four hours after the tap, since subjective impressions from the patient and family are unreliable and a measured improvement of more than about ten per cent is what predicts shunt benefit.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.rationale: Ventriculomegaly is common in older adults and much of it reflects atrophy rather than hydrocephalus, so shunting on imaging and symptoms alone exposes patients with irreversible disease to a procedure carrying real rates of subdural haematoma, infection and shunt failure. Predictive testing precedes surgery. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.rationale: Absent response to an adequate levodopa trial is itself a discriminating finding that argues against idiopathic Parkinson disease, and the preserved arm swing and absent tremor point the same way. Escalating a drug that has already failed adds adverse effects without diagnostic value. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Vascular parkinsonism is the closest differential and can produce an almost identical lower body gait disorder, but it usually follows a stepwise course with extensive white matter disease and often pyramidal signs, whereas his imaging shows only mild change with a narrow callosal angle. Vascular risk management should still occur but would leave a potentially reversible condition untreated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.rationale: Alzheimer disease produces an amnestic profile with impaired recall that does not improve with cueing, and gait disturbance appears late rather than leading the presentation. His preserved recall with attentional and executive losses indicates a subcortical pattern. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.rationale: A magnetic gait with urinary urgency and a subcortical cognitive pattern, with imaging showing a narrow callosal angle and tight high convexity sulci and no levodopa response, fits normal pressure hydrocephalus, but imaging alone predicts shunt response poorly. Removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid with objective gait measurement before and after is the accepted test of reversibility and selects those who will benefit from surgery. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

explanation.summary: Exertional heat stroke is defined by a core temperature above 40 degrees Celsius with central nervous system dysfunction in the context of physical exertion, and it is distinguished from heat exhaustion precisely by that neurological involvement, which may be confusion, combativeness, ataxia, seizure or coma. Sweating is often preserved in the exertional form, so dry skin should never be required to make the diagnosis, and temperature must be measured rectally because oral, tympanic and axillary readings substantially underestimate the core in this setting. Survival correlates with the duration of time spent above a core temperature of about 40 degrees Celsius, which makes immediate on site cooling the single most important intervention and places it before transport in every recommended protocol. Cold water immersion produces the fastest cooling rates and is the method of choice where a tub is available, with cooling stopped at around 38.5 to 39 degrees Celsius to avoid overshoot. Complications include rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hepatic failure and acute respiratory distress syndrome, all of which are less frequent when cooling has been rapid.
key_points: Core temperature above 40 degrees Celsius with neurological dysfunction defines heat stroke
Sweating is often preserved in the exertional form and does not exclude it
Rectal temperature is required; peripheral sites underestimate the core substantially
Cool first and transport second; time above 40 degrees Celsius determines outcome
Antipyretics and dantrolene are ineffective in this condition
explanation.pearls: Cold water immersion achieves cooling rates of roughly 0.2 degrees Celsius per minute compared with about 0.05 for ice packs and evaporative methods, which is why a tub of iced water at an endurance event is a life saving piece of equipment rather than an optional comfort measure.

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have a role in controlling shivering and severe agitation that obstructs cooling, but they are an adjunct rather than the priority. Sedating first and reassessing later delays the intervention that determines survival. (Source: ANZCOR: Heat induced illness)

Exertional heat stroke outcome is determined by the time spent above a core temperature of roughly 40 degrees Celsius, so cooling must begin where the patient is rather than after transport, and cold water immersion achieves the fastest cooling rate of any available method. Stopping at about 39 degrees Celsius avoids overshoot into hypothermia. (Source: ANZCOR: Heat induced illness)

Transport before cooling is the single most consequential error in exertional heat stroke, since every additional minute above 40 degrees Celsius increases the risk of multiorgan failure and death. The rule is to cool first and transport second. (Source: ANZCOR: Heat induced illness)

Antipyretics act on a hypothalamic set point that is not raised in heat stroke and are ineffective while adding hepatotoxic risk in a patient who may develop liver injury. Ice packs and cold fluids cool far more slowly than immersion and are fallbacks when immersion is impossible. (Source: ANZCOR: Heat induced illness)

Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, in which a triggering anaesthetic agent produces muscle rigidity and hypercarbia, and trials have shown no benefit in exertional heat stroke. Fluid is needed but does not substitute for physical cooling. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Accidental hypothermia with cardiac arrest is one of the few situations in which standard advanced life support is deliberately modified, because the profoundly cooled myocardium is refractory to both defibrillation and drugs while cerebral metabolic demand is so reduced that neurologically intact survival after very prolonged resuscitation is well documented. Below about 30 degrees Celsius, current guidance is to limit defibrillation attempts and withhold adrenaline and antiarrhythmics until the core temperature rises, then to give drugs at extended intervals between 30 and 35 degrees Celsius. Extracorporeal life support provides rewarming rates far beyond any other method and carries the best survival with good neurological outcome, so transfer to a centre with that capability should be arranged early rather than after other measures have failed. Prognostication is deliberately conservative, and the serum potassium is the most useful discriminator, since a markedly raised level indicates cell lysis and suggests the patient was asphyxiated or died before cooling, whereas a normal potassium supports continued resuscitation. Handling must also be gentle, because rough movement of a profoundly cold heart can itself precipitate ventricular fibrillation.
key_points: Below 30 degrees Celsius, limit shocks and withhold adrenaline until rewarming begins
Give drugs at extended intervals between 30 and 35 degrees Celsius
Extracorporeal rewarming gives the best survival with intact neurology
A markedly raised potassium suggests the arrest preceded the cooling
Standard prognostic markers including end tidal carbon dioxide are unreliable when cold
explanation.pearls: Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead, and the practical exception is a serum potassium above roughly 12 mmol/L in an avalanche or immersion victim, which indicates hypoxic death before cooling and is the accepted biochemical marker for stopping resuscitation.

options.rationale: External and minimally invasive rewarming achieves only around 1 to 2 degrees Celsius per hour, which is far too slow for a patient in arrest, and a fixed thirty minute limit ignores the neuroprotection that profound hypothermia confers. Prolonged resuscitation with full recovery is well documented in this group. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

The usual prognostic markers are unreliable in profound hypothermia because metabolic rate and carbon dioxide production are markedly reduced, so a low end tidal value reflects the temperature rather than the quality of resuscitation. A normal potassium here is the finding that argues strongly against futility. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

Antiarrhythmic drugs are ineffective in the hypothermic myocardium and accumulate because hepatic metabolism and renal clearance are profoundly slowed. Their delayed effects can provoke arrhythmia during the rewarming phase. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

Below about 30 degrees Celsius the myocardium responds poorly to defibrillation and drugs accumulate without effect while toxicity builds on rewarming, so further shocks and adrenaline are withheld until the core temperature rises. A potassium of 4.1 mmol/L indicates the hypothermia preceded rather than followed the arrest, and extracorporeal rewarming offers the best survival with intact neurology in this situation. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

The standard algorithm assumes a normothermic myocardium, and at 27 degrees Celsius repeated shocks are usually ineffective while repeated adrenaline doses accumulate and can cause toxicity and arrhythmia once the patient is rewarmed. Modification of the algorithm is specifically recommended below 30 degrees Celsius. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

explanation.summary: Chronic digoxin toxicity is a disease of drug interactions and declining renal function rather than of overdose, and it typically presents in older patients with days of nausea, anorexia, lethargy and visual disturbance that are easily attributed to age or to the underlying heart disease. The characteristic rhythm disturbances arise from increased automaticity with impaired conduction, producing bradyarrhythmias, atrial tachycardia with block, and the regularised ventricular response that signals complete atrioventricular block in a patient with atrial fibrillation. Hyperkalaemia reflects inhibition of the sodium potassium pump and is a marker of severity that predicts mortality in acute poisoning. Antibody fragments bind the drug directly and reverse both the arrhythmia and the hyperkalaemia, usually within 30 to 60 minutes. Every subsequent digoxin level is uninterpretable after antidote administration because assays measure bound drug.
key_points: Chronic toxicity is usually caused by interacting drugs and falling renal clearance.
A regularised ventricular response in atrial fibrillation suggests complete heart block from toxicity.
Hyperkalaemia is a severity marker and reverses with antidote administration.
Dialysis is ineffective because of the large volume of distribution.
Levels measured after antidote are uninterpretable as the assay detects bound drug.
explanation.pearls: Review digoxin dosing whenever an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor, spironolactone, amiodarone, verapamil or clarithromycin is added, since each raises the level or reduces clearance and this cluster accounts for most presentations of chronic toxicity.

options.rationale: Calcium is the standard membrane stabiliser for hyperkalaemia but is traditionally avoided in this setting because of concern that it worsens the intracellular calcium overload caused by sodium potassium pump inhibition. The hyperkalaemia here is a marker of severity that resolves as the antidote works. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Shifting potassium intracellularly treats the number rather than the cause, and the potassium will fall once the toxin is bound. These measures are used for hyperkalaemia of other causes or as a temporising step while the antidote is obtained. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

A regularised slow ventricular response in known atrial fibrillation, with visual disturbance, vomiting, a level far above range and potassium above 5 mmol/L, indicates toxicity severe enough to warrant the specific antibody fragment antidote. Both new drugs contributed, the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor by reducing renal clearance and the aldosterone antagonist by raising potassium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Dialysis does not remove this drug to any useful extent because of its very large volume of distribution and extensive tissue binding. It remains the treatment for refractory hyperkalaemia from other causes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Temporary pacing is reserved for haemodynamically significant bradycardia that persists despite the antidote, and wire insertion in a toxic myocardium can provoke ventricular arrhythmias. Antidote administration usually restores conduction within an hour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Proton pump inhibitor associated hypomagnesaemia is an under-recognised complication of long term therapy, typically appearing after a year or more and caused by impaired active intestinal magnesium transport. Magnesium deficiency then produces two secondary problems that dominate the presentation. It causes renal potassium wasting by removing magnesium dependent inhibition of potassium secreting channels, making hypokalaemia refractory to replacement, and it impairs both parathyroid hormone release and end-organ responsiveness, producing hypocalcaemia with an inappropriately normal or low parathyroid hormone. The clinical signs are neuromuscular, with tetany, tremor, weakness and in severe cases seizures and ventricular arrhythmias including torsades de pointes. Treatment is magnesium repletion, usually intravenous when symptomatic, together with withdrawal of the causative drug where possible. Deprescribing acid suppression should be considered in every patient taking it for years without a maintained indication.
key_points: Hypokalaemia will not correct until magnesium is repleted.
Magnesium deficiency causes functional hypoparathyroidism with low or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone.
Long term proton pump inhibitor use impairs intestinal magnesium absorption.
Severe deficiency causes tetany, seizures and torsades de pointes.
Deprescribing the acid suppressing drug is part of the treatment.
explanation.pearls: Check magnesium in any patient whose potassium or calcium refuses to correct with replacement, and remember that serum magnesium underestimates total body stores because less than 1 per cent is extracellular, so a low normal value in a symptomatic patient still warrants repletion.

options.rationale: Potassium replacement fails while magnesium is low because magnesium depletion removes the inhibition of renal outer medullary potassium channels, so the kidney wastes the potassium being given. More of an ineffective therapy is the classic error in refractory hypokalaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Calcium relieves acute tetany and is given if there is carpopedal spasm, seizure or laryngospasm, but the calcium will fall again while the underlying magnesium deficiency continues to impair parathyroid hormone secretion and action. It treats the symptom rather than the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Active vitamin D and oral calcium are used for hypoparathyroidism and chronic kidney disease related mineral disorder, where the parathyroid axis is permanently impaired. Here the parathyroid response is reversibly suppressed and recovers within days of magnesium repletion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Long term proton pump inhibitor use impairs intestinal magnesium absorption, and the resulting deficiency causes both renal potassium wasting and functional hypoparathyroidism, which is why the potassium and calcium will not correct on their own. Repleting magnesium intravenously and removing the cause corrects all three abnormalities together. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Potassium sparing diuretics are useful when renal potassium loss is driven by mineralocorticoid excess, which typically presents with hypertension and metabolic alkalosis. He is normotensive and not alkalotic, so the mechanism does not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Australia has one of the highest rates of asbestos related disease in the world because of decades of domestic use in building products, and the latency from exposure to malignant pleural disease is typically 20 to 50 years, so presentations continue well after the ban. The imaging features that should raise concern are circumferential pleural thickening, nodularity, thickening greater than 1 cm and involvement of the mediastinal pleura, all of which distinguish malignant from benign pleural disease. Fluid cytology is insufficiently sensitive for mesothelioma, so tissue is required, obtained either by image guided cutting needle biopsy or at thoracoscopy, which has the advantage of allowing drainage and talc pleurodesis in the same procedure. Histological subtype has prognostic and therapeutic implications and is also essential for dust diseases compensation, which in most states does not require the person to prove which employer was responsible. Every case warrants referral to a specialist multidisciplinary service and a discussion about compensation entitlements.
key_points: Latency from asbestos exposure to malignant pleural disease is typically 20 to 50 years.
Nodular circumferential thickening with mediastinal involvement suggests malignancy.
Fluid cytology has low sensitivity for mesothelioma, so tissue is required.
Thoracoscopy allows biopsy, drainage and pleurodesis in a single procedure.
Histological confirmation is needed for treatment decisions and for dust diseases compensation.
explanation.pearls: Record a detailed occupational and home renovation exposure history at the first visit, including the years and the materials handled, because compensation schemes in each state rely on that account and it becomes far harder to reconstruct once the patient deteriorates.

options.rationale: Cytological yield is low for tumours that shed few cells into the fluid, and a third sample adds little after two negatives when imaging shows nodular thickening. Repeat cytology is worthwhile for suspected adenocarcinoma, where yield is considerably higher. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pleural disease)

Tuberculous pleuritis also produces a lymphocytic exudate, but smooth rather than nodular thickening, and mycobacterial cultures are negative here. Empirical therapy would delay tissue diagnosis of a condition with major compensation implications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Functional imaging can direct a biopsy and assist staging but cannot provide the histological subtype and immunohistochemistry required for diagnosis, treatment and compensation claims. It is an adjunct to tissue sampling rather than an alternative. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pleural disease)

Diuresis is appropriate for a transudate from heart failure, but the fluid here meets exudative criteria on protein and lactate dehydrogenase ratios. Treating an exudate as a transudate wastes a month in a time-critical diagnosis. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pleural disease)

Nodular circumferential thickening with mediastinal pleural involvement in a man with heavy occupational fibre exposure requires tissue, and image guided cutting needle biopsy of the thickened pleura has a far higher yield than repeated fluid cytology. Thoracoscopic biopsy is the alternative when image guided sampling is non-diagnostic or drainage and pleurodesis are needed at the same time. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pleural disease)

explanation.summary: Familial hypercholesterolaemia affects about one in 250 Australians and remains largely undiagnosed, despite carrying a risk of premature coronary disease many times that of the general population because arterial exposure to high cholesterol begins at birth. Diagnosis is clinical, using criteria that combine untreated low density lipoprotein cholesterol level, physical signs such as tendon xanthomata and corneal arcus before 45, personal or family history of premature coronary disease, and genetic testing where available. Standard absolute cardiovascular risk calculators must not be applied, because they systematically underestimate risk in this group and would justify inaction in a young patient. Treatment is a high intensity statin from diagnosis, with ezetimibe and then a PCSK9 inhibitor added to reach targets, and treatment in children is generally started from around 8 to 10 years of age. Cascade testing of first degree relatives is the single highest yield public health action, since each has a 50 per cent chance of being affected.
key_points: Untreated low density lipoprotein cholesterol above 6.5 mmol/L strongly suggests the diagnosis.
Tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease in relatives support it.
Absolute risk calculators underestimate risk and should not guide treatment here.
High intensity statin therapy aims for at least a 50 per cent reduction from baseline.
Each first degree relative has a 50 per cent chance of being affected and should be tested.
explanation.pearls: Palpate the Achilles tendons in any patient with a low density lipoprotein cholesterol above 5 mmol/L: tendon xanthomata are close to specific for this diagnosis and take the clinical score straight into the definite range, whereas corneal arcus only counts if it appears before the age of 45.

sources.label: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

options.rationale: Low intensity therapy will not approach the target reduction of at least 50 per cent from baseline needed in this condition, and a year of untreated exposure adds to a lifetime cholesterol burden that began at birth. Dose intensity, not simply the presence of a statin, determines outcome here. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

options.rationale: Diet lowers low density lipoprotein cholesterol by roughly 10 per cent at best and cannot correct a genetic receptor defect. Lifestyle measures remain part of management but are never sufficient as sole therapy in this disorder. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

options.rationale: Untreated low density lipoprotein cholesterol above 6.5 mmol/L with tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease in a first degree relative makes familial hypercholesterolaemia the working diagnosis, and treatment is a high intensity statin aiming for at least a 50 per cent reduction, with ezetimibe added if needed. Cascade testing of first degree relatives identifies affected family members, each of whom has a one in two chance of carrying the variant. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

options.rationale: Ezetimibe lowers cholesterol by about 15 to 20 per cent and is used as an addition to a statin rather than as monotherapy except in statin intolerance. Calcium scoring can refine risk in intermediate risk patients but does not change the need to treat this degree of elevation. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

options.rationale: Apheresis is reserved for homozygous disease or for severe heterozygous disease with progressive coronary disease despite maximal drug therapy. It is not a first line intervention in an asymptomatic patient who has not yet been treated. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

explanation.summary: Symptomatic urethral discharge in a man is treated presumptively at the first visit, because delay prolongs infectivity and risks the patient not returning.
