A Gram stain showing intracellular Gram negative diplococci has high specificity in this setting and justifies treating for gonorrhoea immediately, while nucleic acid testing confirms the organism and identifies coinfection. Australian practice uses dual therapy with an injectable third generation cephalosporin plus azithromycin, which addresses both the rising cephalosporin minimum inhibitory concentrations seen internationally and the high rate of chlamydial coinfection. Culture should be collected before treatment where possible, since it is the only way to obtain susceptibility data for surveillance and for treatment failures. Every episode requires testing at all exposed sites, partner notification covering contacts from the preceding two months, a full sexually transmissible infection screen including syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology, discussion of pre-exposure prophylaxis, and a test of cure where pharyngeal infection or treatment failure is a concern.
key_points: Symptomatic urethral discharge is treated presumptively at the first visit.
Intracellular Gram negative diplococci on smear are highly specific in symptomatic men.
Australian therapy is dual, with an injectable cephalosporin plus azithromycin.
Culture before treatment provides the susceptibility data that nucleic acid testing cannot.
Partner notification and a full screen including syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus are part of the episode.
explanation.pearls: Test all exposed sites rather than urine alone, because pharyngeal and rectal gonorrhoea are usually asymptomatic, are missed by urine testing, and are the reservoir from which both onward transmission and cephalosporin resistance emerge.

options.rationale: Doxycycline covers chlamydia and is part of many urethritis regimens, but it does not reliably treat gonococcal infection and Australian resistance patterns make it unsuitable as sole therapy. It is the correct choice when only chlamydia is identified. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Azithromycin monotherapy is inadequate for gonorrhoea and drives macrolide resistance, which is why Australian guidance pairs it with an injectable cephalosporin. The pairing, not either drug alone, is what achieves cure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Waiting two days leaves a symptomatic and infectious man untreated, risks loss to follow up, and ignores a smear finding that is highly specific in symptomatic urethral discharge. Deferring treatment is reasonable only for asymptomatic screening. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI management guidelines)

Intracellular Gram negative diplococci in a symptomatic man are sufficient to treat presumptively, and Australian practice uses intramuscular ceftriaxone with oral azithromycin, which covers the gonococcal infection, limits resistance emergence and treats coexisting chlamydia. Partner notification for contacts in the preceding two months is part of the treatment episode, not an optional extra. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Quinolone resistance in Australian gonococcal isolates is high enough that ciprofloxacin is used only when susceptibility has been demonstrated on culture. That makes it a directed rather than an empirical option. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Ross River and Barmah Forest viruses are the commonest arboviral infections in Australia, transmitted by mosquitoes with reservoirs in macropods, and outbreaks follow flooding and high tides in coastal and inland river systems. The illness typically begins one to three weeks after exposure with symmetrical polyarthralgia affecting wrists, ankles, knees and small joints, accompanied by profound fatigue, myalgia and often a transient maculopapular rash. Diagnosis is serological, with specific immunoglobulin M plus either a rising immunoglobulin G titre or supportive epidemiology, and single immunoglobulin M positivity can persist for many months and must be interpreted cautiously. There is no specific treatment and no vaccine, so management is analgesia, education and graded activity, with most people recovering over three to six months although fatigue and arthralgia occasionally persist longer. It is easily mistaken for the onset of rheumatoid arthritis, leading to disease modifying therapy, and conversely persistent symptoms may be attributed to the virus when a genuine inflammatory arthritis is evolving.
key_points: Incubation is typically one to three weeks after mosquito exposure.
Symmetrical polyarthralgia with profound fatigue and a transient rash is the typical picture.
Diagnosis is serological, and isolated immunoglobulin M can persist for months.
Management is symptomatic, as there is no specific therapy or vaccine.
Most recover within three to six months, with fatigue the last symptom to settle.
explanation.pearls: Warn patients at diagnosis that fatigue and joint pain commonly persist for three to six months, because the single most common reason these patients return distressed is an expectation of recovery within a fortnight.

sources.label: CDNA: Ross River virus infection national guidelines

options.rationale: Corticosteroid is not indicated for a self-limiting post-infectious arthropathy and may prolong symptoms while exposing her to adverse effects. It is reserved for inflammatory arthritis once that diagnosis is established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Rickettsial infection is worth considering after bush exposure but classically produces fever, headache and often an eschar at the bite site, none of which is present ten days into a symmetrical polyarthralgia. Doxycycline would be appropriate if an eschar or ongoing fever were found. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Septic arthritis is almost always monoarticular with a hot, exquisitely tender joint, fever and marked inflammatory response. Symmetrical polyarticular involvement with mild inflammatory markers and no fever makes aspiration unnecessary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Disease modifying therapy is started when persistent inflammatory arthritis is confirmed over weeks with supportive serology and imaging, not at ten days in a post-infectious picture that usually resolves. Starting it now would treat a disease she probably does not have. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Early arthritis)

Symmetrical polyarthralgia with profound fatigue and a transient maculopapular rash three weeks after intense mosquito exposure in an inland river region is the classic Australian arboviral pattern, confirmed by serology showing specific immunoglobulin M with a rising immunoglobulin G titre. Management is symptomatic with simple analgesia, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and graded return to activity, and the illness is notifiable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Alcoholic ketoacidosis develops after a heavy drinking episode ends and is followed by vomiting and starvation, at which point glycogen is depleted, insulin secretion falls, counterregulatory hormones rise and free fatty acids are mobilised. Alcohol metabolism generates a high ratio of reduced to oxidised nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, which favours beta hydroxybutyrate over acetoacetate, so bedside ketone strips measuring acetoacetate can underestimate the severity while blood beta hydroxybutyrate is markedly raised. The acid base picture is frequently mixed, with vomiting adding a metabolic alkalosis and alcohol withdrawal adding a respiratory alkalosis, so the pH can be deceptively close to normal and the anion gap is the more reliable signal. Treatment is dextrose containing saline with thiamine given first, potassium replacement, and treatment of withdrawal, with resolution usually within 12 to 24 hours. Failure to improve should prompt a search for pancreatitis, sepsis, gastrointestinal bleeding or toxic alcohol ingestion.
key_points: A normal or low glucose with a high anion gap ketoacidosis is the defining pattern.
Beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, so acetoacetate based bedside tests underestimate severity.
Treatment is dextrose containing fluid, thiamine first, and potassium replacement.
Insulin is not required and risks hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia.
Failure to resolve within 24 hours suggests an alternative or additional diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Give thiamine before any glucose containing fluid in a malnourished drinker, since a carbohydrate load consumes the last of the thiamine as a cofactor and can precipitate acute thiamine deficient encephalopathy within hours.

options.rationale: Ketoacidosis with a normal glucose after a binge followed by starvation and vomiting is driven by glycogen depletion and a high ratio of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, and it resolves with volume replacement and carbohydrate, which restores insulin secretion and switches off ketogenesis. Thiamine is given before the glucose load and potassium is replaced because it falls further as ketosis clears. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Insulin is the cornerstone of diabetic ketoacidosis, where hyperglycaemia is present and endogenous insulin is absent, but here the glucose is normal and insulin would cause dangerous hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia. The distinguishing feature between these two ketoacidoses is the glucose, not the ketone level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in ketoacidosis at this pH and worsens hypokalaemia and intracellular acidosis. It is reserved for extreme acidaemia, conventionally a pH below 6.9, or for specific poisonings. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Saline restores volume but without a carbohydrate source the ketogenic drive persists, so recovery is slower and hypoglycaemia may supervene. Saline alone is the right approach in hyperglycaemic states where fluid is the first priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dialysis is indicated for toxic alcohol ingestion, severe salicylate poisoning or refractory acidosis with kidney failure, none of which applies to a ketoacidosis that reverses within hours of simple treatment. The osmolar gap and toxicology history are what separate those causes from this one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity follows inadvertent intravascular injection or systemic absorption from a large volume block, and its incidence has fallen with ultrasound guidance but has not disappeared. The classic sequence begins with prodromal neurological symptoms including perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, visual disturbance and agitation, progresses to seizures, and then to cardiovascular toxicity with conduction delay, bradyarrhythmias, ventricular arrhythmias and asystole. Onset is typically within minutes but can be delayed for up to an hour with large volume blocks, so monitoring after the procedure matters. Management combines stopping the injection, airway and ventilation support, seizure control with a benzodiazepine, and lipid emulsion as the specific antidote. Adrenaline is used in reduced doses, propofol is avoided as a lipid substitute, and lidocaine and other sodium channel blocking antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Prolonged resuscitation is justified because recovery after long arrests has been documented, and every clinician performing blocks should know where the lipid emulsion is kept.
key_points: Prodromal perioral numbness, metallic taste and tinnitus precede seizures and cardiac toxicity.
Onset can be delayed up to an hour after a large volume block.
Lipid emulsion 20 per cent is the specific antidote, given as a bolus then an infusion.
Adrenaline is used at markedly reduced doses and lidocaine is contraindicated.
Prolonged resuscitation is warranted because late recovery has been documented.
explanation.pearls: Keep a dedicated lipid emulsion kit wherever regional blocks are performed and rehearse the dose: 1.5 mL/kg of 20 per cent emulsion as a bolus followed by an infusion at 15 mL/kg/hour, with the bolus repeatable twice if circulation has not returned.

sources.label: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation but would remove seizure control in a patient at high risk of further convulsions, and it does nothing for the cardiac toxicity. Airway support is essential but is standard care rather than the specific treatment. (Source: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity)
source_refs: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.rationale: Perioral numbness, metallic taste and auditory change progressing to seizure and then cardiovascular collapse after a large volume block is local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, and 20 per cent lipid emulsion is the specific antidote, given as a bolus followed by an infusion. It acts as a lipid sink that draws the drug away from cardiac sodium channels, and it is given alongside, not instead of, airway support and resuscitation. (Source: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity)
source_refs: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.rationale: Adrenaline is used in this setting but at substantially reduced doses, conventionally 1 microgram per kilogram or less, because large boluses impair resuscitation and worsen arrhythmia in local anaesthetic toxicity. Dose, not the drug, is what makes this option wrong. (Source: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity)
source_refs: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.rationale: Amiodarone is the preferred antiarrhythmic if ventricular arrhythmia occurs in this setting, so it is not wrong in itself, but it does not remove the drug from the sodium channels and should not displace the antidote. Lidocaine and other local anaesthetic antiarrhythmics are specifically contraindicated because they add to the toxic burden. (Source: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity)
source_refs: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is the treatment for sodium channel blockade from tricyclic antidepressant poisoning and is a reasonable adjunct here, but it is not the specific antidote and should not be given first. The two poisonings share a mechanism but differ in the treatment with the strongest evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Syncope occurring during exertion, as opposed to immediately after stopping, is a cardinal warning sign that demands assessment before any return to sport. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the commonest inherited cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes and produces a dynamic outflow murmur that behaves opposite to the murmur of aortic stenosis: it increases when preload or afterload falls, as on standing or during Valsalva, and decreases when preload rises with squatting or handgrip. Electrocardiographic abnormalities precede symptoms in most cases, with deep lateral T wave inversion and voltage criteria being typical, and a completely normal tracing makes the diagnosis unlikely. Echocardiography defines wall thickness, outflow gradient and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging used when windows are poor or apical disease is suspected. Family screening of first degree relatives is mandatory, and risk stratification determines whether an implantable defibrillator is required.
key_points: Syncope during exertion is a red flag, unlike syncope after stopping exercise.
The murmur increases on standing and Valsalva and decreases on squatting.
Deep lateral T wave inversion with voltage criteria is the typical electrocardiographic pattern.
Competitive sport is suspended pending diagnosis, not after it.
First degree relatives require clinical and electrocardiographic screening.
explanation.pearls: Any family history of sudden death under 40, including a death attributed to drowning, a single vehicle accident or unexplained epilepsy, should be treated as a possible inherited arrhythmia syndrome and triggers screening of the whole first degree family.

sources.label: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.rationale: Syncope during rather than after exertion is a red flag for a structural or arrhythmic cardiac cause and is never reassured away, particularly with a family history of sudden death under 40. Post-exertional syncope on stopping is the pattern more often benign. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.rationale: Provoking symptoms in someone with suspected dynamic outflow obstruction risks the very event being investigated, and stress testing is done later, under supervision, for risk stratification once the anatomy is known. Imaging precedes provocation. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.rationale: A murmur that increases when preload falls on standing, lateral T wave inversion with voltage criteria, exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death under 40 together require urgent imaging to define the myocardium and outflow tract. Sport is suspended immediately because the highest risk period is before the diagnosis is established, and continued training while awaiting a scan is what turns this presentation into a death. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.rationale: Beta blockade is a reasonable treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed and symptoms require it, but it does not abolish the risk of sudden arrhythmic death and allowing continued competition is the dangerous element of this option. Treatment follows diagnosis and risk stratification. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring contributes to risk stratification by detecting non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, but it cannot show the structural abnormality and a normal recording would be falsely reassuring. It is part of the assessment after imaging rather than instead of it. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

explanation.summary: Cardiac tamponade is a clinical diagnosis supported by echocardiography rather than a purely echocardiographic one, and in malignancy it often develops gradually, allowing the pericardium to stretch until a critical volume is reached and decompensation becomes abrupt. The physical signs reflect equalisation of diastolic pressures and exaggerated ventricular interdependence: a raised jugular venous pressure with preserved or exaggerated inspiratory rise, quiet heart sounds, tachycardia, hypotension and an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure greater than 10 mmHg. Electrocardiographic low voltage with beat to beat amplitude variation reflects the heart swinging within the fluid. The management principle is that anything reducing preload is harmful, so diuretics, nitrates and positive pressure ventilation are avoided, while cautious fluid loading can temporise in a hypovolaemic patient. Definitive treatment is drainage, and because malignant effusions reaccumulate, a drain is usually left in place with consideration of a pericardial window or sclerosant for recurrence. Fluid is sent for cytology, which also has staging implications.
key_points: Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis confirmed rather than made by echocardiography.
An inspiratory systolic fall above 10 mmHg is a key physical sign.
Diuretics, nitrates and positive pressure ventilation all reduce preload and are harmful.
Echocardiography guided drainage with a catheter left in place is the treatment.
Malignant effusions frequently reaccumulate and may need a window or sclerosant.
explanation.pearls: Chest radiograph enlargement of the cardiac silhouette requires roughly 200 mL or more of pericardial fluid, so a normal sized heart never excludes tamponade when fluid has accumulated rapidly after a procedure or trauma.

options.rationale: Diuresis reduces the filling pressure that is maintaining cardiac output against external compression and can precipitate shock. It is the correct treatment for the pulmonary oedema this presentation mimics, which is excluded by the clear chest and clear lung fields. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Vasodilatation reduces preload and systemic vascular resistance, both of which are supporting circulation in tamponade, so it risks cardiovascular collapse. Nitrates are appropriate for acute pulmonary oedema with a raised blood pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Corticosteroid and radiotherapy have a role in malignant airway or superior vena caval obstruction, but they do nothing for the mechanical problem of fluid under pressure in the pericardial sac. Drainage must come first regardless of the underlying tumour. (Source: eviQ: Oncological emergencies)

An elevated jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration, quiet heart sounds, an inspiratory systolic fall above 10 mmHg and diastolic right atrial collapse establish tamponade, which is relieved only by removing the fluid. Echocardiographic guidance with a drain left in place reduces complications and reaccumulation, which is common in malignant effusions. (Source: eviQ: Oncological emergencies)

Cross sectional imaging adds staging information but delays decompression while the patient sits at the steep part of the pressure volume curve, where small further increases in fluid cause abrupt collapse. Imaging follows stabilisation. (Source: eviQ: Oncological emergencies)

explanation.summary: Carbon monoxide poisoning is the great imitator of winter emergency medicine, presenting with headache, nausea, dizziness, fatigue and confusion that are routinely attributed to viral illness or migraine. Three features should redirect the assessment: more than one person in a household affected, symptoms that improve away from the building and recur on return, and the presence of an unflued or poorly maintained combustion appliance, which in Australia has caused deaths in both rental housing and camping situations with fuel burning devices in enclosed spaces. Standard pulse oximetry is falsely reassuring because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so a blood gas with co-oximetry is required, and the level correlates poorly with symptom severity. Treatment is high flow oxygen, which reduces the elimination half life from several hours in room air to around an hour, continued until symptoms resolve and the level normalises. Hyperbaric therapy is considered for loss of consciousness, neurological signs, myocardial ischaemia, very high levels or pregnancy, and every case requires public health notification and remediation of the source before anyone returns to the building.
key_points: Multiple household members affected with symptoms tied to being at home is the key pattern.
Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal, so co-oximetry on a blood gas is required.
High flow oxygen is started before confirmation and shortens the elimination half life substantially.
Levels correlate poorly with severity, so treatment follows the clinical picture.
The source must be identified and remediated before anyone returns to the premises.
explanation.pearls: Ask explicitly whether the family pet has also been unwell, since small animals with high metabolic rates develop symptoms earlier than people and a sick cat or bird at home is often the first clue to a domestic exposure.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.rationale: A viral illness does not remit at work and recur at home, and it would not affect three adults with a time course tied to the evenings. Symptomatic treatment here would send her back into the exposure that caused the illness. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for focal neurology, altered conscious state or thunderclap onset, none of which is present, and it delays a treatment that is safe to start immediately. Scanning is reasonable later if symptoms fail to resolve with treatment. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.rationale: Triptans treat migraine, which does not spread to housemates or follow the geography of a house. Discharging her with an analgesic returns three people to an ongoing source of exposure that can be lethal during sleep. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.rationale: Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with sudden severe headache in one person, not with three days of building symptoms shared by a household. The shared exposure history is what redirects the workup. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.rationale: Headache and nausea affecting a whole household, worse at home and better away from it, with an unflued combustion heater and soot staining, is carbon monoxide exposure, and treatment is 100 per cent oxygen through a non rebreather mask started before any confirmatory result. A blood gas analysed by co-oximetry is required because standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin and reads falsely normal. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

explanation.summary: Acute severe ulcerative colitis is defined by six or more bloody stools a day with evidence of systemic upset, and it remains a condition with real mortality, so admissions are managed jointly by gastroenterology and colorectal surgery from day one. Intravenous corticosteroid is first line, along with venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, correction of anaemia and electrolytes, exclusion of superimposed Clostridioides difficile and cytomegalovirus infection, and avoidance of opioids, antimotility agents and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The day three assessment is the pivot of the admission: persisting high stool frequency, or intermediate frequency with a raised C-reactive protein, identifies patients who will not respond and who need rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin. Rescue therapy is itself assessed at around day seven, and failure at that point means colectomy. Daily abdominal examination and radiographs when there is concern about dilatation are essential, since colonic dilatation beyond 5.5 cm, perforation or massive haemorrhage mandate immediate surgery regardless of the medical plan.
key_points: Acute severe colitis is six or more bloody stools daily with systemic upset.
Response to intravenous corticosteroid is formally assessed on day three.
More than eight stools daily, or three to eight with C-reactive protein above 45 mg/L, predicts colectomy.
Rescue therapy is infliximab or ciclosporin, with surgical involvement in parallel.
Opioids, antimotility drugs and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided throughout.
explanation.pearls: Colonic diameter above 5.5 cm on abdominal radiograph, or any free gas, converts this from a medical problem to an immediate surgical one, so repeat the film whenever stool frequency falls at the same time as abdominal distension increases, which is the deceptive pattern of evolving toxic megacolon.

options.rationale: More than eight stools a day on day three, or three to eight stools with a C-reactive protein above 45 mg/L, predicts a high likelihood of colectomy during that admission and defines failure of intravenous corticosteroid. Rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin is started at that point, with concurrent surgical review so that a timely operation follows if rescue fails. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

Continuing beyond day three in a non-responder delays rescue therapy and surgery, and prolonged corticosteroid exposure increases postoperative complications if colectomy becomes necessary. Response is formally assessed on day three precisely to prevent this drift. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

Stepping down to oral therapy is appropriate for a patient who has responded, with stool frequency falling and inflammatory markers normalising. Discharging a patient still passing seven bloody stools a day risks readmission with perforation. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

Aminosalicylates maintain remission and treat mild to moderate disease but have no role in acute severe colitis, where they do not alter the trajectory. They are reintroduced once the acute episode is controlled. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

Antimotility agents are avoided in acute severe colitis because they can precipitate toxic megacolon by masking the very stool frequency used to judge response. They remain useful in quiescent disease with functional diarrhoea. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

explanation.summary: Chronic salicylate toxicity occurs in older patients taking regular over the counter analgesia and is frequently missed because there is no history of overdose and the presentation resembles sepsis, delirium or a respiratory illness. Salicylate stimulates the respiratory centre, producing a primary respiratory alkalosis, and uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with fever, sweating and hypoglycaemia, particularly in the brain where cerebrospinal fluid glucose can be low despite a normal serum value. Because the two disturbances oppose each other, the pH can be near normal, so the diagnosis rests on recognising the anion gap and the low carbon dioxide rather than on the pH. Chronic toxicity causes neurological injury at much lower levels than acute overdose, so dialysis criteria are correspondingly lower and altered mental status alone justifies it. Management is alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and generous potassium, volume replacement, glucose supplementation even when the serum glucose is normal, and avoidance of intubation wherever possible.
key_points: A near normal pH with a high anion gap and a low carbon dioxide indicates a mixed disorder.
Chronic toxicity produces neurological injury at far lower levels than acute overdose.
Altered mental status is an indication for dialysis regardless of the measured level.
Alkalinisation fails without adequate potassium replacement.
Intubation removes the compensatory hyperventilation and can be rapidly fatal.
explanation.pearls: Give glucose to any salicylate poisoned patient with altered mental status even when the serum glucose is normal, because cerebral glucose use is uncoupled from the serum level and neuroglycopenia occurs with normal peripheral readings.

options.rationale: Charcoal is useful for recent large ingestions and for ongoing absorption from concretions, but it does nothing for drug already distributed into tissue over four days of accumulation. Using it as the sole measure in a confused patient also risks aspiration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Chronic salicylate toxicity with altered mental status is an indication for haemodialysis regardless of the absolute level, and alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate is started immediately because raising serum and urinary pH keeps salicylate ionised, out of the brain and excreted by the kidney. Potassium must be replaced in the same fluid, since hypokalaemia prevents the kidney from excreting bicarbonate and defeats the alkalinisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Intubation is particularly dangerous in this poisoning, because her hyperventilation is the compensation keeping her pH survivable, and any period of apnoea or conventional ventilator settings precipitates a catastrophic fall in pH that drives salicylate into the brain. If intubation is unavoidable, it is done with bicarbonate loading and very high minute ventilation matched to her own. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Volume replacement is necessary because these patients are markedly dehydrated, but fluid alone does not enhance elimination and observation wastes the window in which neurological injury is preventable. Fluid is a component of the correct plan rather than the whole of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning, which is worth excluding given the additional chemist powder, but it has no role against this drug. Confusing the two analgesic poisonings is a recognised error when a patient has been taking several over the counter products. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating hydrocephalus in which cerebrospinal fluid pressure measured at a single point is within the normal range, and it matters disproportionately because it is one of the few treatable causes of gait disturbance and cognitive decline in older people. The classic triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment is present in full in only a minority, and the sequence carries more diagnostic weight than the completeness, since gait almost always comes first and a case where cognition leads should be doubted. The gait is broad based, short strided and magnetic with marked start hesitation and difficulty turning, and it is distinguished from parkinsonian gait by the wide base and by the absence of rest tremor, rigidity and asymmetry, although the overlap is real enough that the two are often confused. Imaging shows ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy, conventionally with an Evans index above 0.3, but imaging alone cannot distinguish it from the ventricular enlargement of cerebral atrophy, so a cerebrospinal fluid drainage trial is used to demonstrate reversibility. Gait improvement after high volume drainage is the best predictor of benefit from ventriculoperitoneal shunting, and gait responds better than cognition, so realistic expectations are set before surgery.
key_points: Gait disturbance almost always precedes the urinary and cognitive features.
A wide base with no rest tremor, rigidity or asymmetry separates it from Parkinson disease.
Ventriculomegaly alone cannot be distinguished from atrophy without a drainage trial.
Gait responds to shunting better than cognition does, which shapes expectations.
explanation.pearls: Time and video the gait over a fixed distance before and immediately after removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid, because a measurable improvement in walking speed and turning is the best available predictor of who will benefit from a shunt, and unrecorded clinical impression is unreliable.

options.rationale: Shunting is the definitive treatment, but imaging and clinical features alone predict response poorly and the operation carries risks of subdural haematoma, infection and shunt failure. Demonstrating reversibility first is what selects the patients who benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Treating the bladder in isolation ignores the gait and cognitive features that share a single cause, and anticholinergic drugs worsen cognition in older adults and add falls risk. The urinary urgency here is a central rather than a bladder problem. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Gait disturbance preceding urinary and cognitive symptoms, with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, is the picture of normal pressure hydrocephalus. Removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid with timed and videoed gait assessment either side is the standard test of reversibility and predicts response to shunting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Parkinson disease is the principal differential because both cause a shuffling gait with start hesitation and turning difficulty, and it is separated here by the absence of rest tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and asymmetry, and by a wide rather than narrow base. A levodopa trial would delay a potentially reversible diagnosis by six weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Alzheimer disease impairs delayed recall early and affects gait only late, whereas his memory is preserved and the gait changed first by many months. Treating this as a primary dementia misses the reversible cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia is defined as a single oral temperature of 38.3 degrees Celsius or more, or 38.0 degrees Celsius sustained for an hour, together with an absolute neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L or below 1.0 x10^9/L and predicted to fall. The nadir typically falls between seven and fourteen days after cytotoxic chemotherapy, which makes the timing in the history a diagnostic feature in its own right. Clinical signs of infection are attenuated because the inflammatory response depends on the neutrophils that are absent, so pus, consolidation on auscultation and localised erythema may all be missing, and no source is identified in around half of episodes. Empirical therapy is an antipseudomonal beta lactam such as piperacillin with tazobactam or cefepime given within an hour, with vancomycin added for suspected line or skin infection, for haemodynamic instability or for known resistant Gram positive colonisation, and an aminoglycoside added for shock or known resistant Gram negative organisms. Risk stratification tools such as the Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer score identify a low-risk subgroup suitable for oral therapy and early discharge, but that decision follows the first dose rather than preceding it.
key_points: Fever with a neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L is an emergency requiring antibiotics within an hour.
Signs of infection are blunted because the inflammatory response requires neutrophils.
Empirical cover must include Pseudomonas aeruginosa; vancomycin alone is inadequate.
No source is found in around half of episodes and cultures are often negative.
explanation.pearls: The chemotherapy nadir at 7 to 14 days after treatment means a patient who telephones with fever in that window is told to come in immediately rather than to take paracetamol and see how they go, since antipyretics mask the only reliable sign they have.

options.rationale: Oral therapy with amoxicillin and clavulanate plus ciprofloxacin is an option only for carefully selected low-risk outpatients with a favourable risk score, adequate support and reliable follow-up. This regimen also lacks pseudomonal cover, which is the reason antipseudomonal agents are mandated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Colony stimulating factor shortens the duration of neutropenia and has a place in primary and secondary prophylaxis, but it does not treat established infection and has no demonstrated mortality benefit in this setting. It is an adjunct, never the initial intervention. (Source: eviQ: Febrile neutropenia)

Vancomycin covers Gram positive organisms only and leaves the Gram negative bacilli, particularly Pseudomonas aeruginosa, that cause the most rapidly fatal episodes entirely untreated. Vancomycin is added to a beta lactam for suspected line infection, skin or soft tissue infection or haemodynamic instability rather than used alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Fever with an absolute neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L is febrile neutropenia, a medical emergency in which empirical broad spectrum antipseudomonal beta lactam therapy is given within an hour of presentation. Cultures are drawn immediately before the first dose, from both a peripheral vein and each lumen of the central device, but they must not delay it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Cultures take 24 to 48 hours and are negative in around 70 per cent of episodes, while mortality in untreated neutropenic sepsis rises sharply with every hour of delay. Waiting for microbiological confirmation is the central error this presentation tests. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Cluster headache is the commonest trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia and is defined by severe strictly unilateral orbital, supraorbital or temporal pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes untreated, occurring from every other day to eight times daily, with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features or a sense of restlessness. Three features separate it from migraine at the bedside, namely the restlessness and pacing where migraine sufferers lie still in the dark, the prominent ipsilateral autonomic signs, and the striking circadian and circannual periodicity that wakes patients at the same time each night. A partial Horner syndrome is common and usually resolves between attacks, although it can persist. Acute treatment must act within minutes, which restricts the effective options to oxygen at 12 to 15 litres per minute by non-rebreather mask and to subcutaneous or intranasal triptans, and oral agents of any kind are too slow. Verapamil is the preventive of choice with electrocardiographic monitoring during titration because of dose-related atrioventricular block, a tapering corticosteroid course or greater occipital nerve block can bridge the gap, and smoking cessation and alcohol avoidance during a bout are advised.
key_points: Restlessness during attacks distinguishes cluster headache from migraine, where patients lie still.
Attacks last 15 to 180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic features and circadian periodicity.
Acute treatment must act in minutes: high flow oxygen and subcutaneous or nasal triptan.
Verapamil is the preventive of choice and requires electrocardiographic monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Oxygen for cluster headache must be 12 to 15 litres per minute through a non-rebreather mask with a reservoir bag, because nasal prongs or a simple mask deliver too low a fraction of inspired oxygen to abort the attack and are the usual reason a patient reports that oxygen did not work.

options.rationale: Oral triptans take 30 to 60 minutes to act, by which time an attack is already resolving, and the same drug given subcutaneously acts within about ten minutes. The difference is entirely one of route and pharmacokinetics rather than of drug choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia, which produces brief electric shock-like paroxysms lasting seconds, triggered by touching the face, and without autonomic features or nocturnal periodicity. The attack duration alone separates the two conditions. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

A tapering corticosteroid course is a legitimate transitional treatment used to suppress attacks while a preventive agent is titrated, but it does not abort the attack he is having now. Its place is bridging rather than acute relief. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Propranolol prevents migraine and has no established role in cluster headache, where verapamil is the preventive agent of choice. Eight weeks is also longer than the bout is likely to last, so the review would follow spontaneous remission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Strictly unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features and agitation in circadian nocturnal attacks is cluster headache, and high flow oxygen with subcutaneous sumatriptan are the two acute treatments with the strongest evidence. Both work within minutes, which matters when attacks peak in under a quarter of an hour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: The combination of a renin angiotensin system inhibitor, a diuretic and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is often called the triple whammy and is one of the commonest preventable causes of community-acquired acute kidney injury in older Australians. The three act at different points on the same autoregulatory system, since the diuretic depletes intravascular volume, the non-steroidal blocks the prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilatation that maintains glomerular perfusion when volume is low, and the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor blocks the efferent arteriolar constriction that would otherwise preserve filtration pressure. Each is well tolerated alone in a euvolaemic patient, which is why the combination is so often overlooked until an intercurrent illness removes the volume reserve, and gastroenteritis, vomiting, febrile illness and hot weather are the usual triggers. A bland urinary sediment with an unobstructed tract and clinical volume depletion establishes a prerenal picture without further investigation, and management is to withhold all three agents and restore volume. Sick day guidance is the durable lesson, with patients on these agents told which medicines to pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever, and over-the-counter anti-inflammatory purchase asked about directly since it will not appear on the medication list.
key_points: Diuretic, renin angiotensin inhibitor and non-steroidal disable renal autoregulation together.
An intercurrent illness removing volume reserve is the usual precipitant.
A bland sediment with no obstruction establishes a prerenal cause without further tests.
Over-the-counter anti-inflammatory use must be asked about, as it is absent from the list.
explanation.pearls: Give written sick day guidance to every patient on a renin angiotensin inhibitor plus a diuretic, naming the medicines to pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever and when to restart them, because the combination is safe until the day the patient cannot keep fluids down.

options.rationale: Volume depletion with a bland urinary sediment and an unobstructed tract indicates prerenal acute kidney injury, and all three drugs are contributing by different mechanisms that each disable glomerular autoregulation. Withholding the whole combination while restoring volume is the treatment, with reintroduction once renal function has recovered. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

Stopping one agent leaves the other two mechanisms operating, with the diuretic continuing to deplete volume and the anti-inflammatory continuing to constrict the afferent arteriole. The injury arises from the combination rather than from any single drug. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

Drug-induced interstitial nephritis is worth considering with any new medication, but it typically produces sterile pyuria, white cell casts, eosinophiluria, a rash or fever, and her sediment and examination are bland. Corticosteroid would add hyperglycaemia and immunosuppression without addressing the volume deficit. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

Catheterisation and imaging are the right moves when obstruction is suspected, and obstruction has already been excluded by an ultrasound showing no hydronephrosis with a non-palpable bladder. An unnecessary catheter carries a real risk of urinary infection in this age group. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

Biopsy is reserved for suspected intrinsic glomerular or interstitial disease where the cause remains unclear after non-invasive assessment, particularly with an active sediment or systemic features. A clear precipitant with a bland sediment does not warrant an invasive procedure with a bleeding risk. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the constellation of fluid and electrolyte shifts that follows reintroduction of nutrition after a period of starvation, driven by the switch from fat and protein catabolism back to carbohydrate metabolism and the resulting insulin surge. Insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells at a time when total body stores are already depleted despite normal or near-normal admission levels, and it simultaneously promotes sodium and water retention, producing the oedema and cardiac failure seen here. Hypophosphataemia is the biochemical hallmark and it causes the clinical syndrome, since adenosine triphosphate and 2,3-diphosphoglycerate synthesis both fail, producing respiratory muscle weakness, cardiac failure, rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis, seizures and arrhythmia. Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and is consumed rapidly as carbohydrate metabolism restarts, so it is given before or with the first feed to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. Prevention is what matters most, with identification of high-risk patients by body mass index, weight loss, duration of negligible intake and pre-existing electrolyte abnormality, starting feeds at a fraction of the requirement and building up over days, with daily electrolyte monitoring throughout the first week.
key_points: Insulin release after refeeding drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells.
Hypophosphataemia impairs adenosine triphosphate synthesis, causing cardiac and respiratory failure.
Thiamine is given before or with the first feed to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
Prevention means starting at reduced calories and building up with daily monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Start feeding a patient at high refeeding risk at about 5 to 10 kcal per kilogram per day and build to full requirement over four to seven days, with daily phosphate, potassium and magnesium for the first week, since normal admission electrolytes say nothing about total body stores.

options.rationale: The route of feeding is not the problem and parenteral nutrition carries higher refeeding risk along with line-related complications. Adding exogenous insulin would drive further intracellular shift of the very electrolytes that are already dangerously low. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

A falling phosphate with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and new fluid overload after reintroducing nutrition to a severely malnourished patient is refeeding syndrome. Management is to reduce the caloric load, aggressively replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and give thiamine, which is consumed rapidly as carbohydrate metabolism resumes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Oral phosphate is slow, causes diarrhoea at the doses needed and is inadequate for a level of 0.38 mmol/L with respiratory and cardiac manifestations. Continuing full-rate feeding sustains the insulin-driven intracellular shift that caused the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Stopping feeding altogether prolongs malnutrition and sets up a repeat episode when it is restarted, and the evidence supports continuing at a reduced rate while replacing electrolytes. The feed should be reduced, not abandoned. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Increasing the caloric load intensifies the insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and will deepen every abnormality present. Starting at full requirement was itself the precipitant in this case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects a substantial proportion of commercial drivers and is associated with a two to threefold increase in motor vehicle crash risk, concentrated in those with excessive daytime sleepiness rather than in everyone with a raised apnoea hypopnoea index. The Australian standard set out in Assessing Fitness to Drive is stricter for commercial vehicle drivers than for private drivers and turns primarily on symptoms, so a driver reporting sleepiness while driving, or a recent episode of falling asleep at the wheel, does not meet the standard regardless of what a sleep study eventually shows. The legal framework places the obligation to report a relevant medical condition on the driver, while the treating doctor is responsible for assessing fitness, giving clear advice, and documenting both, with direct notification to the licensing authority permitted and appropriate where a driver continues to drive against advice. Continuous positive airway pressure is the definitive treatment and drivers can usually return to commercial driving once symptoms are controlled and adherence is demonstrated objectively, typically with downloaded device data showing regular use. Weight loss, positional therapy, mandibular advancement splints and treatment of contributory hypothyroidism or alcohol use are adjuncts, and the associated hypertension frequently improves with effective treatment.
key_points: Commercial driving standards turn on daytime sleepiness rather than on the apnoea index alone.
Falling asleep at the wheel means the standard is not met, before any sleep study is done.
The driver holds the reporting obligation; the doctor advises, documents and may notify.
Return to commercial driving requires symptom control with demonstrated device adherence.
explanation.pearls: An Epworth Sleepiness Scale of 16 or more, or any episode of falling asleep at the wheel, disqualifies a commercial driver under the Austroads standard immediately, so the certificate is withheld on the day rather than held open pending the polysomnogram.

options.rationale: Wake-promoting agents are reserved for residual sleepiness that persists despite adequate treatment of the underlying disorder, and using one to mask sleepiness in an untreated driver is unsafe. It also has no effect on the apnoeas, the hypoxaemia or the blood pressure. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Weight loss is genuinely disease-modifying and bariatric referral is reasonable in the longer term, but surgery is months away at best and does nothing about tomorrow night's shift. The immediate hazard is not addressed. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

Severe excessive daytime sleepiness with a recent episode of falling asleep at the wheel means he does not meet the commercial vehicle standard, and the advice to cease driving applies immediately rather than after the sleep study. Australian practice places the reporting obligation on the driver, with the doctor responsible for giving and documenting clear advice. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

A fourteen week wait means fourteen more weeks of overnight heavy vehicle driving by a man who has already fallen asleep at the wheel, and fitness to drive turns on demonstrated sleepiness rather than on a numerical apnoea index. Deferring the decision to the test misunderstands what the standard measures. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

Reporting to the licensing authority is permitted where a driver continues to drive against advice, but it follows rather than replaces giving the advice, and doing it covertly is not supported. The first step is always an explicit conversation with the patient. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: Behcet disease is a variable vessel vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all sizes, with a marked geographic distribution along the historical Silk Road from the eastern Mediterranean through to East Asia, and a strong association with HLA-B51. The International Study Group criteria require recurrent oral ulceration at least three times a year plus two of recurrent genital ulceration, eye lesions, skin lesions and a positive pathergy test, in which a sterile pustule forms at a needle prick site within 48 hours. Ocular involvement occurs in around half of patients, is typically a bilateral relapsing panuveitis with retinal vasculitis rather than isolated anterior uveitis, and was historically a leading cause of blindness in young adults in endemic regions. Other major manifestations are venous thrombosis, arterial aneurysm including the pulmonary arteries, central nervous system parenchymal and venous sinus disease, and gastrointestinal ulceration that can perforate. Treatment is stratified by organ involvement, with colchicine and topical measures for mucocutaneous disease, and systemic corticosteroid combined with azathioprine, ciclosporin, interferon alfa or a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor for ocular, neurological and vascular disease.
key_points: Recurrent oral ulceration plus two of genital ulcers, eye, skin or pathergy meets criteria.
Pathergy is a sterile pustule forming at a needle prick site within 48 hours.
Ocular disease is a relapsing panuveitis with retinal vasculitis, not isolated anterior uveitis.
Sight-threatening or neurological disease requires systemic immunosuppression, not colchicine alone.
explanation.pearls: Look at the cannula sites before ordering a pathergy test: a sterile pustule that appeared at a venepuncture or cannulation site within 48 hours is the same phenomenon and is often already documented in the nursing notes as a line-site reaction.

options.rationale: Topical therapy penetrates adequately for anterior uveitis only, and posterior segment inflammation requires systemic treatment. A month of observation in a condition that causes irreversible visual loss within days is the central hazard here. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

Recurrent herpetic ulceration also causes oral and genital ulcers together, and it is excluded here by a negative polymerase chain reaction from the ulcer base, by the scarring pattern and by the accompanying erythema nodosum and pathergy, which herpes does not produce. Repeating a negative test delays treatment of the eye. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Colchicine is a reasonable first-line agent for mucocutaneous and joint manifestations and would be appropriate if ulcers were the only problem. It is inadequate as sole therapy once sight-threatening ocular disease is present. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

Inflammatory bowel disease can produce oral ulceration and erythema nodosum and warrants consideration, but he has no bowel symptoms and endoscopy will take weeks. The eye cannot wait for a differential diagnosis to be narrowed by an unrelated investigation. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

Recurrent oral and genital ulceration with erythema nodosum, a positive pathergy response and new ocular symptoms indicates Behcet disease with probable posterior uveitis, which is sight-threatening and can destroy vision within days. Same-day ophthalmological assessment with systemic corticosteroid, followed by a steroid-sparing agent, is the appropriate response. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

explanation.summary: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis accounts for under 1 per cent of strokes but occurs in a much younger population, with a median age around 35 and a marked female predominance driven by oestrogen-containing contraception, pregnancy and the puerperium. Presentation is protean and often subacute, and the four recognised syndromes are isolated intracranial hypertension with headache and papilloedema, focal deficits, seizures, and encephalopathy, with headache the presenting symptom in around 90 per cent. Two features on plain imaging should raise the diagnosis, namely a parenchymal haemorrhage or infarct that does not respect arterial territory boundaries, particularly when parasagittal or temporal, and a hyperdense cord or delta sign, though the unenhanced scan is normal in up to a third of cases so a negative scan does not exclude it. Confirmation is by computed tomography venography or magnetic resonance venography, and treatment is therapeutic anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin even in the presence of haemorrhagic venous infarction, a counterintuitive principle supported by trial and registry data because the bleeding is a consequence of venous congestion that anticoagulation relieves. Endovascular thrombectomy is reserved for deterioration despite anticoagulation, and thrombophilia screening, cessation of oestrogen-containing contraception and three to twelve months of oral anticoagulation follow.
key_points: Oestrogen-containing contraception, pregnancy and the puerperium are the major risk factors.
A haemorrhage or infarct crossing arterial territory boundaries suggests a venous cause.
Anticoagulation is given despite haemorrhagic venous infarction, which is the key principle.
A normal unenhanced scan occurs in up to a third of cases and does not exclude the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: A headache that is worse lying flat, worse on coughing or straining and worst on waking is the raised intracranial pressure pattern, and in a young woman on the combined pill it should trigger venographic imaging rather than a diagnosis of migraine, whatever the unenhanced scan shows.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: Progressive positional headache with papilloedema, a focal seizure and a parenchymal haemorrhage that crosses arterial boundaries in a woman on oestrogen indicates cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Venography confirms it and therapeutic anticoagulation is the established treatment, since the haemorrhage is venous infarction caused by the clot rather than a contraindication to treating it. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: Randomised and observational evidence both support anticoagulating despite haemorrhagic venous infarction, because relieving the venous outflow obstruction is what stops the bleeding from extending. Withholding treatment allows the thrombus to propagate and the infarct to enlarge. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: Decompressive surgery is reserved for impending herniation from a large venous infarct with a deteriorating conscious state, and she is fully oriented with normal limb power. Osmotic therapy also does not address the underlying occlusion. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: An antiseizure medication is appropriate after a seizure with a supratentorial lesion and is part of the plan. The distinction is that it treats a complication while leaving the thrombosis undiagnosed and untreated, and a repeat unenhanced scan cannot demonstrate the occluded sinus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Antiplatelet therapy and carotid imaging belong to the workup of arterial ischaemic stroke, which this is not, since the lesion crosses arterial territory boundaries and the presentation is dominated by raised intracranial pressure. Carotid disease is also vanishingly rare at this age. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

explanation.summary: Malignant spinal cord compression complicates around 5 per cent of cancers, most often from prostate, breast, lung, myeloma and renal primaries, and results from vertebral metastasis expanding into the epidural space or from vertebral collapse. Back pain precedes neurological signs by a median of several weeks and has characteristic features, being worse on lying flat, waking the patient at night and worsened by coughing or straining, which together distinguish it from mechanical pain that eases with rest. The single strongest predictor of whether a patient walks afterwards is whether they were walking when treatment started, so this is a presentation where hours matter and where waiting for the morning list costs function that does not return. Dexamethasone is given immediately at high dose to reduce vasogenic oedema, whole spine magnetic resonance imaging is obtained urgently because multilevel disease is common and changes the treatment field, and definitive treatment is decided jointly between radiation oncology and spinal surgery. Surgical decompression with stabilisation followed by radiotherapy gives better ambulatory outcomes than radiotherapy alone in selected patients with a single level of compression, good performance status, a reasonable prognosis and spinal instability or a radioresistant tumour.
key_points: Pain worse lying flat and waking the patient is the warning that precedes neurological signs.
Ambulatory status at the start of treatment is the strongest predictor of final function.
Image the whole spine, since around a third of patients have multilevel compression.
Dexamethasone is given before imaging, not after it.
explanation.pearls: The sensory level in cord compression sits at or below the compressive lesion and never above it, so a level at the umbilicus corresponding to the tenth thoracic dermatome means imaging the thoracic and cervical spine as well, and a lumbar-only request will miss the lesion entirely.

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is the right modality, but this plan fails on two counts. The whole spine must be imaged because a third of patients have compression at more than one level, some of it remote from the symptomatic site, and the timeframe must be hours rather than a week. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

Back pain with upper motor neuron signs, a sensory level and urinary retention in a man with bone metastases is malignant spinal cord compression, and neurological outcome depends almost entirely on how much function remains when treatment begins. High dose dexamethasone is given immediately to reduce peritumoural oedema while magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine is arranged. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

Plain films miss around a fifth of compressive lesions, cannot show the cord or the epidural space, and would be imaging the wrong region given a sensory level at the umbilicus corresponding to the tenth thoracic dermatome. A normal film would falsely reassure. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

Analgesia is necessary but does nothing for the compression, and an outpatient referral introduces a delay measured in days when the window for preserving ambulation is measured in hours. Established paraplegia is rarely reversible. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

A bone scan shows osseous metastatic activity but gives no information about the epidural space or the degree of cord compression, and it cannot guide the radiotherapy field or a surgical decision. It answers a question that has already been answered. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

explanation.summary: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction in which antibodies form against complexes of platelet factor 4 and heparin, and those immune complexes cross-link platelet Fc receptors to cause platelet activation, thrombin generation and thrombosis, with the thrombocytopenia arising from consumption rather than from impaired production. The paradox that defines it clinically is that bleeding is rare while thrombosis occurs in up to half of untreated patients, so a falling platelet count on heparin is a thrombotic emergency rather than a bleeding one. The 4Ts score structures the pretest assessment using the degree of thrombocytopenia, the timing at five to ten days after first exposure or sooner with recent prior exposure, the presence of thrombosis or skin necrosis, and the absence of other causes, and a high score mandates immediate action before any laboratory confirmation. Confirmatory testing proceeds in two steps, with a sensitive but non-specific immunoassay for platelet factor 4 antibodies followed by a functional assay such as serotonin release or heparin induced platelet activation, but results take days and treatment cannot wait. Anticoagulation continues for at least four weeks in isolated thrombocytopenia and three months where thrombosis has occurred, and the event is documented prominently as an adverse drug reaction because re-exposure years later can provoke rapid-onset recurrence.
key_points: It causes thrombosis rather than bleeding despite a falling platelet count.
The 4Ts score drives immediate management before laboratory confirmation returns.
All heparin preparations cross-react, so switching to unfractionated heparin is futile.
Warfarin before platelet recovery risks venous limb gangrene through protein C depletion.
explanation.pearls: Delay warfarin until the platelet count is above 150 x10^9/L and overlap it with the non-heparin anticoagulant for at least five days, because starting it early depletes protein C before the procoagulant factors fall and has caused venous limb gangrene requiring amputation.

options.rationale: Warfarin given before the platelet count has recovered depletes protein C faster than the procoagulant factors and can precipitate venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis, which makes this the most dangerous of the wrong answers. Warfarin is introduced only once the platelet count exceeds 150 x10^9/L, overlapped with the non-heparin agent. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

High dose immunoglobulin has a role in severe or refractory disease by saturating the Fc receptors that mediate platelet activation, so it is a legitimate adjunct. The distinction is that it never substitutes for stopping the heparin, and continuing the causative drug guarantees progression. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

A platelet fall of more than 50 per cent beginning on day five to ten of heparin exposure with new thrombosis and no alternative cause gives a high 4Ts score, and the disorder is profoundly prothrombotic despite the low count. Stopping every heparin preparation and starting a full therapeutic dose of a non-heparin agent such as danaparoid, argatroban or fondaparinux is the immediate step. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

Platelet transfusion adds substrate to a process that is driving thrombosis rather than bleeding and has been associated with arterial thrombotic events in this setting. It is reserved for active major bleeding, which is absent here. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

The antibody is directed against platelet factor 4 bound to heparin and cross-reacts across all heparin preparations, so unfractionated heparin perpetuates rather than resolves the process. Unfractionated heparin in fact carries a higher risk of causing the syndrome than the low molecular weight form. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

explanation.summary: Lofgren syndrome is an acute form of sarcoidosis defined by the combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and periarticular ankle inflammation, often with fever, and it is one of the few presentations in which the clinical picture alone is considered diagnostic without histology. That exception exists because the specificity of the triad approaches 95 per cent and because the prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous resolution in around 90 per cent within two years, particularly in those carrying HLA-DRB1 03. The ankle involvement is a periarthritis of the soft tissues around the joint rather than a true synovitis, which is why it is warm and tender but not destructive. Initial assessment still includes chest radiography, lung function with gas transfer, serum calcium, renal and liver function, an electrocardiogram and ophthalmological review, because asymptomatic cardiac, renal and ocular involvement determine whether treatment is needed. Corticosteroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease rather than given routinely, and in this presentation non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with rest and planned review are sufficient, with colchicine or a short steroid course used if symptoms are severe.
key_points: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle periarthritis define the syndrome.
The triad is diagnostic without biopsy, unlike other presentations of sarcoidosis.
Around 90 per cent remit spontaneously within two years.
Steroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease, not for the syndrome itself.
explanation.pearls: Symmetry of the hilar lymphadenopathy is what earns the clinical diagnosis: asymmetrical or unilateral hilar nodes, or any accompanying weight loss and night sweats, take the presentation out of Lofgren syndrome and back to tissue sampling for lymphoma and tuberculosis.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.rationale: Tuberculous lymphadenopathy is characteristically unilateral or asymmetrical and accompanied by constitutional symptoms, and her interferon gamma release assay is negative with no exposure history. Empirical antituberculous therapy carries substantial hepatotoxicity for a diagnosis that is not supported. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Corticosteroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease such as significant pulmonary impairment, cardiac or neurological involvement, hypercalcaemia or sight-threatening uveitis, none of which is present given normal lung function and a normal calcium. Steroids may also prolong the course in an otherwise self-limiting presentation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.rationale: Lymphoma typically produces asymmetrical or bulky mediastinal nodes with constitutional symptoms rather than symmetrical hilar enlargement with erythema nodosum and periarticular ankle inflammation. Surgical biopsy would subject her to a general anaesthetic for a clinical diagnosis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.rationale: Erythema nodosum with symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle periarthritis in a well patient is Lofgren syndrome, an acute presentation of sarcoidosis with a distinctive natural history of spontaneous remission in around 90 per cent within two years. The constellation is sufficiently specific that tissue diagnosis is not required, and symptomatic treatment with observation is appropriate. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.rationale: Tissue sampling is indicated where the presentation is atypical, where lymphoma or malignancy is a genuine concern, or where treatment decisions depend on it, and it is the standard route to a sarcoidosis diagnosis in other presentations. The distinguishing point is that this specific triad is diagnostic on its own and biopsy adds procedural risk without changing management. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome follows massive release of intracellular contents from rapidly dividing cells, classically in bulky high grade lymphoma and acute leukaemias within 12 to 72 hours of treatment, producing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and secondary hypocalcaemia, with acute kidney injury from urate and calcium phosphate deposition. Prevention rests on risk stratification, aggressive hydration and a urate-lowering agent, with allopurinol for intermediate risk and rasburicase for high risk or established disease. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase that converts urate to the far more soluble allantoin, and because that reaction generates hydrogen peroxide it causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in people who cannot regenerate reduced glutathione, making glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency an absolute contraindication. The deficiency is X-linked and common in people of Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian ancestry, and a family history of haemolysis after primaquine or fava beans is strong enough evidence to withhold the drug while testing proceeds. The management of hypocalcaemia in this syndrome is also counterintuitive, since correcting it in the face of a high phosphate drives calcium phosphate deposition, so calcium is given only for arrhythmia, tetany or seizures rather than for the number.
key_points: Rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
Hypocalcaemia is treated only for arrhythmia, tetany or seizures, not for the value alone.
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended as it promotes calcium phosphate deposition.
Volume expansion with allopurinol is the safe route when enzyme status is unknown.
explanation.pearls: A family history of haemolysis after primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin or fava beans is enough to withhold rasburicase before any test result is available, because the resulting haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia are more dangerous than the hyperuricaemia the drug was going to treat.

sources.label: HSANZ: Supportive care in haematological malignancy

options.rationale: The hypocalcaemia here is secondary to hyperphosphataemia, and giving calcium while the phosphate is 2.4 mmol/L promotes calcium phosphate precipitation in the renal tubules and soft tissues, worsening the kidney injury. Calcium is reserved for cardiac membrane stabilisation with electrocardiographic changes or for symptomatic tetany or seizures, and a Trousseau sign alone does not meet that threshold. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Alkalinisation increases urate solubility but simultaneously reduces calcium phosphate solubility, promoting nephrocalcinosis in a patient whose phosphate is already markedly raised, and it is no longer recommended. A diuretic in a patient who is becoming oliguric with a rising creatinine risks compounding hypovolaemia. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Renal replacement therapy is indicated for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia, fluid overload or oliguria persisting despite adequate volume expansion, and none of those thresholds has yet been reached with a normal electrocardiogram and fluids not yet maximised. It remains a real possibility over the next hours if the response is inadequate. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Rasburicase is the standard agent for established tumour lysis with a urate this high, and it would be the answer in almost any other patient, which is what makes it the tempting branch here. Its metabolism generates hydrogen peroxide, and in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, which this family history strongly suggests, it precipitates severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia and is contraindicated. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

With urine output falling and creatinine rising, intensified volume expansion is the immediate priority, and allopurinol is continued because it blocks further urate formation without the oxidative risk. Testing glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status is what determines whether rasburicase can ever be used, and treatment proceeds on the safe assumption of deficiency until it returns. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)
