explanation.pearls: Test for post exercise facilitation by eliciting an absent reflex, having the patient sustain a maximal contraction of that muscle group for ten to fifteen seconds, then immediately re-testing; return of the reflex points to a presynaptic disorder and should trigger chest imaging for small cell lung cancer.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.rationale: This pairing targets the postsynaptic disorder, in which fatigable ptosis and diplopia dominate, reflexes are preserved and strength worsens rather than improves with repeated effort. The two conditions are distinguished by the direction of the response to exercise, and here strength and reflexes both improve. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.rationale: Oligoclonal bands support a central demyelinating process, which would give upper motor neuron signs rather than absent reflexes. Nerve conduction studies alone, without repetitive stimulation protocols, will not capture the presynaptic abnormality. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.rationale: A cord or cauda equina lesion could produce lower limb weakness with areflexia and bladder or bowel disturbance, which gives this option some surface plausibility. It would not produce dry mouth, would not improve with sustained contraction and would be expected to give sensory and sphincter findings that he does not have. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy is a standard differential for subacute proximal weakness, but the creatine kinase is already within normal limits and a primary muscle disease does not explain the autonomic symptoms or the facilitation. Biopsy would subject him to a procedure that does not address the discriminating findings. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

Proximal weakness with autonomic features and post exercise facilitation of reflexes indicates a presynaptic defect of acetylcholine release, which in a heavy smoker of this age is paraneoplastic in around half of cases and most often driven by a small cell lung carcinoma. The tumour frequently precedes the neurological presentation and a plain radiograph is insufficiently sensitive to exclude it. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

explanation.summary: Cystic fibrosis related diabetes arises from progressive destruction of the pancreatic islets by the same fibrotic process that causes exocrine insufficiency, and it affects a substantial proportion of adults with the condition, with prevalence rising steeply with age. It sits apart from both type 1 and type 2 diabetes: insulin deficiency is partial so ketoacidosis is rare, insulin resistance fluctuates with infection and corticosteroid use, and the earliest abnormality is postprandial rather than fasting hyperglycaemia. Its clinical importance is that unexplained weight loss, a decline in lung function and increasing exacerbation frequency precede the diagnosis by up to several years, and these outcomes improve with insulin therapy, which is the treatment of choice rather than oral agents. Annual screening with an oral glucose tolerance test from about ten years of age is standard, with additional testing whenever there is unexplained decline. Glycated haemoglobin is specifically not recommended as the screening test because red cell turnover in this population makes it falsely reassuring.
key_points: Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in cystic fibrosis because of shortened red cell survival
The oral glucose tolerance test is the annual screen and the diagnostic standard
Postprandial hyperglycaemia precedes any fasting abnormality
Unexplained weight loss, falling lung function and more frequent exacerbations are the clinical prompts
Insulin, not an oral agent, is the treatment of choice
explanation.pearls: In cystic fibrosis related diabetes the decline in weight and forced expiratory volume in one second begins two to four years before the glucose tolerance test becomes diagnostic, so an unexplained fall in either is itself the indication to test regardless of the annual schedule.

options.rationale: The oral glucose tolerance test is the standard annual screen from adolescence in this population and is the appropriate test now, because the characteristic early abnormality is postprandial hyperglycaemia with a preserved fasting glucose. Unexplained weight loss and a rising exacerbation frequency are the classic prompts to test outside the annual schedule. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia)

Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in this population because shortened red cell survival from chronic inflammation and recurrent infection falsely lowers the result, so a value within normal limits does not exclude the diagnosis. Repeating an insensitive test after a further three months of weight loss compounds the delay. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia)

The fasting glucose remains within normal limits until relatively late in this condition because residual insulin secretion covers the basal state while failing to cover meals. Relying on it misses the window in which treatment protects lung function and weight. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society)

Continuous monitoring detects postprandial excursions sensitively and is increasingly used in this group. It has not replaced the glucose tolerance test as the diagnostic standard, and the diagnostic thresholds that direct insulin therapy are defined against the tolerance test. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society)

A random glucose lacks the sensitivity to establish the diagnosis and ketosis is characteristically absent in this form of diabetes because insulin deficiency is partial rather than complete. A negative result would provide false reassurance. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis evolves through three overlapping phases: an allergic phase with adult onset asthma and sinonasal disease, an eosinophilic phase with peripheral eosinophilia and tissue infiltration producing migratory pulmonary infiltrates or eosinophilic gastroenteritis, and a vasculitic phase with neuropathy, purpura, cardiac and renal involvement. The asthma label typically precedes the vasculitis by several years, which is why the condition is so often first recognised at the moment a patient labelled asthmatic develops a neurological deficit. Mononeuritis multiplex, meaning deficits in two or more separately named peripheral nerves, is the classic neurological signature and occurs in the majority. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are positive in only about forty per cent and a negative result therefore cannot exclude the diagnosis, which is a frequent source of delay. Cardiac involvement, which may present with only a raised troponin, is the principal cause of mortality and shifts treatment toward combined corticosteroid and cyclophosphamide or rituximab.
key_points: Adult onset asthma with nasal polyps plus eosinophilia plus neuropathy is the defining combination
Mononeuritis multiplex means deficits in two or more separately named nerves
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are positive in only about forty per cent
Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death and may show only as a raised troponin
Send strongyloides serology in parallel with, not instead of, starting corticosteroid
explanation.pearls: A peripheral eosinophil count above 1.5 x10^9/L in someone carrying an asthma label who develops a new foot drop should prompt same day corticosteroid and vasculitis referral, because an infarcted nerve left untreated beyond a few weeks recovers poorly.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy
Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.rationale: Treating this as refractory eosinophilic asthma addresses the wheeze while leaving a vasculitis to infarct further nerves and myocardium. Biologic therapy targeting interleukin 5 does have a role in this condition, but as a steroid sparing agent after remission is induced, not as the acute response to progressive nerve and cardiac involvement. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

Late onset asthma with nasal polyps, marked eosinophilia, palpable purpura and mononeuritis multiplex constitutes an eosinophilic small vessel vasculitis with active neurological and probable cardiac involvement, which is an indication for immediate corticosteroid while specialist assessment and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing proceed. Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death in this condition and drives the urgency. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

Nerve conduction studies will confirm the pattern of multiple separate named nerve lesions and are worth obtaining, but the tempo is wrong. Each week of untreated disease risks a further infarcted nerve with incomplete recovery, and the raised troponin signals organ involvement that will not wait. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.rationale: Excluding strongyloides before immunosuppression is genuinely important because hyperinfection can be fatal, and serology should be sent today, but it is drawn in parallel rather than used to delay treatment. He has no overseas travel or endemic residence, and the neurological progression will not pause for a serology result. (Source: Australian Society for Infectious Diseases)

Allergy testing addresses the atopic label he has carried rather than the vasculitic process now causing his deficits. Leukotriene antagonists have historically been associated with unmasking this condition when corticosteroid is reduced, and they have no therapeutic role in the acute vasculitis. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

explanation.summary: Infiltrative cardiomyopathy should be suspected whenever increased left ventricular wall thickness coexists with low QRS voltages, because hypertensive and hypertrophic disease both produce high voltages in proportion to muscle mass and the discordance signals that the thickening is deposited material rather than myocyte hypertrophy. Apical sparing on longitudinal strain imaging, biatrial enlargement, a persistently raised troponin without a rise and fall pattern and disproportionately elevated natriuretic peptides complete the echocardiographic and biochemical picture. The critical fork is between the light chain form arising from a clonal plasma cell population and the transthyretin form, because the first is treated with anti plasma cell therapy and carries a far worse untreated prognosis measured in months, while the second is treated with a transthyretin stabiliser. Extracardiac features separate them: macroglossia, periorbital purpura and nephrotic range proteinuria are essentially specific to the light chain form, while bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and lumbar spinal stenosis years earlier suggest transthyretin disease. Blood pressure also often falls and antihypertensives are withdrawn in the year before diagnosis, and autonomic involvement produces the postural drop seen here.
key_points: Increased wall thickness with low QRS voltage is the signature discordance of infiltration
Apical sparing on strain imaging and biatrial enlargement support the diagnosis
Macroglossia, periorbital purpura and nephrotic proteinuria indicate the light chain form
Exclude a plasma cell disorder before interpreting bone scintigraphy as transthyretin disease
A persistently raised troponin without a rise and fall pattern reflects infiltration, not plaque rupture
explanation.pearls: Serum free light chains with serum and urine immunofixation together detect over ninety per cent of light chain amyloidosis, whereas serum protein electrophoresis alone misses roughly a third, so ordering electrophoresis by itself is the commonest way this diagnosis is delayed.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Bone avid tracer uptake identifies the transthyretin form of the disease and is an excellent non-invasive test for it, which makes this the strongest competing answer. It must not be used alone, because a positive scan is only interpretable as transthyretin disease once a plasma cell disorder has been excluded, and the extracardiac features here point to the light chain form. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Diffuse subendocardial late enhancement with abnormal gadolinium kinetics supports infiltration and refines the cardiac assessment, so this is a reasonable investigation at some point. It cannot distinguish the light chain from the transthyretin form, and that distinction is the one that changes treatment. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Macroglossia, periorbital purpura and nephrotic range proteinuria alongside an infiltrative cardiomyopathy indicate light chain deposition from an underlying plasma cell disorder, and the light chain assay with immunofixation is both the most sensitive screen and the test that determines treatment. Identifying the clonal process is what separates a haematologically treatable disease from an untreatable one, and it must precede or accompany any bone scintigraphy. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: A renal biopsy would demonstrate the deposits and is sometimes how the diagnosis is first made, but it is invasive and carries bleeding risk that is increased in this disease by factor X deficiency and vascular fragility. A blood and urine based assay answers the same question first. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

The persistently raised troponin without a rise and fall pattern reflects ongoing myocardial injury from infiltration rather than plaque rupture, and the preserved ejection fraction with marked wall thickening and biatrial enlargement is not an ischaemic pattern. Angiography also exposes him to contrast with an already reduced filtration rate. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus, most often by a large central disc prolapse, and it is one of the few genuine neurosurgical emergencies arising from a common presentation. The features to elicit are bilateral radicular pain or weakness, saddle sensory disturbance, reduced anal tone, and bladder dysfunction that progresses from difficulty initiating micturition and loss of the sense of fullness to painless retention with overflow. Painless retention with overflow incontinence indicates established damage and carries a far worse prognosis than the earlier phase of altered urinary sensation, which is why asking about the quality of bladder sensation matters more than asking only about incontinence. A post-void residual measured by bladder scan is a quick objective addition to the examination. Red flags for other serious causes of back pain, namely fever, injected drug use, known malignancy, unexplained weight loss, age over fifty with new pain and prolonged corticosteroid use, are screened for at the same time.
key_points: Bilateral symptoms, saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone and urinary change define the syndrome
Magnetic resonance imaging is the only adequate study and is arranged emergently
Painless retention with overflow already indicates established injury
A bladder scan residual is a fast objective bedside measure
Corticosteroid before imaging belongs to malignant cord compression, not disc prolapse
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the patient can feel urine passing and whether they feel the bladder filling, because loss of urethral and filling sensation precedes retention by hours to days and identifies the window in which decompression preserves continence.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: Bilateral radicular pain with saddle sensory loss, reduced anal tone and urinary retention is a surgical emergency, and magnetic resonance imaging is the only study that shows the disc, the thecal sac and the nerve roots well enough to plan decompression. Outcomes for bladder and sexual function deteriorate with every hour of delay, so the scan is arranged now rather than booked. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Computed tomography shows bone well but resolves the disc, ligament and neural elements poorly, so a normal study cannot exclude compression and an abnormal one rarely gives the surgeon what is needed. It is the fallback only when magnetic resonance imaging is contraindicated or unavailable. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid is given ahead of imaging for malignant spinal cord compression to reduce peritumoural oedema, and the absence of any cancer history, fever, weight loss or raised inflammatory markers argues against that mechanism here. Steroid does not relieve mechanical compression by disc material. (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online)

Plain films do not image neural tissue at all and change management in acute back pain only when a fracture or gross instability is suspected. Ordering them here consumes time in a condition measured in hours. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: Conservative management is right for mechanical back pain without neurological compromise, but retention with a 620 mL residual and saddle anaesthesia are the specific findings that take this out of that category. Missing them is the commonest cause of permanent bladder dysfunction in this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Alpha one antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited disorder of the principal circulating antiprotease, and without it neutrophil elastase released in the lung destroys alveolar tissue unopposed. The severe deficiency phenotype is the commonest clinically significant form, and smoking accelerates decline so steeply that smoking status largely determines whether an affected person presents in their forties or remains well into old age. The radiological signature is panlobular emphysema with a basal predominance, which contrasts with the apical centrilobular pattern of ordinary smoking related disease and is one of the most useful discriminators available. Liver disease arises by a different mechanism, from polymerisation and accumulation of the abnormal protein within hepatocytes, and it can present as neonatal cholestasis, childhood liver disease or adult cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Diagnosis matters for the patient's own management, for smoking cessation emphasis and occupational advice, and because first degree relatives should be offered testing and counselling.
key_points: Suspect it in emphysema before fifty, in never or light smokers, and with a basal distribution
Unexplained liver disease in the patient or a relative is a strong pointer
Measure the level and phenotype, since the level rises as an acute phase reactant
Lung disease comes from unopposed elastase; liver disease from protein accumulation in hepatocytes
Test first degree relatives once a severe deficiency phenotype is confirmed
explanation.pearls: The basal panlobular distribution is the single most useful radiological clue, because ordinary smoking related emphysema is centrilobular and apical, so a lower zone predominant pattern should prompt the test even when the smoking history seems adequate to explain the disease.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: This combination investigates allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, which arises in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis and produces central bronchiectasis with mucus plugging rather than basal emphysema. She has no history of asthma and no wheeze. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Emphysema before fifty with a trivial smoking history, a lower zone rather than apical distribution, and unexplained liver disease in a first degree relative is the pattern of this inherited protease inhibitor deficiency. Phenotyping is added because the level alone can be misleading during any acute phase response. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Late presenting cystic fibrosis is a real entity but produces bronchiectasis with chronic productive cough, sinus disease and pancreatic insufficiency rather than isolated basal emphysema with a normal body mass index. Her computed tomography shows destruction rather than airway dilatation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Small vessel vasculitis of the lung presents with haemoptysis, nodules or cavities, alveolar haemorrhage and usually renal involvement, none of which is present, and it does not cause fixed airflow obstruction with basal emphysema. The absence of systemic features argues against it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

Exercise testing quantifies the limitation and distinguishes cardiac from respiratory causes of breathlessness, but the spirometry and imaging have already established that the problem is emphysema. It measures severity rather than identifying an aetiology. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterised by ventricular enlargement with a normal opening pressure and the triad of gait disturbance, urinary dysfunction and cognitive slowing, and it matters disproportionately because it is one of the few causes of dementia and gait failure that can be improved by treatment. The gait is the earliest and most responsive element, described as magnetic or apraxic, with a broad base, reduced step height, difficulty initiating and marked trouble turning. Cognitive change is typically subcortical, with slowing, apathy and reduced attention rather than the amnesia of Alzheimer disease, and urinary urgency precedes frank incontinence. Ventriculomegaly alone is not sufficient for the diagnosis because it is common in ageing brains, so response to cerebrospinal fluid removal is used to identify who will benefit from shunting. Reversible mimics including vitamin B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, neurosyphilis, cervical myelopathy and medication effects are excluded first.
key_points: Gait disturbance is the earliest feature and the most likely to improve with treatment
Cognitive impairment is subcortical slowing rather than early amnesia
Ventriculomegaly alone does not make the diagnosis
High volume cerebrospinal fluid removal with objective gait testing predicts shunt response
Exclude vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and cervical myelopathy first
explanation.pearls: Time a ten metre walk and count steps before and about two to four hours after removing thirty to fifty millilitres of cerebrospinal fluid, because a fall in walking time of more than about ten to twenty per cent is the objective threshold used to select patients for shunting.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.rationale: Carotid disease causes focal hemispheric events rather than a symmetrical gait disorder with urinary and cognitive change, and he has had no transient ischaemic attack or stroke. The study would not explain a progressive eight month syndrome. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia)

A levodopa trial is reasonable where parkinsonism is suspected, but bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor are all absent and his arm swing is preserved, so the cardinal features are not there to respond. Lower body predominant gait failure without upper limb signs points away from Parkinson disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Removing thirty to fifty millilitres of cerebrospinal fluid and measuring gait speed and step length before and several hours afterwards is the standard test of whether shunting is likely to help, and the gait component is the feature that responds best. Objective timed measurement is essential because subjective impressions of improvement are unreliable. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.rationale: Ventriculomegaly is common in older people and much of it reflects atrophy rather than a treatable disturbance of cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, so operating on the scan alone subjects many patients to a procedure with real infection, haemorrhage and over drainage risks for no benefit. The correct answer is the test that selects who will respond. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.rationale: Non convulsive status can cause fluctuating confusion but does not produce a steadily progressive gait disorder with urinary urgency over eight months. His clear orientation and preserved handling of the household accounts argue against an ongoing ictal state. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary hypertension is defined haemodynamically by a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg measured at right heart catheterisation, and the pre capillary form additionally requires a wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg with an elevated pulmonary vascular resistance. Echocardiography is the screening test and estimates right ventricular systolic pressure from the tricuspid regurgitant jet, but it systematically over and under estimates in individual patients and cannot distinguish the groups that require entirely different treatment. The classification into five groups drives management: arterial disease, disease due to left heart failure, disease due to lung disease or hypoxia, chronic thromboembolic disease, and multifactorial causes. Chronic thromboembolic disease is specifically excluded with a ventilation perfusion scan rather than a computed tomography angiogram, because the scan is more sensitive for the chronic organised thrombus that is potentially curable by surgical endarterectomy. Exertional syncope, right heart failure and a rapidly falling exercise capacity all mark high risk disease requiring urgent specialist referral.
key_points: Catheterisation defines the diagnosis; echocardiography only screens
A wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg separates pre from post capillary disease
Ventilation perfusion scanning, not computed tomography, excludes chronic thromboembolic disease
Exertional syncope indicates severely limited cardiac output and high mortality
Targeted pulmonary vasodilators are started only after haemodynamic confirmation
explanation.pearls: A ventilation perfusion scan showing mismatched segmental defects identifies chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, the one form that is potentially curable by pulmonary endarterectomy, which is why it is never omitted even when a computed tomography angiogram is clean.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Sleep apnoea can contribute to pulmonary hypertension but rarely produces pressures of this magnitude with right ventricular failure in a young non obese woman, and her partner reports no witnessed apnoea. It is a contributor to look for, not the explanation for this picture. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Serial imaging defers action in a woman who has already had exertional syncope, which is a marker of severely limited cardiac output and of high short term mortality. Untreated disease of this type progresses over months, so waiting is itself a decision against treatment. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Cardiac magnetic resonance characterises right ventricular volumes and function superbly and is used for prognostication and follow up, but it does not measure pressures directly and so cannot establish the haemodynamic diagnosis. The distinction from the correct answer is measured pressure against inferred structure. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Echocardiography estimates rather than measures pressure and cannot separate pre from post capillary disease, so catheterisation with direct measurement of mean pulmonary artery pressure, wedge pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance is required before any targeted therapy is started. Acute vasoreactivity testing at the same sitting identifies the small group who respond to calcium channel blockade. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Pulmonary vasodilators given without a confirmed haemodynamic diagnosis can precipitate pulmonary oedema if the elevation turns out to be post capillary from left heart disease, and they are prescribed in Australia through specialist centres after catheterisation. Treating before measuring risks harming the patient it is meant to help. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is an antibody mediated astrocytopathy directed at the aquaporin four water channel, and separating it from multiple sclerosis is one of the more consequential diagnostic distinctions in neurology because the treatments diverge and several multiple sclerosis therapies make it worse. The features that point away from multiple sclerosis are a cord lesion extending three or more vertebral segments, severe and often bilateral optic neuritis with poor recovery, area postrema syndrome with intractable hiccups or vomiting, absent oligoclonal bands, and a cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis above fifty cells or containing neutrophils. Attacks are more severe and recover less completely than multiple sclerosis relapses, so disability accumulates through attacks rather than through progression between them, which makes rapid attack treatment and effective relapse prevention the whole of management. Acute attacks are treated with high dose methylprednisolone and plasma exchange for severe or steroid refractory episodes. A separate antibody against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein defines an overlapping but distinct disease with a different prognosis, and is tested when the aquaporin four antibody is negative.
key_points: Three or more contiguous vertebral segments defines a longitudinally extensive cord lesion
Absent oligoclonal bands and a neutrophilic pleocytosis argue against multiple sclerosis
Interferon beta and some other multiple sclerosis therapies worsen this disease
Disability accrues through incomplete recovery from attacks rather than by progression
Test myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody when the aquaporin four antibody is negative
explanation.pearls: Intractable hiccups or vomiting lasting more than forty eight hours, from a lesion in the area postrema of the dorsal medulla, is a recognised presenting syndrome and is frequently investigated as a gastrointestinal problem for weeks before the neurological diagnosis is considered.

options.rationale: Evoked potentials can document a previous optic neuritis but her clinical history and afferent pupillary defect have already done so, and the test does not distinguish between the conditions under consideration. It would add confirmation of something already known. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Serial brain imaging is the approach to demonstrating dissemination in time in multiple sclerosis, but a cord lesion spanning six segments, a cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis of this degree with neutrophils, and absent oligoclonal bands are all atypical for that disease. Waiting three months in a relapsing condition that causes stepwise permanent disability is also unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Connective tissue disease can cause a myelitis and the panel is reasonable to include in a broad screen, but she has none of the sicca, cutaneous, mucosal or articular features that would suggest it. It does not test the leading diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

Beyond being a treatment rather than an investigation, interferon beta is specifically harmful in the condition that this presentation suggests and has been reported to precipitate relapses. Starting a multiple sclerosis therapy before distinguishing the two diseases is the central error to avoid here. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Physicians)

A longitudinally extensive cord lesion of three or more vertebral segments with optic neuritis, absent oligoclonal bands and a marked cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis is the pattern of aquaporin four antibody disease, and the cell based assay is substantially more sensitive and specific than older enzyme immunoassays. A positive result changes acute and long term treatment immediately. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Physicians)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy occurs in a substantial minority of patients with advanced cancer and carries a poor prognosis, marking disease progression as often as it marks a treatable metabolic emergency. Three mechanisms account for nearly all cases: secretion of parathyroid hormone related peptide by solid tumours, local osteolysis from bone metastases or myeloma, and excess calcitriol production in lymphoma and granulomatous disease, and the last of these is the one that responds to corticosteroid. A suppressed parathyroid hormone distinguishes these from primary hyperparathyroidism, which remains the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia overall and is usually mild and chronic rather than acute. The clinical syndrome of drowsiness, confusion, nausea, constipation, polyuria and polydipsia is explained by a calcium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that produces a vicious cycle of volume depletion and rising calcium. Management is therefore sequential: restore volume first, then give a bisphosphonate or denosumab to switch off osteoclastic resorption, then treat the underlying cancer.
key_points: Volume replacement comes before any bone directed agent
A suppressed parathyroid hormone separates malignant from primary hyperparathyroid hypercalcaemia
Bisphosphonates take two to four days to act and need renal dose adjustment
Corticosteroids work only in calcitriol mediated disease such as lymphoma or sarcoidosis
Loop diuretics are reserved for fluid overload during rehydration
explanation.pearls: Denosumab is the alternative when renal impairment precludes a bisphosphonate or when hypercalcaemia recurs despite one, because it is not renally cleared, but it carries a substantial risk of delayed hypocalcaemia and calcium must be monitored for several weeks afterwards.

options.rationale: Hypercalcaemia drives a nephrogenic concentrating defect and vomiting, so these patients are always profoundly volume depleted, and restoring circulating volume alone lowers calcium by improving glomerular filtration and urinary calcium excretion. It must precede bone directed therapy because a bisphosphonate given to a hypovolaemic patient with an acute kidney injury risks worsening renal function. (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online)

A bisphosphonate is the definitive treatment and will be given, but it takes two to four days to work, requires dose reduction in renal impairment and is relatively contraindicated until volume has been restored. Giving it first treats the number while leaving the physiology that caused it uncorrected. (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online)

Loop diuretics were once routine but worsen volume depletion and electrolyte disturbance, and they are now reserved for fluid overload developing during rehydration in a patient with cardiac or renal impairment. Using one in a hypotensive hypovolaemic patient will make both the kidney injury and the calcium worse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Corticosteroids are effective where the mechanism is excess calcitriol production, as in lymphoma, myeloma and granulomatous disease, but her suppressed parathyroid hormone with bone metastases indicates a parathyroid hormone related peptide or local osteolytic mechanism. The steroid is aimed at the wrong pathway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dialysis is reserved for life threatening hypercalcaemia with established kidney failure or heart failure that prevents adequate fluid loading, and her kidney injury is pre renal and expected to reverse with fluid. Escalating to dialysis before a saline challenge subjects her to an invasive procedure she is likely not to need. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction distinguished from ordinary drug exanthems by fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, haematological abnormality and internal organ involvement. Its defining feature is a long latency of two to eight weeks from starting the drug, far longer than the four to fourteen days of a simple morbilliform eruption, so the drug started most recently is frequently exonerated wrongly and an older one overlooked. Allopurinol, the aromatic anticonvulsants including carbamazepine, lamotrigine and phenytoin, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline account for most cases. The liver is the organ most often involved and hepatitis is the usual cause of death, while kidney, lung, heart and thyroid involvement also occur. Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses is characteristic and contributes to the prolonged and relapsing course, which is why corticosteroid is weaned slowly over weeks to months and follow up thyroid function is checked months after apparent recovery.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks separates it from a simple drug exanthem
Fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy and eosinophilia are the recognition tetrad
Liver involvement is commonest and drives the mortality
Absent mucosal erosions and a negative Nikolsky sign exclude epidermal necrolysis
Relapse on steroid weaning and late autoimmune thyroid disease are characteristic
explanation.pearls: Check thyroid function two to three months after apparent recovery, because autoimmune thyroiditis develops weeks to months later in a recognised minority of patients and is easily missed once the rash has settled and the patient has been discharged.

options.rationale: Continuing the responsible drug in a reaction with fever, organ involvement and eosinophilia allows it to progress, and the mortality of this syndrome is around ten per cent, driven largely by liver failure. Antihistamine and topical treatment is the management of a simple morbilliform drug eruption, which this is not. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Withdrawal of the causative drug plus systemic corticosteroid is the standard treatment when there is significant organ involvement, and his transaminases at seven times the upper limit qualify. Monitoring continues for weeks after the drug is stopped because relapse and late thyroiditis are characteristic. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Burns unit transfer is the pathway for epidermal necrolysis, which presents with painful dusky skin, mucosal erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign, all of which are explicitly absent here. His rash is inflammatory rather than necrolytic and his skin barrier is intact. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Immunoglobulin has been used in refractory cases and in epidermal necrolysis but has no established first line role in this syndrome, and it carries thrombotic and renal risks. It would be considered only after corticosteroid failure. (Source: National Blood Authority Australia)

Cellulitis is unilateral, tender and sharply demarcated rather than a symmetrical confluent eruption with facial oedema, and it does not cause eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes or hepatitis. Adding a new beta lactam during a severe drug reaction also risks a second sensitisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand, and unlike bisphosphonates it is not incorporated into bone, so its effect disappears entirely once dosing stops. The result is a rebound in osteoclast activity that overshoots baseline, producing rapid loss of the bone mineral density gained and a characteristic pattern of multiple vertebral fractures appearing within one to two years of the last injection. The risk is highest in those who had vertebral fractures before treatment and in those treated for longer, and a single late or missed dose is enough to begin the process. This makes denosumab a treatment that should not be started unless continuity can be assured, and it means a missed appointment carries a clinical consequence rather than an administrative one. When denosumab is deliberately stopped, a bisphosphonate is given as follow on therapy, usually starting around six months after the last injection, and bone turnover markers or densitometry are used to check that the rebound has been suppressed.
key_points: The denosumab effect ends completely when dosing stops, unlike a bisphosphonate
Rebound produces multiple vertebral fractures within one to two years
A single missed or delayed dose can initiate the rebound
Follow on bisphosphonate is mandatory whenever denosumab is ceased
Anabolic therapy given straight after denosumab without cover loses hip bone density
explanation.pearls: Denosumab injections are due every six months and are given within a four week window, so a patient who is more than a month overdue needs active recall rather than being left until the next routine visit.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: Supplements support but do not substitute for antiresorptive therapy, and a woman who has already sustained two vertebral fractures has severe established disease with a high risk of further fractures within the next twelve months. Doing nothing active is the option with the highest short term fracture risk. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

Fracture healing is not impaired by antiresorptive therapy and delaying treatment prolongs exactly the window of accelerated bone turnover that produced these fractures. The rebound is time limited but intense, so the delay is the harm. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

Stopping denosumab releases a burst of osteoclast activity that produces rapid bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures within one to two years, and the treatment is to restore antiresorptive suppression without further delay. The lasting fix is that denosumab is never simply ceased, and a bisphosphonate is given as follow on therapy whenever it is discontinued. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

Vertebral augmentation has not shown consistent benefit over sham in randomised trials and is considered only for intractable pain unresponsive to conservative measures. It also addresses the two fractures already sustained rather than the accelerated bone loss that will cause the next ones. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: Anabolic therapy has a place in severe osteoporosis with multiple fractures, but given immediately after denosumab and without antiresorptive cover it produces transient loss of hip bone density because it amplifies the already elevated turnover. The sequence of agents matters as much as the choice. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

explanation.summary: Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are a single disease separated by the extent of epidermal detachment, under ten per cent for the former, over thirty per cent for the latter, and the overlap band between them. Onset is typically one to four weeks after starting the responsible drug, with the aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, nevirapine and oxicam anti inflammatories the commonest culprits. A prodrome of fever, sore throat and painful eyes precedes the rash by one to three days and is routinely mistaken for a viral illness. Lamotrigine is a particular risk when titrated faster than the recommended schedule or combined with valproate, which inhibits its metabolism, so titration errors are a recurring cause. Mortality is predicted by the SCORTEN score using age, malignancy, heart rate, detached surface area, urea, bicarbonate and glucose, and early withdrawal of the causative drug is one of the few interventions with a clear survival benefit.
key_points: Detachment under ten per cent, ten to thirty per cent and over thirty per cent define the spectrum
Latency is one to four weeks and a febrile prodrome precedes the rash
Mucosal involvement at two or more sites with a positive Nikolsky sign is characteristic
Stopping the drug early is one of the few interventions that improves survival
Ophthalmology review within days prevents permanent ocular scarring
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine must be titrated slowly over at least six weeks, and the starting dose is halved when it is combined with valproate, because valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles its concentration.

options.rationale: Ambulatory management is unsafe with twelve per cent epidermal detachment, since fluid loss, hypothermia, infection and ocular scarring all progress over the following days. The role of systemic corticosteroid in epidermal necrolysis also remains contested, unlike its accepted role in the eosinophilic drug syndrome. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Topical treatment is appropriate for inflammatory drug eruptions with an intact epidermis, whereas she has lost her skin barrier across a large area and needs the fluid, thermal, analgesic and ocular care of a specialist unit. Applying steroid to denuded dermis does not address any of those problems. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is the near diagnosis to exclude, but it occurs almost entirely in young children, spares the mucosae and splits the epidermis at a very superficial level without the dusky targetoid macules seen here. Prophylactic antibiotics are also avoided in epidermal necrolysis because they select resistant organisms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Immediate withdrawal of the causative drug improves survival, and detachment of this extent requires the fluid balance, temperature control, analgesia, wound handling and ophthalmic review that only a specialist unit provides. Ocular involvement in particular causes permanent scarring and vision loss unless assessed within the first days. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Biopsy confirms the level of the split and is usually performed, but it is done alongside rather than before the decisions that determine survival. Waiting for histology delays drug withdrawal and transfer in a condition whose mortality tracks with how quickly the drug is stopped. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

explanation.summary: Acute intermittent porphyria is the commonest of the acute hepatic porphyrias and results from partial deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase, so that induction of hepatic haem synthesis floods the pathway with neurotoxic porphyrin precursors. Attacks are provoked by anything that induces the rate limiting enzyme, principally drugs including sulfonamides, barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin and progestogens, along with fasting or carbohydrate restriction, alcohol, infection and the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. The attack is neurovisceral rather than cutaneous: severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and no peritonism, autonomic overactivity with tachycardia and hypertension, a predominantly motor and often proximal neuropathy that can ascend to respiratory failure, hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuresis, and psychiatric disturbance ranging from anxiety to frank psychosis. Patients are characteristically investigated repeatedly and frequently undergo a negative laparotomy or laparoscopy before the diagnosis is considered, so a history of recurrent unexplained abdominal pain with normal imaging is itself a diagnostic clue. Treatment is withdrawal of the precipitant, high carbohydrate intake, and intravenous haem arginate, with careful attention to using only drugs known to be safe in porphyria.
key_points: Pain out of proportion with a soft abdomen and normal imaging is the hallmark
Autonomic features, motor neuropathy, hyponatraemia and psychiatric change complete the syndrome
Sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, rifampicin, progestogens, fasting and alcohol precipitate attacks
Urinary porphobilinogen during the attack is the diagnostic test and the sample must be light protected
Treatment is removal of the precipitant, carbohydrate loading and intravenous haem arginate
explanation.pearls: Every drug prescribed during and after an attack must be checked against a porphyria safe list, and among the analgesics morphine and paracetamol are safe while among the antiemetics ondansetron is safe but metoclopramide is a recognised precipitant.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: A normal contrast study three days into the illness, a soft abdomen without peritonism and a previously normal laparoscopy together make an intra abdominal structural cause very unlikely. Repeating the scan will not explain the hyponatraemia, the hypertension or the motor weakness. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.rationale: Lead poisoning is the closest mimic, causing colicky abdominal pain with a motor neuropathy, but it produces a microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling and does not cause a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and her haemoglobin and film are normal. It is also not precipitated by starting a drug or by fasting. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

options.rationale: An acute motor neuropathy makes Guillain Barre syndrome a reasonable thought, but that illness is ascending and predominantly distal, does not begin with four days of abdominal pain, and does not cause hypertension with hyponatraemia. Her weakness is proximal and upper limb predominant, which is the opposite of the usual pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Paired osmolalities would confirm inappropriate antidiuresis but stop at describing a mechanism that is itself a manifestation of the underlying disease rather than an answer. Investigating the sodium in isolation leaves the pain, the hypertension and the weakness unexplained. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

Recurrent severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging, autonomic features of tachycardia and hypertension, a motor neuropathy, hyponatraemia and psychiatric disturbance, all following a sulfonamide and a period of carbohydrate restriction, is the acute neurovisceral attack of a hepatic porphyria. Porphobilinogen rises markedly during an attack and the sample is shielded from light because the porphyrins degrade on exposure. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in an adult man or a postmenopausal woman is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and the absence of visible bleeding or altered bowel habit is expected rather than reassuring. Right sided colonic tumours characteristically present exactly this way, with occult blood loss and anaemia rather than obstruction, because the caecum is capacious and the stool is liquid there. Bidirectional endoscopy is the standard investigation, because upper and lower tract lesions are both common and synchronous pathology occurs. Coeliac serology should be checked, as here, since coeliac disease is a treatable non bleeding cause. Iron replacement is started at the same time as referral, never instead of it.
key_points: Iron deficiency anaemia in men and postmenopausal women mandates investigation of the gastrointestinal tract.
Right sided colonic tumours bleed occultly without altering bowel habit or producing visible blood.
Bidirectional endoscopy is required because upper and lower lesions are both common and may coexist.
Faecal occult blood testing adds nothing once iron deficiency anaemia is established.
Coeliac serology should be checked as a treatable non bleeding cause of iron deficiency.
explanation.pearls: Never accept a normal rectal examination and a normal bowel habit as a reason to skip colonoscopy in a man with iron deficiency anaemia, because a caecal carcinoma bleeds into liquid stool in a capacious lumen and typically declares itself only as breathlessness and a low ferritin.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia
Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.rationale: Iron replacement is certainly needed and will correct the haemoglobin, and giving it without investigating the cause allows a colonic malignancy to progress while the blood count normalises and falsely reassures both of you. Replacement and investigation proceed together rather than one instead of the other. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.rationale: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man or a postmenopausal woman is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and bidirectional endoscopy is the standard investigation because a right sided colonic carcinoma can bleed occultly for months without altering bowel habit or producing visible blood. His family history of colectomy in his sixties raises that risk further, and iron is started at the same time rather than afterwards. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.rationale: Faecal occult blood testing is a population screening tool for asymptomatic people, and using it in someone who already has established iron deficiency anaemia adds nothing, because the anaemia is itself the evidence of blood loss. A negative result would not exclude a tumour and would delay endoscopy. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.rationale: Electrophoresis distinguishes thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency in an unexplained microcytosis, and that question is already answered here by a ferritin of 7 micrograms/L with a transferrin saturation of 6 percent. Thalassaemia trait also does not deplete iron stores. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.rationale: Intravenous iron is appropriate where oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, or where rapid correction is needed, and the route of replacement is not the issue in this case. Whichever route is chosen, the underlying source of loss still has to be found. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

explanation.summary: Triple assessment of a breast lump comprises clinical examination, imaging and tissue sampling, and its central principle is concordance: if any component raises suspicion, the workup continues until that suspicion is resolved by histology. This woman has a firm irregular tethered mass, which is a clinically suspicious finding regardless of what the imaging shows. Mammographic sensitivity is substantially reduced in heterogeneously dense breast tissue, and invasive lobular carcinoma characteristically infiltrates in single file without forming a discrete mass on either mammography or ultrasound. A normal screening mammogram eighteen months earlier does not exclude an interval cancer. Core biopsy rather than fine needle aspiration is the sampling method, because it distinguishes invasive from in situ disease and provides grade and receptor status.
key_points: Triple assessment requires concordance, and any suspicious component mandates tissue sampling.
Mammographic sensitivity is substantially reduced in dense breast tissue.
Invasive lobular carcinoma may infiltrate without forming a discrete mass on mammography or ultrasound.
Core biopsy is preferred over fine needle aspiration because it provides grade, invasion status and receptor status.
Serum tumour markers have no role in diagnosing early breast cancer.
explanation.pearls: Refer a clinically suspicious breast lump for core biopsy even when mammography and ultrasound are both reported as normal, because discordance is resolved by histology and invasive lobular carcinoma in dense tissue is the classic cancer that both imaging modalities miss.

sources.label: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.rationale: Triple assessment requires clinical examination, imaging and tissue sampling to be concordant, and when any one component is suspicious the assessment is incomplete until tissue has been obtained regardless of how reassuring the others are. Mammographic sensitivity falls substantially in dense breast tissue and some cancers, particularly invasive lobular carcinoma, infiltrate diffusely without forming a discrete sonographic mass, so a negative scan cannot override a tethered irregular lump. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.rationale: Interval review is appropriate for a clinically benign finding such as a soft mobile lump in a younger woman with concordant normal imaging. Discordance between a suspicious examination and negative imaging is the specific situation in which reassurance is unsafe, and three months allows nodal progression. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.rationale: Tomosynthesis does improve cancer detection in dense tissue and would be a sensible adjunct at the time of assessment rather than a reason to wait half a year. Repeating imaging also cannot substitute for the histology that a palpable suspicious mass requires. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.rationale: Fine needle aspiration can confirm malignancy but cannot distinguish invasive carcinoma from ductal carcinoma in situ, and it does not provide receptor status or grade, which now guide neoadjuvant decisions. Core biopsy has superseded it as the sampling method for a solid breast mass. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.rationale: Serum markers such as CA15-3 have no role in the diagnosis of breast cancer because they lack both sensitivity and specificity in early disease, and they are used only for monitoring established metastatic disease. A normal result would wrongly reassure everyone involved. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

explanation.summary: Most syncope is reflex and benign, so the clinical task is to identify the minority in whom it signals a risk of sudden death. The high risk features present here are syncope occurring during exertion rather than after it, complete absence of a prodrome, recurrence, and a family history of sudden death under 50 years. Examination adds a murmur that becomes louder on standing from squatting and on Valsalva, which indicates dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction because reduced preload worsens it, in contrast to aortic stenosis where the murmur softens. The electrocardiogram showing left ventricular hypertrophy with deep lateral T wave inversion supports hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Brief myoclonic jerking during syncope is common and does not indicate epilepsy, and these patients need admission, telemetry and echocardiography rather than outpatient investigation.
key_points: Syncope during exertion, without prodrome, or with a family history of sudden death is high risk.
A murmur that increases with reduced preload indicates dynamic outflow obstruction rather than valvular stenosis.
Left ventricular hypertrophy with deep lateral T wave inversion suggests hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Brief stiffening and jerking occur commonly in syncope and do not indicate a seizure.
Tongue biting, incontinence and prolonged postictal confusion distinguish a genuine seizure from syncope.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the collapse happened during exertion or after it, because syncope during exertion points to a structural or arrhythmic cause needing admission, whereas syncope immediately after stopping exercise is usually reflex and benign.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Reflex syncope is common and is managed this way, and it is identified by a prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating or visual greying, by an upright provoking situation such as prolonged standing or venepuncture, and by a normal heart and electrocardiogram. Syncope occurring during exertion without any prodrome is the opposite pattern and is never attributed to a reflex cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Tilt testing is used for recurrent unexplained syncope where a reflex mechanism is suspected and the cardiac workup is clean. Using it in a man with exertional syncope, a family history of sudden death and an abnormal electrocardiogram risks a falsely reassuring positive result while he remains at risk of sudden death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Brief stiffening with a few jerks is common in syncope of any cause once cerebral perfusion falls, and it is not evidence of epilepsy. A genuine seizure is suggested by tongue biting, incontinence and postictal confusion lasting minutes, and he recovered fully within thirty seconds. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Syncope during exertion with no prodrome, a family history of sudden death under 50, a murmur that increases with reduced preload and an electrocardiogram showing hypertrophy with lateral T wave inversion together identify a structural cardiac cause with a real risk of ventricular arrhythmia. Admission with telemetry protects him while echocardiography defines the outflow tract and wall thickness, and this pathway also captures the family screening that a heritable cardiomyopathy requires. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Ambulatory monitoring is reasonable for infrequent palpitations or for syncope judged to be low risk, and a 24 hour recording is very unlikely to capture an event that has occurred three times in a year. Sending him home while awaiting the result leaves him unmonitored during the interval in which he is most at risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Incidental pulmonary nodules are found frequently as computed tomography use increases, and management is determined by nodule size, attenuation, morphology and the patient's risk of lung cancer. Comparison with any earlier imaging is the single most valuable first step because documented stability over two years effectively excludes malignancy in a solid nodule, and here no earlier imaging exists. For a solid nodule of this size in a person with a smoking history, interval computed tomography surveillance is recommended, with the interval determined by diameter and risk. Positron emission tomography is unreliable below about 8 to 10 mm because of partial volume effects, and biopsy of a 7 mm target has a high non diagnostic rate. Subsolid and part solid nodules follow different and longer surveillance schedules because indolent adenocarcinoma can grow very slowly.
key_points: Nodule size, attenuation, margin morphology and smoking history together determine management.
Documented stability of a solid nodule over two years effectively excludes malignancy.
Positron emission tomography is unreliable below about 8 to 10 mm because of partial volume effects.
Spiculated margins, upper lobe location and larger size increase the probability of malignancy.
Subsolid and part solid nodules require longer surveillance because indolent adenocarcinoma grows slowly.
explanation.pearls: Hunt for any previous chest imaging before arranging surveillance for an incidental nodule, because two years of documented stability on an old scan resolves a solid nodule immediately and spares the patient a further two years of interval computed tomography.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy is used for larger or more suspicious peripheral lesions where a tissue diagnosis will direct treatment, and at 7 mm the target is small enough that the non diagnostic rate is high while the pneumothorax risk is unchanged. Sampling is not justified before surveillance has shown whether the nodule is growing. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

Functional imaging is valuable for nodules above about 8 to 10 mm, and below that size its spatial resolution produces frequent false negatives because partial volume effects understate uptake. A negative scan at 7 mm would provide false reassurance rather than information. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

Bronchoscopic sampling is suited to central lesions and to mediastinal nodal staging, and the yield for a small peripheral nodule without a bronchus leading to it is poor. There is also no nodal disease here to stage. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

Discharge without follow up is appropriate for a nodule below about 5 mm in a low risk person, or for one with benign features such as dense central or laminated calcification or macroscopic fat. A 7 mm solid nodule in a former smoker with a substantial history sits above the threshold at which surveillance is recommended. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

A solid nodule of this size carries a low but not negligible malignancy risk, and growth over time is the most useful discriminator available, so serial thin section computed tomography at intervals set by size and risk is the accepted approach. Surveillance continues for around two years because stability of a solid nodule over that period effectively excludes malignancy, whereas any interval growth prompts escalation to functional imaging or sampling. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when rapid cell death releases intracellular contents, producing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and consequent hypocalcaemia, with acute kidney injury from urate and calcium phosphate deposition in the tubules. Risk is determined by tumour bulk, proliferation rate, baseline lactate dehydrogenase and urate, and pre-existing renal impairment, and this man is high risk on every count. Allopurinol prevents new urate formation and suits lower risk patients, whereas rasburicase enzymatically degrades urate already present and is indicated for high risk disease. Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase status must be established first because rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and causes severe haemolysis in deficient individuals, who are more commonly of Mediterranean, African or South East Asian ancestry. Urinary alkalinisation has been abandoned because it promotes calcium phosphate precipitation, and vigorous hydration with close biochemical monitoring remains the foundation of prevention.
key_points: The metabolic signature is hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and hypocalcaemia.
Allopurinol prevents new urate formation while rasburicase degrades urate already present.
Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is a contraindication to rasburicase because of severe haemolysis.
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended because it promotes calcium phosphate deposition.
Vigorous intravenous hydration with frequent biochemical monitoring is the foundation of prevention.
explanation.pearls: Check glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase status before giving rasburicase, because the drug generates hydrogen peroxide and causes life threatening haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in deficient patients, who are disproportionately of Mediterranean, African or South East Asian ancestry.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase and so prevents the formation of new urate, which makes it appropriate prophylaxis for low and intermediate risk disease. It cannot remove the urate that has already accumulated, and oral fluids are inadequate for a patient whose urate is already raised with a rising creatinine. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Dialysis is used for established tumour lysis syndrome with refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload or oliguric renal failure. Inserting a line and dialysing prophylactically exposes him to procedural risk when pharmacological prevention has not yet been tried. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Urinary alkalinisation was standard practice and has been abandoned because raising the urinary pH increases the deposition of calcium phosphate in the renal tubules, worsening nephrocalcinosis in a patient who is already hyperphosphataemic. It also exacerbates the hypocalcaemia. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Delay would be reasonable for a slow growing tumour requiring optimisation, and a high grade lymphoma with this proliferation index can double in days, so waiting increases both the tumour burden and the eventual lysis risk. The metabolic risk is managed alongside treatment rather than by postponing it. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

Bulky rapidly proliferating disease with a markedly raised lactate dehydrogenase, an elevated urate and impaired renal function places him at high risk, and rasburicase converts existing urate to the far more soluble allantoin rather than merely preventing further production. Vigorous intravenous hydration to maintain high urine output is given alongside, and confirming glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase status first matters because rasburicase causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in deficient patients. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

explanation.summary: Hepatitis B is never fully eradicated after infection, because covalently closed circular viral DNA persists in hepatocyte nuclei and is held in check by immune surveillance rather than removed. A surface antigen negative, core antibody positive pattern therefore represents resolved rather than absent infection, and immunosuppression can allow reverse seroconversion with reappearance of surface antigen and a viral load. Rituximab and other B cell depleting agents carry among the highest reactivation risks, and the resulting hepatitis may be severe or fatal. All patients should be screened for surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody before immunosuppression, and those at high risk receive entecavir or tenofovir prophylaxis started before treatment and continued for at least twelve months afterwards. Monitoring alone is reserved for low risk regimens, because viral load rises before transaminases do.
key_points: Covalently closed circular viral DNA persists in hepatocytes for life, so infection is controlled rather than cleared.
Core antibody positivity with a negative surface antigen indicates resolved infection at risk of reactivation.
Rituximab and other B cell depleting agents carry the highest reactivation risk.
Prophylaxis starts before immunosuppression and continues at least twelve months after the last dose.
Screening before immunosuppression should include surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody.
explanation.pearls: Order hepatitis B core antibody rather than surface antigen alone before any B cell depleting therapy, because a patient who has cleared surface antigen still harbours intranuclear viral DNA and rituximab can drive reverse seroconversion into a fulminant hepatitis.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Hepatitis B

options.rationale: A negative surface antigen with positive core antibody means the virus is controlled by the immune system rather than eradicated, because covalently closed circular viral DNA persists in hepatocyte nuclei indefinitely. Removing B cell mediated immune control is precisely what allows that reservoir to reactivate. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.rationale: Vaccination generates surface antibody, which he already has at a protective level, and it does nothing about the intranuclear viral reservoir that reactivation arises from. Response to vaccination is also poor once chemotherapy has begun. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.rationale: Rituximab depletes B cells and carries one of the highest risks of hepatitis B reactivation of any agent, including reverse seroconversion in people whose surface antigen is negative and core antibody positive, and the resulting hepatitis can be fulminant and fatal. Entecavir or tenofovir started before the first cycle prevents this and is continued for at least twelve months after the last dose, because the risk persists while B cell recovery is incomplete. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.rationale: Monitoring with on demand treatment is an accepted strategy only for patients at low reactivation risk, and it fails with rituximab because the viral load rises before the transaminases and the hepatitis can progress to liver failure faster than a monthly test detects. Waiting for enzyme rise means waiting for hepatocyte destruction to have begun. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.rationale: Rituximab substantially improves survival in this lymphoma and omitting it would trade a curable cancer outcome for a risk that effective prophylaxis reduces to a very low level. The hepatitis risk is managed pharmacologically rather than by compromising the oncological regimen. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

explanation.summary: Elective repair of an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm is offered at a maximum diameter of 5.5 cm in men, at around 5.0 cm in women, for expansion exceeding 1 cm per year, or for symptoms or tenderness regardless of size. Below those thresholds the annual rupture risk is lower than the perioperative mortality of repair, so surveillance is the correct approach, with ultrasound intervals shortening as the diameter increases. This man is at 4.8 cm with 0.2 cm of growth over eleven months, which is well within the surveillance range. The most effective intervention available to him is smoking cessation, which slows expansion and reduces rupture risk, and he has already achieved it. Optimising blood pressure and lipids matters because most patients with an aneurysm die of coronary disease rather than of rupture.
key_points: Repair thresholds are 5.5 cm in men, around 5.0 cm in women, growth over 1 cm per year, or symptoms.
Below the threshold the perioperative mortality of repair exceeds the annual rupture risk.
Smoking cessation is the single most effective measure for slowing aneurysm expansion.
Beta blockers have been trialled for expansion and do not slow it.
Most patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm die of coronary disease rather than of rupture.
explanation.pearls: Treat an incidentally found aneurysm below 5.5 cm as a cardiovascular diagnosis rather than a surgical one, because the patient is statistically far likelier to die of coronary disease than of rupture, and smoking cessation does more to slow expansion than any drug that has been trialled.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.rationale: Urgent repair is indicated for a symptomatic, tender or ruptured aneurysm, and he has no pain and no tenderness with a stable growth rate. Operating at 4.8 cm exposes him to perioperative mortality that exceeds his current annual rupture risk. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.rationale: Symptom triggered imaging fails because the first symptom of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is frequently rupture, which carries a mortality of around eighty percent when all prehospital deaths are counted. Surveillance exists precisely because the condition is silent until it is catastrophic. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery
