options.rationale: Repair is offered at 5.5 cm in men, for growth exceeding 1 cm in a year, or for symptoms, and at 4.8 cm growing 0.2 cm over eleven months he meets none of these, so surveillance at intervals of around six months is correct. The active part of management is cardiovascular, since smoking cessation is the single most effective measure for slowing expansion and statin and antihypertensive treatment address the coronary disease that is the commonest cause of death in these patients. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.rationale: Beta blockade was studied for this purpose on the rationale of reducing aortic wall stress and randomised trials showed no reduction in expansion rate or rupture. It remains appropriate if indicated for another reason such as ischaemic heart disease, which he does not have. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.rationale: Computed tomography angiography is the planning study once the repair threshold is reached, as it defines neck anatomy and iliac access for stent grafting. Performing it eight months before he is likely to need it adds contrast and radiation exposure without changing anything today. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

explanation.summary: Persistent or recurrent symptoms after a coeliac diagnosis are common, and continuing gluten exposure accounts for the large majority of cases. Serology is the most useful objective guide: antibody titres should fall progressively and normalise within about twelve months of strict adherence, so a plateau or a rise indicates ongoing exposure even when the patient believes the diet is strict. Common sources are cross contamination in shared kitchens and restaurants, and gluten in sauces, thickeners, medications and supplements, none of which emerge without a detailed dietary review. Refractory coeliac disease and enteropathy associated T cell lymphoma are important but rare, and both are pursued only after adherence has been verified or when alarm features are present. Coexisting functional gut symptoms are considered once exposure has been excluded.
key_points: Ongoing gluten exposure explains most persistent symptoms after a coeliac diagnosis.
Antibody titres should fall progressively and normalise within about twelve months of strict adherence.
A plateau or rise in serology is objective evidence of continuing exposure.
Refractory coeliac disease requires demonstrated persistent villous atrophy with verified adherence.
Weight loss, fever, night sweats, pain or falling albumin are alarm features prompting imaging for lymphoma.
explanation.pearls: Plot the coeliac serology trend rather than reading a single value, because a titre that falls and then plateaus or rises is objective evidence of continuing gluten exposure and sends the patient to a dietitian rather than to repeat endoscopy.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.rationale: Continuing gluten exposure, usually inadvertent, accounts for the great majority of persistent symptoms after diagnosis, and a serology that has plateaued and then risen rather than normalising is the objective marker of ongoing exposure. Cross contamination in restaurant kitchens, shared toasters and gluten in sauces, medications and supplements are not identifiable without a specialist dietary history, which is why this precedes any further investigation. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.rationale: Refractory coeliac disease is treated with corticosteroid and is diagnosed only after persistent villous atrophy is demonstrated on repeat biopsy with strict adherence confirmed, which has not been established here. It is also rare, affecting a very small proportion of patients, and her rising serology points to exposure rather than to true refractoriness. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.rationale: Enteropathy associated T cell lymphoma is a recognised complication and is sought when there are alarm features such as weight loss, fever, night sweats, abdominal pain or a falling albumin. She has none of these and her weight, albumin and inflammatory markers are all normal. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.rationale: Functional gut symptoms genuinely coexist with coeliac disease and a low fermentable carbohydrate approach helps those patients, and it is considered only once ongoing gluten exposure has been excluded. Layering a second restrictive diet onto an incompletely implemented first one makes both harder to follow. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.rationale: Repeat biopsy has a place in assessing mucosal healing and is essential before diagnosing refractory disease, and performed while adherence is unverified it cannot distinguish ongoing exposure from true refractoriness. The dietary assessment should come first so the biopsy, if still needed, can be interpreted. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

explanation.summary: Hypertriglyceridaemia is the third commonest cause of acute pancreatitis after gallstones and alcohol, and the risk becomes appreciable above about 10 mmol/L and substantial above 20 mmol/L, when chylomicrons obstruct pancreatic capillaries and liberated free fatty acids injure acinar cells. Grossly lipaemic serum, eruptive xanthomas and a family history point to an underlying genetic predisposition unmasked by acquired factors, which here are alcohol, poorly controlled diabetes and obesity. Fibrates are the most effective triglyceride lowering drugs and are first line for preventing recurrence, with omega 3 fatty acids as a possible adjunct. Statins lower triglycerides only modestly and are prescribed for cardiovascular risk rather than for pancreatitis prevention. Controlling the acquired drivers is as important as the drug, because the genetic component alone rarely produces these concentrations.
key_points: Pancreatitis risk rises above about 10 mmol/L and becomes substantial above 20 mmol/L.
Eruptive xanthomas and lipaemic serum indicate chylomicronaemia.
Fibrates lower triglycerides by up to half and are first line for preventing recurrence.
Statins lower triglycerides only modestly and address cardiovascular rather than pancreatitis risk.
Alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes, obesity and certain drugs are the acquired drivers that must be corrected.
explanation.pearls: Treat the alcohol and the diabetes with the same urgency as the fibrate after hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, because a genetic predisposition rarely produces a triglyceride concentration above 20 mmol/L without an acquired driver, and the drug alone will not keep him below the threshold for recurrence.

options.rationale: Fibrates activate peroxisome proliferator activated receptor alpha and are the most effective agents for lowering triglycerides, reducing them by up to half, which is what is needed to move him below the threshold at which pancreatitis recurs. The drug alone is insufficient because alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes and dietary fat are each driving the hypertriglyceridaemia, so treating all four factors together is what prevents another episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Statins are the cornerstone of cardiovascular risk reduction and lower triglycerides only modestly, typically by ten to thirty percent, which is insufficient at this concentration. He will need one for cardiovascular protection, but it does not address the pancreatitis risk that is the immediate problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption and lowers low density lipoprotein cholesterol with minimal effect on triglycerides. It addresses the wrong lipid fraction for a man whose risk comes from chylomicronaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Apheresis removes triglycerides rapidly and has a role in severe acute hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, particularly with organ failure, and in refractory familial chylomicronaemia. As ongoing outpatient therapy it is invasive and resource intensive when modifiable drivers have not yet been addressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Gallstones are the commonest cause of pancreatitis in Australia and cholecystectomy would be correct if they were present, and his ultrasound shows no stones and no biliary dilatation. Operating would not address the triglyceride concentration that caused this episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotics that block the dopamine D2 receptor remove the tonic inhibition of lactotrophs by hypothalamic dopamine and raise prolactin, with risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride the worst offenders while aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine are comparatively sparing. The difficulty is that drug induced elevation and a prolactinoma present identically with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea, so the magnitude of the elevation is used as a guide. Drug induced levels usually remain below about 2 000 mIU/L, and levels above that range warrant pituitary imaging before the elevation is attributed to medication. Prolonged hypo-oestrogenism carries real consequences for bone density, so the problem cannot simply be accepted. Management requires collaboration with the psychiatrist, since both switching the antipsychotic and adding a dopamine agonist risk destabilising the underlying illness.
key_points: Dopamine D2 blockade removes tonic inhibition of lactotrophs and raises prolactin.
Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin most, while aripiprazole and quetiapine spare it.
Drug induced elevation usually stays below about 2 000 mIU/L, and higher levels warrant pituitary imaging.
Macroprolactin causes spuriously raised results but does not cause galactorrhoea or amenorrhoea.
Prolonged hypo-oestrogenism from hyperprolactinaemia accelerates bone loss and must be addressed.
explanation.pearls: Image the pituitary rather than blaming the antipsychotic when prolactin exceeds about 2 000 mIU/L, and never stop or add to a psychotropic regimen unilaterally, because both switching the agent and starting a dopamine agonist can precipitate relapse of a psychotic illness that has been stable for a year.

options.rationale: Antipsychotic induced elevation usually sits below about 2 000 mIU/L, so a level above that range does not safely exclude a coexisting adenoma and imaging is required before the elevation is attributed to the drug. The psychiatrist must be involved because the alternatives, switching to a prolactin sparing agent such as aripiprazole or adding a dopamine agonist, both carry a risk of destabilising a psychotic illness that has been well controlled for over a year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Withdrawing the antipsychotic does test the hypothesis, and stopping it unilaterally in a woman whose psychotic illness has been stable for fourteen months risks relapse with far greater consequences than amenorrhoea. Any change to her antipsychotic belongs to a shared decision with the prescriber. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dopamine agonists lower prolactin effectively and are first line for a true lactotroph adenoma, and in a patient on an antipsychotic they directly oppose the dopamine blockade that is treating her illness and can precipitate psychotic relapse. They are used in this setting only with psychiatric agreement and after imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Attributing it to the drug without imaging accepts a diagnosis that the level does not support, and it also leaves prolonged hypo-oestrogenism untreated, which causes accelerated bone loss in a woman of 28. An expected adverse effect still requires management when it is causing harm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Macroprolactin is a biologically inactive complex that causes a spuriously high result and is worth excluding in an asymptomatic patient with an unexplained elevation. She has galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and a low oestradiol, which demonstrate that the circulating prolactin is biologically active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Deprescribing in frail older people works best when it is mechanism driven rather than list driven, starting with the drug most closely linked to the presenting harm. This woman has symptomatic orthostatic hypotension with a 36 mmHg systolic drop that reproduces her symptoms, and her falls all occur on standing. Alpha one blockers such as doxazosin and prazosin directly prevent the reflex vasoconstriction that maintains blood pressure on standing, which makes them the most potent orthostatic offenders among common antihypertensives. The temporal association with its introduction three months ago and the weakness of its indication strengthen the case further. Several of her other medicines are legitimate deprescribing targets and should be addressed sequentially afterwards, changing one drug at a time so that the effect of each withdrawal can be judged.
key_points: Alpha one blockers impair reflex vasoconstriction and are potent causes of orthostatic hypotension.
A symptomatic postural drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic defines orthostatic hypotension.
Deprescribing should start with the drug most closely linked to the presenting harm.
Temporal association between starting a drug and the onset of symptoms is strong supporting evidence.
Withdraw one drug at a time so that the effect of each change can be attributed.
explanation.pearls: Measure lying and standing blood pressure before choosing which medicine to stop in a falling older patient, and start with the alpha blocker when there is a symptomatic postural drop, because alpha one blockade abolishes the reflex vasoconstriction that other antihypertensives leave intact.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.rationale: Statins are frequently reviewed in frail older people and may reasonably be stopped where life expectancy is short or the indication is primary prevention. They do not cause orthostatic hypotension, so withdrawing the statin would not address the mechanism producing her falls. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.rationale: Long term proton pump inhibitor use without a continuing indication is a legitimate deprescribing target, associated with hip fracture, hypomagnesaemia and enteric infection. It is not a cause of postural blood pressure drop and is therefore not the first priority in a patient falling because of orthostatic symptoms. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.rationale: Amlodipine contributes to her overall blood pressure lowering and is a reasonable later target as her regimen is simplified. Dihydropyridines cause considerably less orthostatic hypotension than alpha blockade because they do not impair the reflex vasoconstriction that maintains pressure on standing. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.rationale: Alpha one blockade prevents the peripheral vasoconstriction that normally maintains blood pressure on standing, making it the drug most specifically responsible for a symptomatic 36 mmHg systolic drop, and the temporal link to its introduction three months ago matches the onset of her falls. It also has the weakest indication in the list, having been started for nocturia in a woman for whom safer alternatives exist. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.rationale: Benzodiazepine withdrawal is an important goal in anyone over 65 who is falling and this drug should certainly come out in due course. It is taken only intermittently and at night, whereas her falls occur on standing during the day with a reproducible postural drop, which points to a different mechanism. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

explanation.summary: Amiodarone contains a large iodine load and is highly lipophilic, and it causes thyrotoxicosis by two mechanisms that require opposite treatments. Type 1 is iodine induced excess synthesis in a gland with pre-existing pathology such as a nodular goitre or latent Graves disease, and it shows normal or increased vascularity on colour flow Doppler with often positive antibodies, responding to thionamides with or without perchlorate. Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis in which preformed hormone leaks from a damaged gland, showing absent vascularity, negative antibodies, no goitre and often a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and it responds to corticosteroid. Mixed forms occur and are treated with both. Radioiodine is ineffective because the iodine load suppresses uptake, and stopping amiodarone produces no rapid benefit given a half life of around one hundred days, so the decision to continue it rests on the cardiac indication.
key_points: Type 1 is iodine induced hormone synthesis in an abnormal gland with preserved or increased Doppler vascularity.
Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis with absent vascularity, negative antibodies and no goitre.
Thionamides treat type 1 and corticosteroid treats type 2, with both used in mixed disease.
Radioiodine is ineffective because the amiodarone iodine load suppresses thyroidal uptake for months.
Amiodarone has a half life of about one hundred days, so cessation gives no rapid biochemical benefit.
explanation.pearls: Use colour flow Doppler to separate the two forms of amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis before prescribing, because absent parenchymal vascularity means a destructive thyroiditis that needs corticosteroid rather than carbimazole, and stopping the amiodarone changes nothing for months while risking the arrhythmia it was prescribed for.

options.rationale: Thionamides block new hormone synthesis and are the treatment where excess iodine drives an overactive gland, typically in a patient with a pre-existing nodular goitre or latent Graves disease and preserved or increased Doppler flow. They cannot help where the gland is not synthesising hormone at all but is releasing preformed stores as it is destroyed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Absent parenchymal vascularity with negative antibodies, no goitre and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate in an iodine replete patient indicates a destructive thyroiditis releasing preformed hormone, which responds to corticosteroid rather than to synthesis blockade. Whether to stop amiodarone is a separate cardiological judgement rather than an automatic step, because its half life of around one hundred days means cessation gives no rapid biochemical benefit while withdrawal risks recurrence of the ventricular tachycardia his defibrillator is already treating. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Stopping the drug is often appropriate in principle and achieves nothing quickly, because amiodarone is highly lipophilic with a half life measured in months, so tissue iodine loading persists long after the last dose. Observation also leaves a thyrotoxic state that is actively destabilising his ventricular arrhythmia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Radioiodine requires the gland to take up iodine, and the enormous iodine load delivered by amiodarone saturates the sodium iodide symporter and suppresses radioiodine uptake to negligible levels for many months. The treatment is therefore ineffective in this setting regardless of which subtype is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Perchlorate competitively inhibits iodide transport into the thyroid and is used as an adjunct in the iodine induced subtype or in mixed disease unresponsive to first line therapy, often alongside a thionamide. Blocking uptake is illogical in a destructive process where stored hormone is leaking from a gland that is not trapping iodide. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Alcoholic ketoacidosis develops when a person with alcohol dependence stops eating and drinking, typically because of vomiting, and presents with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, strongly positive ketones and a blood glucose that is normal or even low. The mechanism is glycogen depletion combined with a raised ratio of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide from ethanol metabolism, which suppresses gluconeogenesis and shifts the redox state towards beta hydroxybutyrate. Because beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, urine ketone dipsticks that detect acetoacetate may substantially understate the ketosis. Treatment is intravenous glucose and saline, which suppresses ketogenesis by restoring substrate and stimulating insulin, together with potassium, magnesium and phosphate replacement. Thiamine must precede the glucose, and toxic alcohol ingestion should be excluded by checking the osmolar gap.
key_points: A high anion gap ketoacidosis with a normal or low glucose distinguishes this from diabetic ketoacidosis.
Glycogen depletion and a raised reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide ratio drive the ketogenesis.
Beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, so acetoacetate based urine dipsticks understate the ketosis.
Treatment is glucose and saline rather than insulin, with potassium, magnesium and phosphate replacement.
A normal osmolar gap argues against toxic alcohol ingestion as the cause of the acidosis.
explanation.pearls: Give thiamine before any glucose containing fluid in a patient with alcohol dependence, because glucose consumes the last of the thiamine as a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in someone who arrived neurologically intact.

options.rationale: Insulin is the treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis, where hyperglycaemia drives the osmotic diuresis and insulin deficiency drives the ketogenesis. This man has a normal blood glucose and is not insulin deficient, so an insulin infusion would cause profound hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidaemia below a pH of about 7.1 with haemodynamic compromise, and it does not address the underlying ketogenesis. In this condition the acidosis resolves rapidly once substrate and volume are restored, so bicarbonate would risk rebound alkalosis and hypokalaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Toxic alcohol poisoning produces a high anion gap acidosis and must always be considered, and it characteristically raises the osmolar gap and is not accompanied by strongly positive ketones. His osmolar gap is normal and there is no history of ingestion, which together make this very unlikely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Restoring carbohydrate is the right principle and the oral route is unreliable in a man who has been vomiting for two days and is clinically dehydrated. He needs intravenous volume and substrate, and observation alone would leave both the ketosis and the volume deficit uncorrected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Starvation and alcohol deplete glycogen and raise the ratio of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, driving ketogenesis with a normal glucose, so the treatment is carbohydrate and volume rather than insulin. Thiamine must be given before the glucose because it is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and a glucose load in a depleted patient consumes the remaining stores and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Denosumab inhibits osteoclast formation but is not incorporated into bone, so its effect depends entirely on continued dosing and disappears once it stops. Cessation is followed by a sharp rebound in bone turnover, loss of the accumulated density within about twelve months, and multiple vertebral fractures in a meaningful proportion of patients, often occurring together. This distinguishes it sharply from the bisphosphonates, which bind to bone mineral and continue to act for years after the last dose, allowing a planned drug holiday. Anyone stopping denosumab therefore needs an antiresorptive to follow it, usually an oral bisphosphonate or a zoledronic acid infusion, started around the time the next injection would have fallen due. Even routine delays of more than a month beyond the due date are associated with increased vertebral fracture risk.
key_points: Denosumab is not incorporated into bone and its effect stops when dosing stops.
Cessation causes rebound turnover and multiple vertebral fractures in a substantial minority.
Bisphosphonates bind to bone and permit a planned drug holiday, which this drug does not.
Follow on antiresorptive treatment is started around the time the next dose was due.
Delaying a dose beyond about a month is itself associated with vertebral fracture.
explanation.pearls: Treat a missed denosumab appointment as urgent rather than routine, because the fractures that follow cluster in the months after a delayed or abandoned dose and typically present as several vertebral fractures at once in a woman who had been doing well.

options.rationale: Teriparatide is an anabolic agent reserved for severe osteoporosis with fractures despite antiresorptive treatment, and it is not funded in this situation. Giving it after this drug also produces a transient fall in bone density at the hip, which makes it a poor choice for the sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

Stopping this drug without replacement produces a rebound in bone turnover that returns density to baseline within a year and causes multiple vertebral fractures in a substantial minority of women. Following it with a bisphosphonate started around the time the next dose was due preserves the gain she has made and is the specific measure that prevents the rebound. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

The suppression of bone turnover wanes markedly by about seven months after a dose, so a twelve monthly interval delivers a rebound period twice a year rather than avoiding one. Delay of more than a month beyond the due date is itself associated with vertebral fracture. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Denosumab)

Long term continuation is a reasonable plan for many patients and avoids the problem altogether, but it is not the only safe option and it disregards a clear preference she has expressed. The requirement is not that she continues forever, only that she does not stop without cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

Simply stopping is safe with the bisphosphonates, where the drug remains bound to bone for years and a drug holiday is a recognised strategy. It is unsafe with this agent, whose effect disappears entirely once dosing ceases, and a scan in two years would document the fractures rather than prevent them. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

explanation.summary: Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure above target despite three agents from different classes, including a diuretic, at maximum tolerated doses. Before adding a fourth drug, three things must be established: that the readings are real rather than white coat, that the patient is actually taking the medicines, and that contributing causes such as non-steroidal anti inflammatories, alcohol, sleep apnoea, renal artery disease and primary aldosteronism have been considered. Once that groundwork is done, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is the fourth agent with the best evidence, outperforming both a beta blocker and an alpha blocker when tested directly in this population. The main hazard is hyperkalaemia, particularly alongside an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor or in renal impairment, so electrolytes are checked within one to two weeks of starting and after any dose increase. A starting potassium at the lower end of normal, as here, makes the choice comfortable.
key_points: Resistant hypertension means above target on three agents including a diuretic.
Confirm adherence and exclude contributing causes before adding a fourth drug.
A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist outperforms a beta blocker or alpha blocker at this step.
Hyperkalaemia is the main hazard, so electrolytes are checked within one to two weeks.
Combining an angiotensin receptor blocker with a converting enzyme inhibitor is avoided.
explanation.pearls: Check the dispensing history before calling any hypertension resistant, because roughly half the patients referred for resistant hypertension are not taking what is on the list, and adding a fourth drug to a regimen nobody is taking achieves nothing but hyperkalaemia risk.

options.rationale: In resistant hypertension where adherence is confirmed and secondary causes have been addressed, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist lowers blood pressure more than a beta blocker or an alpha blocker added at the same point. His potassium at 3.9 mmol/L and preserved renal function make it safe to start, with a check within a fortnight because the combination with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor raises the risk of hyperkalaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Resistant hypertension)

Combining an angiotensin receptor blocker with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor gives little additional blood pressure reduction while significantly increasing hyperkalaemia, acute kidney injury and hypotension. This combination is avoided in current practice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypertension)

An alpha blocker is an accepted later line option and is useful where prostatic symptoms coexist. It is less effective than the preferred agent at this step and causes postural hypotension, so it sits behind it in the sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Resistant hypertension)

A beta blocker is a reasonable fourth agent where there is a compelling indication such as angina, prior myocardial infarction or heart failure, and it remains an option if the preferred agent cannot be used. Compared head to head at this point in the sequence it produces a smaller blood pressure reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Resistant hypertension)

Swapping between thiazide type diuretics is worth considering when the current one is poorly tolerated, and indapamide is at least as effective as hydrochlorothiazide. Exchanging one for the other adds no blood pressure reduction and delays the step that will. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Subclinical hypothyroidism is a biochemical diagnosis defined by a raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine, and it is common enough that the first question is always whether the result is real and persistent. Up to a third of elevations resolve spontaneously, and acute illness in particular disturbs the axis, so a single abnormal sample taken during a viral illness cannot support a decision about lifelong treatment. The repeat is taken after six to eight weeks, alongside thyroid peroxidase antibodies, which identify autoimmune disease and predict progression to overt hypothyroidism. If the elevation persists above 10 mIU/L, treatment is generally offered even without symptoms. Different thresholds apply in pregnancy or when conception is planned, where treatment is started at lower levels and sooner.
key_points: Subclinical hypothyroidism means a raised stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine.
Up to a third of elevations resolve spontaneously, particularly after acute illness.
Confirm persistence at six to eight weeks before committing to lifelong replacement.
Thyroid peroxidase antibodies predict progression to overt hypothyroidism.
Pregnancy and planned conception use lower thresholds and earlier treatment.
explanation.pearls: Ask why the test was ordered before you act on it, because a thyroid stimulating hormone measured during an acute illness is the commonest reason a well person ends up on thyroxine for life, and the repeat six weeks later is normal surprisingly often.

options.rationale: Persistent elevation above 10 mIU/L is an accepted indication to treat, so this is the right destination if the result is confirmed. Starting on a single sample taken during an acute illness commits an asymptomatic woman to lifelong medicine on a result that may well normalise by itself. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

Ultrasound assesses a palpable nodule or goitre and does not contribute to the assessment of thyroid function, since the biochemistry and antibodies establish the diagnosis. She has a normal neck on examination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

A raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine resolves spontaneously in up to a third of people, particularly when the sample was taken during or shortly after an acute illness, which is what happened here. Confirming that the elevation persists before starting lifelong replacement is the point of the repeat, and the antibody result predicts who will progress to overt disease and therefore how closely to follow her. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

Waiting for symptoms is appropriate for a mildly raised result in the range up to about 7 mIU/L in an older person, where the finding often reflects normal ageing. At this level the chance of progression to overt disease is considerably higher, so the result needs following up rather than discarding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

Free triiodothyronine is useful in suspected thyrotoxicosis, where it can be raised while thyroxine remains normal. It stays within range until hypothyroidism is far advanced and adds nothing to the assessment of an underactive gland. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Thyroid hormones)

explanation.summary: Metformin interferes with calcium dependent uptake of the vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor complex in the terminal ileum, and the resulting deficiency becomes common after several years of treatment, with risk rising with both dose and duration. Three features here argue against attributing the neuropathy to diabetes: glycaemic control has been excellent for years, the mean cell volume is raised, and the examination shows dorsal column involvement with a positive Romberg test and upper limb symptoms rather than a purely distal small fibre pattern. Deficiency is confirmed with a serum level, and methylmalonic acid or homocysteine resolve borderline results, because the serum assay is insensitive at the lower end of the range. Treatment is straightforward and neurological recovery depends heavily on how early it starts, since subacute combined degeneration of the cord becomes irreversible. Haematological abnormalities may be entirely absent even with established neurological disease.
key_points: Metformin impairs ileal absorption of vitamin B12 with risk rising over years of use.
Dorsal column signs and a positive Romberg test point away from diabetic neuropathy.
Macrocytosis may be present without anaemia, and may be absent altogether.
Methylmalonic acid or homocysteine clarify borderline serum levels.
Neurological recovery depends on early treatment before cord damage becomes fixed.
explanation.pearls: Check vitamin B12 in anyone who has taken metformin for more than four years and develops numb feet, because attributing it to diabetic neuropathy is the default that lets subacute combined degeneration progress to a deficit that replacement will never reverse.

options.rationale: Nerve conduction studies are valuable where the pattern is atypical, asymmetrical or progressing rapidly and the diagnosis remains unclear after blood tests. They cannot identify the cause of a symmetrical sensory neuropathy, and doing them first delays a result that is available from a single tube of blood. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Peripheral neuropathy)

Poor glycaemic control is the usual driver of diabetic neuropathy and improving it slows progression, which makes this a reflex answer in a diabetic patient. His control has been excellent for six years, and diabetic neuropathy does not explain a raised mean cell volume or prominent proprioceptive loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Diabetic neuropathy)

Metformin reduces ileal absorption of vitamin B12 and the risk rises with dose and duration, making deficiency likely after nine years of treatment. The raised mean cell volume, the dorsal column signs with a positive Romberg test and the upper limb involvement all point away from diabetic neuropathy and toward a treatable deficiency that causes irreversible cord damage if missed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Vitamin B12 deficiency)

A paraprotein is a recognised cause of neuropathy and belongs in the second line workup, particularly in an older patient when the common causes have been excluded. It does not account for the macrocytosis and is far less likely than the deficiency his medicine predicts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Peripheral neuropathy)

Spinal imaging is indicated for asymmetrical signs, a sensory level, bladder or bowel disturbance or upper motor neurone findings, none of which he has. A symmetrical length dependent pattern with fingertip involvement does not localise to the lumbar spine. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Peripheral neuropathy)

explanation.summary: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing, and the absence of a compensatory tachycardia here suggests the response is blunted by his medicines. Five of his drugs contribute: three lower blood pressure directly, the benzodiazepine impairs postural reflexes and increases night time falls, and the anticholinergic adds cognitive impairment and further postural drop. Medication review with staged withdrawal has the strongest evidence of any single intervention for falls of this kind, and the timing of his falls at night and after meals fits the pattern precisely. Exercise programs, home hazard assessment and vitamin D where deficient are complementary rather than alternatives. Cardiac and neurological investigation is reserved for syncope without warning, exertional symptoms or focal signs.
key_points: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes.
An absent compensatory tachycardia suggests drugs or autonomic impairment.
Benzodiazepines and anticholinergics contribute to falls independently of blood pressure.
Medication reduction has the strongest single evidence for preventing falls of this type.
Postprandial and nocturnal timing supports a postural rather than a cardiac mechanism.
explanation.pearls: Measure lying and standing blood pressure at three minutes rather than immediately, because the drop that explains the falls frequently appears only after the first minute and a normal reading taken straight after standing sends the patient off for a Holter monitor they do not need.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.rationale: Cardiac investigation is warranted for syncope without warning, exertional symptoms, palpitations or an abnormal electrocardiogram, since arrhythmia and outflow obstruction are dangerous causes. His symptoms occur only on standing, reproduce with a documented postural drop and come with a normal trace, so the cause is already demonstrated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Syncope)

Fludrocortisone has a place in orthostatic hypotension that persists after culprit drugs have been removed, usually where there is autonomic failure. Using it to counteract medicines that could simply be reduced adds supine hypertension, oedema and hypokalaemia to the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.rationale: Imaging is indicated after a fall with head injury on anticoagulation, with focal neurological signs or with unexplained cognitive decline. A normal neurological examination and a clear postural mechanism do not justify it, and a chronic subdural collection would not produce symptoms confined to the act of standing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.rationale: A fall of 34 mmHg systolic on standing without a compensatory rise in heart rate confirms orthostatic hypotension, and three antihypertensives together with a sedative and an anticholinergic explain it entirely. Medication reduction is the intervention with the best evidence for preventing falls in this situation, and the withdrawal is staged because stopping a benzodiazepine abruptly causes its own problems. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.rationale: Strength and balance exercise reduces falls in older people and should form part of his plan alongside the medication review. On its own it does nothing about a blood pressure that drops 34 mmHg every time he stands up at night. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is diagnosed clinically from an urge to move the legs with an unpleasant sensation that is worse at rest, worse in the evening and relieved by movement. Iron status is the single most useful investigation because brain iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis, and deficiency is the commonest reversible cause even when the patient is not anaemic. Replacement is aimed at a ferritin well above the laboratory lower limit, commonly taken as at least 75 micrograms per litre, and often resolves symptoms without any further treatment. Where drug treatment is needed, an alpha 2 delta ligand such as gabapentin or pregabalin is preferred over a dopamine agonist, because agonists cause augmentation over time, with symptoms starting earlier in the day, spreading to the arms and becoming worse than before treatment. Contributing medicines such as antihistamines, antidepressants and dopamine blocking antiemetics are reviewed at the same time.
key_points: The diagnosis is clinical: urge to move, worse at rest and in the evening, relieved by movement.
Iron deficiency is the commonest reversible cause and occurs without anaemia.
Replacement targets a ferritin above about 75 micrograms per litre, not merely within range.
Dopamine agonists cause augmentation and are no longer first line.
Antihistamines, antidepressants and dopamine blocking antiemetics can precipitate symptoms.
explanation.pearls: A ferritin of 22 micrograms per litre is reported as only mildly low but is emphatically abnormal for this condition, where the treatment target is 75 or above, so read the number against the neurological target rather than against the laboratory range.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for restless legs

options.rationale: Dopamine agonists work quickly and were once first line, which is why they remain a tempting answer. Long term use causes augmentation, in which symptoms begin earlier in the day, spread to the arms and become more severe than before treatment, so they are no longer preferred and are never started before iron status is corrected. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for restless legs)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for restless legs

options.rationale: Iron deficiency is the commonest reversible cause of these symptoms because brain iron is required for dopamine synthesis, and replacement often resolves them without any specific drug. The treatment target is higher than the laboratory lower limit, around 75 micrograms per litre or more, and her heavy periods with a low mean cell volume explain the deficiency and need addressing in their own right. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

Sedatives may help a patient sleep through mild symptoms and are occasionally used as an adjunct in specialist practice. They do not address the urge to move, and starting a benzodiazepine in a woman facing months of symptoms risks dependence for a condition with a treatable cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

The diagnosis is clinical, resting on an urge to move with an unpleasant sensation, worse at rest and in the evening and relieved by movement. A sleep study is reserved for suspected coexisting sleep apnoea or an unclear picture, and periodic limb movements are neither necessary nor sufficient for the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

An alpha 2 delta ligand is an appropriate pharmacological first line when symptoms persist after iron repletion, and it does not cause augmentation. Starting it now would treat the symptom while leaving the deficiency that is generating it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

explanation.summary: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, which lowers intraglomerular pressure and produces an immediate fall in filtration rate alongside the long term reduction in albuminuria and in progression to kidney failure. A creatinine rise of up to thirty per cent within the first two to four weeks is therefore expected and is a marker that the drug is working rather than a sign of injury. The drug is continued and the result rechecked to confirm it has stabilised. Cessation is warranted when the rise exceeds thirty per cent, continues to climb, or is accompanied by hyperkalaemia above the acceptable range, and a steep early rise raises the possibility of bilateral renal artery stenosis or volume depletion. Stopping for a stable rise within the expected range removes one of the few treatments that alters the trajectory of diabetic kidney disease.
key_points: Efferent arteriolar dilatation lowers intraglomerular pressure and raises creatinine acutely.
A stable rise up to thirty per cent is expected and the drug is continued.
Recheck renal function and potassium within two weeks to confirm stability.
A rise above thirty per cent, a continuing climb or hyperkalaemia prompt cessation.
A steep early rise suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
explanation.pearls: Calculate the percentage rise rather than reacting to the absolute number, because 88 to 106 micromol/L looks alarming on a report and is twenty per cent, which is exactly what a drug that is protecting her kidneys is supposed to do.

sources.label: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.rationale: Dose reduction is a reasonable response when the rise approaches the threshold or when symptomatic hypotension limits treatment. Here it sacrifices part of the dose-dependent reduction in albuminuria for a change that is within the expected range. (Source: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.rationale: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors do cause an initial dip in filtration rate through a similar haemodynamic mechanism, and that dip is likewise expected and reversible. Both drugs reduce kidney disease progression and neither is stopped for the anticipated early change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Chronic kidney disease)

A steep rise, often above thirty per cent and occurring within days, does raise the possibility of bilateral renal artery stenosis and warrants imaging. Her ultrasound showed symmetrical kidneys of normal size and her rise is within the expected range, so this is not indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Chronic kidney disease)

A creatinine rise of about twenty per cent reflects the expected fall in intraglomerular pressure that produces the long term kidney protection, and rises of up to thirty per cent that stabilise are acceptable and are not a reason to stop. Her potassium is within range and she is euvolaemic, so the drug continues and the result is simply confirmed as stable. (Source: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.rationale: Cessation is warranted when the rise exceeds thirty per cent, when it keeps climbing on repeat testing or when potassium rises above the acceptable range. Stopping for a stable twenty per cent rise removes the treatment that most reduces her progression to kidney failure and is the commonest error made at this point. (Source: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

explanation.summary: Sulfonylurea induced hypoglycaemia differs from insulin induced hypoglycaemia in that the drug continues to stimulate endogenous insulin secretion for as long as it remains in the circulation, and correcting the glucose does nothing to shorten that. The modified release preparation acts for more than twenty four hours, and acute kidney injury from poor intake prolongs it further, so recurrence is the rule rather than the exception. Anyone with sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia needs admission for a glucose infusion and regular monitoring for at least twenty four hours, and longer if renal function is impaired. Octreotide suppresses insulin release and is reserved for episodes that recur despite adequate glucose replacement. A glycated haemoglobin of 6.4 per cent in a frail older woman indicates overtreatment, and relaxing the glycaemic target is part of preventing the next episode.
key_points: Sulfonylureas keep stimulating insulin release long after the glucose has been corrected.
Modified release preparations act for more than twenty four hours.
Renal impairment prolongs the effect and makes recurrence more likely.
Octreotide is reserved for hypoglycaemia recurring despite adequate glucose replacement.
A low glycated haemoglobin in a frail older person indicates overtreatment.
explanation.pearls: Never discharge a sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia from the emergency department on the strength of a normal glucose, because the drug outlasts the observation period by a day or more and the second episode typically happens overnight at home with nobody there.

options.rationale: Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen and is valuable where intravenous access is difficult, particularly in the community. Its effect is brief, glycogen stores are already depleted in someone who has been eating poorly for days, and it can provoke further insulin release in sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Sulfonylureas)

Two hours of stability is a reasonable discharge rule after hypoglycaemia caused by short-acting insulin, where the effect is over and the cause is understood. It is unsafe with a long-acting sulfonylurea in renal impairment, since the drug continues to stimulate insulin release long after the observation period ends. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

The modified release preparation acts for well over twenty four hours and her reduced renal clearance prolongs it further, so a single correction treats the reading rather than the cause and the recurrence at four hours confirms it. Admission with a glucose infusion and regular monitoring covers the many hours of continuing insulin secretion, and she cannot be observed at home with her daughter leaving tonight. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

Reducing or stopping the sulfonylurea is certainly part of the plan, and a glycated haemoglobin of 6.4 per cent indicates she is overtreated for her age in any case. Dose adjustment does nothing about the drug already circulating, which will keep causing hypoglycaemia through tonight. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

Octreotide suppresses pancreatic insulin release and is the targeted treatment for sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia, used when episodes recur despite adequate glucose. It is reserved for refractory cases rather than started at the first recurrence, and it does not remove the need for admission and monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Levodopa has a short plasma half life and in advanced Parkinson disease the response follows the dosing schedule closely, so delays of even an hour produce disabling off periods. Interrupting treatment altogether can precipitate an akinetic crisis, with severe rigidity, inability to swallow, hyperthermia and a picture resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which carries a real mortality. A nil by mouth order therefore does not extend to levodopa, which is given through a nasogastric tube at the patient's own times, or delivered by a rotigotine patch when no enteral route exists. Dopamine antagonists must be avoided, so metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol are replaced by ondansetron or domperidone for nausea and by quetiapine if an antipsychotic is unavoidable. Charting the home regimen exactly, rather than mapping it onto standard ward drug rounds, is the single most important prescribing decision at admission.
key_points: Levodopa has a short half life and the dosing schedule determines mobility.
Interruption can precipitate an akinetic crisis resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Nil by mouth does not include levodopa, which is given by nasogastric tube.
A rotigotine patch is the alternative when no enteral route is available.
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol are avoided as central dopamine antagonists.
explanation.pearls: Chart the patient's own times rather than three times daily on admission, and cross off any metoclopramide, because those two entries on the drug chart cause more avoidable deterioration in Parkinson disease than anything that happens in theatre.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for Parkinson disease

options.rationale: Withholding oral medicines is standard for most drugs before an operation and is what the nil by mouth order is usually taken to mean. Levodopa is a specific exception because interruption for even a day risks an akinetic crisis, aspiration and a syndrome resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

A transdermal dopamine agonist is the accepted alternative when no enteral route is available at all, and calculating the equivalent dose requires specialist input. He has a working nasogastric tube, and leaving a centrally acting dopamine antagonist charted undermines whatever dopaminergic treatment is given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

Standard ward drug rounds are convenient and adequate for most medicines, which is exactly how this error is made. In advanced disease the interval between doses determines whether the patient can move at all, and shifting a five times daily schedule onto the ward round produces hours of immobility each day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

Apomorphine is a potent dopamine agonist given subcutaneously rather than intravenously, and it is used for sudden off periods under specialist supervision with premedication against severe vomiting. It is not a ward level substitute for restoring the regular schedule. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for Parkinson disease)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for Parkinson disease

options.rationale: Missed or delayed doses in advanced Parkinson disease cause rapid deterioration and can precipitate an akinetic crisis with rigidity, swallowing failure and aspiration, so the home schedule is maintained through the tube with the tube clamped briefly after each dose. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that crosses into the brain and will worsen his rigidity, so it is replaced with an antiemetic that does not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

explanation.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia is treated according to severity, and Australian practice uses a severity tool to decide between oral outpatient therapy, intravenous inpatient therapy and intensive care level treatment with broadened cover. Standard moderate severity treatment combines a beta lactam for typical organisms with doxycycline or a macrolide for atypical organisms. A genuine immediate hypersensitivity reaction, characterised by urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm or hypotension within an hour of a dose, excludes the whole beta lactam group including cephalosporins in the acute setting, and a respiratory fluoroquinolone becomes the appropriate substitute because it covers both halves of the usual regimen. Distinguishing this from a delayed non-severe rash matters greatly, since the majority of patients labelled penicillin allergic are not, and inaccurate labels lead to worse outcomes through use of broader and less effective agents. Formal allergy assessment and delabelling should be arranged after recovery.
key_points: Severity assessment determines route, spectrum and site of care
Standard moderate therapy pairs a beta lactam with atypical cover
Immediate hypersensitivity excludes the beta lactam group in the acute setting
A respiratory fluoroquinolone covers both typical and atypical organisms alone
Most patients labelled penicillin allergic are not, and delabelling improves outcomes
explanation.pearls: A documented reaction with hypotension and angioedema within an hour is an immediate hypersensitivity that rules out cephalosporins acutely, whereas an isolated delayed maculopapular rash does not and should prompt referral for delabelling rather than lifelong avoidance.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Penicillin allergy

options.rationale: Cephalosporins retain a beta lactam ring and, although cross reactivity with later generation agents is lower than once believed, they are avoided after a documented anaphylactic reaction. The atypical cover is appropriate but the primary agent is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This is the standard regimen for moderate community-acquired pneumonia but is absolutely contraindicated by his documented anaphylaxis to a penicillin. Rechallenge risks a fatal reaction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vancomycin has no activity against the Gram negative and atypical organisms relevant here and does not cover the common causative pathogen adequately in this context. It is reserved for suspected resistant staphylococcal infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A respiratory fluoroquinolone covers both typical and atypical pathogens and avoids the beta lactam ring entirely, which is necessary after a documented immediate hypersensitivity reaction. Monotherapy is adequate because its spectrum replaces both components of the standard combination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Oral monotherapy with an agent lacking reliable pneumococcal activity is insufficient for pneumonia requiring inpatient intravenous treatment. Severity determines the route as well as the spectrum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Management of an elevated international normalised ratio on warfarin is determined by two variables: whether the patient is bleeding, and how high the value is. In the absence of bleeding, values up to about 4.5 are managed by withholding doses and rechecking, values between roughly 4.5 and 10 warrant withholding plus a low oral dose of vitamin K, and values above 10 warrant a somewhat larger oral dose. Any significant bleeding changes the approach entirely, requiring intravenous vitamin K together with prothrombin complex concentrate for major or life threatening haemorrhage. The reason low dose oral vitamin K is preferred when there is no bleeding is that larger parenteral doses cause over-correction and resistance to re-anticoagulation for several days, which matters for a patient who needs to return to therapeutic range. Identifying the precipitant is equally important, and antibiotics, particularly trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole and metronidazole, are among the commonest causes through inhibition of warfarin metabolism.
key_points: Management depends on the presence of bleeding and on the height of the value
Withholding alone suffices below about 4.5 without bleeding
Low dose oral vitamin K is added between roughly 4.5 and 10
Large parenteral doses cause resistance to re-anticoagulation for days
Antibiotics are among the commonest precipitants through metabolic inhibition
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is one of the most potent potentiators of warfarin, and an international normalised ratio check within three to five days of starting it prevents exactly this presentation.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Australia: Patient blood management

options.rationale: Omitting doses alone is the correct approach for modest elevation below about 4.5, but at this level the correction is too slow. The bleeding risk during the delay is what makes it inadequate. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

At this degree of over-anticoagulation without bleeding, withholding doses alone corrects too slowly and leaves a period of substantial bleeding risk, so a small oral dose of vitamin K is added. Low dose oral therapy avoids the prolonged warfarin resistance that follows larger parenteral doses. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A large parenteral dose over-corrects and produces warfarin resistance lasting up to a week, which is a particular problem before planned surgery requiring bridging. The high dose is reserved for major bleeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Factor concentrate is reserved for major or life threatening bleeding, or for urgent surgery that cannot wait, and carries thrombotic risk. She is not bleeding and her surgery is three weeks away. (Source: National Blood Authority Australia: Patient blood management)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Australia: Patient blood management

options.rationale: Continuing any warfarin while the level is this high prolongs the period of excess anticoagulation. Dose adjustment addresses future stability rather than the present risk. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Muscle symptoms are the commonest reason patients stop statins, yet blinded rechallenge studies consistently show that the great majority of such symptoms occur equally on placebo, meaning they are often not caused by the drug. The clinically important distinction is between statin associated muscle symptoms with a normal creatine kinase and preserved power, which are common and manageable, and true myopathy or rhabdomyolysis with objective weakness and a markedly raised enzyme, which is rare and requires immediate cessation. A third entity, immune mediated necrotising myopathy, presents with proximal weakness and a very high creatine kinase that persists after stopping the drug and requires immunosuppression. The recommended approach to the common presentation is to exclude contributors such as hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, renal impairment and interacting drugs, then to stop the statin for a washout, confirm symptom resolution, and rechallenge with a lower dose or an alternative agent. Alternate day dosing of a long-acting statin is often tolerated when daily dosing is not.
key_points: Most statin attributed muscle symptoms are not reproduced on blinded rechallenge
Normal creatine kinase with preserved power excludes true myopathy
Immune mediated necrotising myopathy persists after the drug is stopped
Exclude hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency and interacting drugs first
Alternate day dosing of a long-acting statin is often tolerated
explanation.pearls: A creatine kinase that stays markedly elevated weeks after the statin is stopped, with genuine proximal weakness, points to immune mediated necrotising myopathy rather than ordinary intolerance, and that patient needs immunosuppression rather than a rechallenge.

options.rationale: Abandoning statin therapy after a myocardial infarction removes a treatment with a clear mortality benefit on the basis of symptoms that are frequently not drug related. Lifestyle measures alone will not achieve his lipid targets. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Coenzyme Q10 has not been shown in randomised trials to relieve statin associated muscle symptoms and adds cost without benefit. Continuing unchanged also ignores his stated intention to stop. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Invasive investigation is reserved for objective weakness with a markedly raised creatine kinase, which would raise the possibility of an immune mediated necrotising myopathy. His examination and enzymes do not support that. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

These agents are reserved for patients with a documented inability to tolerate statins after adequate rechallenge, and Australian subsidy requires that demonstration. Moving to them first bypasses a necessary step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

A normal creatine kinase with preserved power excludes true myopathy, and most such symptoms are not reproduced on blinded rechallenge, so permanent avoidance forfeits substantial mortality benefit unnecessarily. A structured washout and rechallenge establishes whether the drug is genuinely responsible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Cobalamin deficiency is frequently missed because the haematological and neurological manifestations do not track together, and neurological disease can be well advanced while the blood count remains entirely normal. The serum assay is an imperfect test because it measures total rather than metabolically available cobalamin, so patients with genuine tissue deficiency can return values within the reference range. Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine rise when the vitamin dependent reactions fail and therefore demonstrate functional deficiency, with methylmalonic acid the more specific of the two since homocysteine also rises in folate deficiency. Metformin impairs calcium dependent absorption of the cobalamin intrinsic factor complex in the terminal ileum and is a well recognised cause after several years of use, alongside pernicious anaemia, gastric surgery, ileal disease and dietary restriction. Subacute combined degeneration produces a characteristic mixture of dorsal column loss with upper motor neuron signs and a peripheral neuropathy, and neurological recovery depends heavily on how early replacement begins.
key_points: Neurological disease can precede any haematological abnormality
A serum level within range does not exclude functional deficiency
Methylmalonic acid is more specific than homocysteine for cobalamin deficiency
Long term metformin impairs ileal absorption of the vitamin
Neurological recovery depends on how early replacement is started
explanation.pearls: Absent ankle reflexes with brisk knee reflexes is the signature of subacute combined degeneration, where a peripheral neuropathy and a corticospinal tract lesion coexist in the same patient.

options.rationale: The serum assay measures total cobalamin including an inactive protein bound fraction and is insensitive at the lower end, which is exactly why the metabolite was measured. A normal range result does not exclude functional deficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Diabetic neuropathy does not usually produce dorsal column signs with brisk knee reflexes, and his glycaemic control has been consistently good. Symptomatic treatment would leave a reversible cause untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

A raised methylmalonic acid demonstrates functional deficiency at tissue level even though the serum level sits within the reference range, and the combination of dorsal column and peripheral nerve signs indicates established neurological involvement. Delay risks irreversible cord damage, so replacement begins immediately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Folate given to a cobalamin deficient patient can correct the blood picture while the neurological damage continues to progress unchecked. His folate is in any case normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Imaging may show dorsal column signal change but does not alter the decision to replace, and waiting for it delays treatment of an evolving cord lesion. The biochemistry has already established the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors can precipitate a ketoacidosis in which the glucose is normal or only mildly elevated, because urinary glucose loss masks the hyperglycaemia that would normally prompt the diagnosis. The mechanism combines reduced insulin secretion, increased glucagon and a shift toward fatty acid oxidation, and it is triggered by any state of physiological stress or reduced carbohydrate intake, with surgery, acute illness, fasting and very low carbohydrate diets the usual precipitants. Because the glucose looks unremarkable, the diagnosis is regularly missed or attributed to a surgical complication, so ketones must be measured in any unwell patient on these drugs who is acidotic or has an unexplained raised anion gap. Treatment is an insulin infusion with co-administered glucose, since insulin is needed to suppress ketogenesis but the glucose is not high enough to tolerate insulin alone. Australian practice is to withhold the drug for at least two days before planned surgery and during acute illness.
key_points: Ketoacidosis can occur with a normal or mildly raised glucose with this drug class
Surgery, fasting, acute illness and low carbohydrate diets are the usual triggers
Measure ketones in any acidotic patient taking these agents
Insulin with co-administered glucose is required to suppress ketogenesis
Withhold the drug for at least two days before planned surgery
explanation.pearls: Any patient on a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor with a raised anion gap and a normal lactate needs a beta hydroxybutyrate measured before the acidosis is attributed to a surgical complication, because a glucose of 9 mmol/L will otherwise argue the diagnosis away.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Peri-operative use of SGLT2 inhibitors

options.rationale: Fluid replacement alone does not suppress ketogenesis, which requires insulin, so the acidosis will persist. Volume repletion is necessary but not sufficient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Bicarbonate does not address the underlying ketogenesis and may worsen intracellular acidosis and hypokalaemia. It is considered only at extremely low pH values alongside definitive therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

A leak or ischaemia would be expected to raise the lactate and produce peritonism, and his lactate is normal with a benign abdomen. The ketone level already identifies the mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Ketoacidosis can occur at near normal glucose with this drug class because glycosuria suppresses the glucose while ketogenesis continues unchecked. Insulin is required to switch off ketone production, and glucose is co-infused so that insulin can be given at an adequate rate without hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Intermittent subcutaneous dosing cannot deliver the sustained insulin concentration needed to suppress ketogenesis reliably in an unwell patient. An infusion allows titration against the ketone level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: A microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia should immediately narrow the differential to the thrombotic microangiopathies, and normal coagulation studies with a normal fibrinogen are the finding that separates these from disseminated intravascular coagulation. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura arises from deficiency of the enzyme that cleaves von Willebrand factor multimers, usually through an acquired autoantibody, allowing ultra large multimers to accumulate and trap platelets in the microvasculature. The classical pentad of fever, neurological signs, renal impairment, thrombocytopenia and haemolysis is present in a minority, so waiting for it causes fatal delay, and the combination of fragments with thrombocytopenia alone should trigger treatment. Plasma exchange transformed untreated mortality of around ninety per cent into survival for the majority and should begin within hours, with corticosteroids and often rituximab as adjuncts, while an enzyme activity assay is sent but not waited for. Platelet transfusion is specifically avoided because it adds fuel to the microvascular thrombosis.
key_points: Fragments with thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation indicate thrombotic microangiopathy
A normal fibrinogen and international normalised ratio exclude disseminated intravascular coagulation
The classical pentad appears in a minority and waiting for it is dangerous
Plasma exchange should start within hours and is life saving
Platelet transfusion is avoided as it worsens microvascular thrombosis
explanation.pearls: Send the enzyme activity assay but never wait for it: plasma exchange started within hours of recognising fragments with a platelet count below 30 x10^9/L is what determines survival in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Australia: Patient blood management

options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in this condition can precipitate worsening neurological and renal ischaemia by adding substrate to ongoing microthrombosis. It is reserved for life threatening bleeding or before an invasive procedure. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

Microangiopathic haemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation indicates a thrombotic microangiopathy driven by platelet consumption in microthrombi rather than by a coagulation defect. Plasma exchange is life saving and platelets are withheld because transfused platelets fuel further microvascular thrombosis. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

Disseminated intravascular coagulation would show a prolonged international normalised ratio and a low fibrinogen, and both are normal here. Plasma infusion is inferior to exchange, which also removes the causative antibody. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

Corticosteroids are given as an adjunct but are wholly inadequate as sole therapy for a condition with very high untreated mortality. Immunosuppression alone does not remove the circulating multimers. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

Meningoencephalitis is a reasonable thought in a confused patient but she is afebrile with no meningism, and lumbar puncture at this platelet count risks spinal haematoma. The haematological findings explain the picture. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary embolism is stratified by haemodynamic consequence rather than by clot burden, and this patient sits in the high risk group defined by sustained hypotension with echocardiographic and biochemical evidence of right ventricular strain. High risk embolism carries a mortality that justifies reperfusion rather than anticoagulation alone, and systemic thrombolysis is ordinarily the default. The difficulty here is that the same event that caused the embolism, recent major intracranial surgery, also creates an absolute contraindication to systemic lysis, and postoperative intracranial haemorrhage after alteplase in this context is usually fatal. When reperfusion is indicated but systemic lysis is contraindicated, catheter directed therapy using mechanical fragmentation, aspiration or low dose local lytic, or surgical embolectomy where cardiothoracic services exist, provides the reperfusion without a systemic lytic state. Supportive care matters alongside this, with cautious fluid and early vasopressor support to protect the failing right ventricle, while an inferior vena cava filter addresses future emboli only and is not a substitute for reperfusion.
key_points: High risk embolism is defined by haemodynamic compromise, not clot burden
Reperfusion rather than anticoagulation alone is indicated in shock
Recent intracranial surgery is an absolute contraindication to systemic lysis
Catheter directed or surgical removal reperfuses without a systemic lytic state
Cautious fluid with early vasopressor support protects the failing right ventricle
explanation.pearls: Giving more than about 500 mL of fluid to a patient in obstructive shock from pulmonary embolism can worsen cardiac output by overdistending the right ventricle and shifting the septum, so noradrenaline is started earlier than instinct suggests.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism

options.rationale: Recent intracranial surgery with residual blood is an absolute rather than relative contraindication, and intracranial haemorrhage in this setting is usually fatal. Haemodynamic severity does not convert an absolute contraindication into a relative one. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism

options.rationale: Anticoagulation prevents further clot but does not relieve the existing obstruction, and mortality in shocked patients treated with anticoagulation alone is high. It is the correct sole therapy for intermediate rather than high risk embolism. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism

options.rationale: She has high risk pulmonary embolism with obstructive shock and needs reperfusion, but intracranial surgery within the preceding month with blood already in the resection cavity is an absolute contraindication to systemic lysis. Catheter directed or surgical removal delivers reperfusion while avoiding a systemic lytic state. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism
